$$ X_{a_{1}i}^{4}\cdots X_{a_{s}i}^{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert S_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}}}\right\rvert^{2}\prec\sum_{\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}, $$

uniformly in $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}\}$ (we absorb another combinatorial factor into $\prec$ ). Combining these with (7.6), we find

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{s}}X_{a_{1}i}^{4}\cdots X_{a_{s}i}^{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert S_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}}}\right\rvert^{2} \displaystyle\prec\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{s}}\sum_{\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}=\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}, $$

Now we apply Cauchy-Schwarz to (7.5) and use these estimates to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{k_{1},k_{2},s}s!}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{s}}1\cdot(X_{a_{1}i}^{2}\cdots X_{a_{s}i}^{2}S_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}})}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{d^{s/2}\alpha_{k_{1},k_{2},s}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{s}}X_{a_{1}i}^{4}\cdots X_{a_{s}i}^{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert S_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}}}\right\rvert^{2}}}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\prec\frac{d^{s/2}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}}}\right)^{1/2}. $$

Suppose without loss of generality that $k_{1}\leqslant k_{2}$ . Then we apply the partial Ward inequality, Lemma 5.2, to each fixed $\mu$ (recall that $T$ is diagonal, so that $(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\nu}=G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}$ whenever $\mu\neq\nu$ ); since the result is uniform in $\mu$ , we can also sum over $\mu$ in the sense of stochastic domination to find

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{d^{s/2}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}}\frac{\im G^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}}{\eta}d^{\max(-s,\ell-k_{2})}}}\right)^{1/2}. $$

Recall that $\eta$ is order one, and that (6.7) yields

$$ \im G^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}=\im(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{N}{d^{k_{1}}}. $$

Notice also that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{k_{1}}$ , and that $s\leqslant k_{2}-1$ (indeed, either $k_{1}<k_{2}$ , in which case $s\leqslant k_{1}<k_{2}$ , or $k_{1}=k_{2}$ , in which case $s\leqslant k_{2}-1$ because of the $\mu\neq\nu$ restriction explained above); thus

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{d^{s/2}}{N}(Nd^{\max(-s,\ell-k_{2})})^{1/2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}d^{\frac{1}{2}\max(0,s+\ell-k_{2})}\leqslant\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}d^{\frac{1}{2}\max(0,\ell-1)}\prec d^{\frac{1}{2}\max(-\ell,-1)}, $$

which finishes the proof that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{1}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{-\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}$ .

Next we estimate $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ . Again it is convenient to split the sum over all $\mu$ ’s into finitely many partial sums

$$ \mathcal{E}_{2,k}=\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu} $$

and show

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{2,k}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} $$

for each $k$ . Fix $\varepsilon$ and $D$ ; since $G^{(i)}$ is independent of $U_{i}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{2,k}}}\right\rvert>d^{\varepsilon-1/2}) \displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{E}_{G^{(i)}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbb{E}_{U_{i}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbf{1}\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{2,k}}}\right\rvert>d^{\varepsilon-1/2}\}}}\right]\mathbf{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{N}{d^{k}}d^{\varepsilon/2}}}\right\}}}\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\geqslant\frac{N}{d^{k}}d^{\varepsilon/2}}}\right). $$

Applying Lemma 7.2 below and (6.7) to the first and second terms on the right-hand side, respectively, we find that each is at most some $C_{\varepsilon,D}d^{-D}$ . This gives $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{2}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ as claimed.

Finally we estimate $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ , again splitting $\mathcal{E}_{3}=\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\mathcal{E}_{3,k}$ with

$$ \mathcal{E}_{3,k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}(G^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}-G_{\mu\mu}). $$

From (6.6) we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{3,k}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{d^{k}}{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}-G_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{N}, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 7.2.

Fix $k$ , and fix some deterministic sequence $(b_{\mu}=b^{(d)}_{\mu})_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}$ of complex numbers with

$$ \sup_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert b_{\mu}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\alpha_{d} $$

for some sequence $(\alpha_{d})_{d=1}^{\infty}$ (recall that the set $\mathbf{M}_{k}$ depends on $d$ ). Then

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)b_{\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{d^{k}\alpha_{d}}{N\sqrt{d}} $$

uniformly in $(b_{\mu})$ subject to (7.11).

#### Proof of Lemma 7.2.

The proof goes by high moments: For $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)b_{\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2p}}}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{\mu_{1},\mu^{\prime}_{1},\mu_{2},\mu^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,\mu_{p},\mu^{\prime}_{p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu^{\prime}_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]\prod_{j=1}^{p}b_{\mu_{j}}\overline{b_{\mu^{\prime}_{j}}} \displaystyle\leqslant(\alpha_{d})^{2p}\sum_{\mu_{1},\mu^{\prime}_{1},\mu_{2},\mu^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,\mu_{p},\mu^{\prime}_{p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu^{\prime}_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=(\alpha_{d})^{2p}\sum_{\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]}}\right\rvert $$

where the last equality is just a convenient relabeling (after we stop distinguishing the complex conjugates between $b_{\mu_{j}}$ and $\overline{b_{\mu^{\prime}_{j}}}$ , we no longer need to pair the terms $\mu_{j}$ and $\mu^{\prime}_{j}$ ).

Given a tuple of tuples $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p})\in(\mathbf{M}_{k})^{2p}$ , we say that some tuple $\mu_{j}$ is isolated if $\max_{m\neq j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu_{j},\mu_{m}}}\right\rangle=0$ , i.e., if $\mu_{j}$ has its own set of $X$ ’s, none of which appears in any other tuple $\mu_{m}$ . Consider the set

$$ \mathcal{G}^{2p}=\{(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p})\in(\mathbf{M}_{k})^{2p}:\text{No $\mu_{j}$ is isolated}\}. $$

On the complement of this set, at least one tuple $\mu_{j}$ is isolated in this sense, meaning that at least one $(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N})$ is independent of everything else; since these variables have mean zero, such expectations vanish, meaning that

$$ \sum_{\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]}}\right\rvert=\sum_{(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p})\in\mathcal{G}^{2p}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]}}\right\rvert. $$

Furthermore, we claim that

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{G}^{2p}}}\right\rvert\leqslant C_{2p}d^{2pk-p}. $$

Indeed, the total number of tuples $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p})\in(\mathbf{M}_{k})^{2p}$ is at most $d^{2pk}$ , because each of the $2p$ $\mu_{j}$ ’s includes $k$ $X$ ’s. To ensure that none is isolated, while using as many $X$ ’s as possible, each $\mu_{j}$ should use $k-1$ of its own $X$ ’s and have a final $X$ which it shares with exactly one other tuple $\mu_{j^{\prime}}$ ; this pairing subtracts $p$ off the naive count, while adding a combinatorial factor $C_{2p}$ tracking which $\mu_{j}$ ’s pair.

At the same time, we claim that for each $p$ there exists $C_{2p}$ with

$$ \sup_{\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{2p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)}}\right]}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{C_{2p}}{N^{2p}} $$

Indeed, writing $A_{j}\vcentcolon=U_{\mu_{j}i}^{2}-1/N$ , we can use the generalized Hölder’s inequality $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j=1}^{2p}A_{j}]}}\right\rvert\leqslant\prod_{j=1}^{2p}(\mathbb{E}[A_{j}^{2p}])^{1/2p}$ , then the triangle inequality: $(\mathbb{E}[A_{j}^{2p}])^{1/2p}=\|U_{i}^{2}-1/N\|_{2p}\leqslant\|U_{i}^{2}\|_{2p}+1/N\leqslant C_{k,p}/N$ .

Combining (7.12), (7.13), and (7.14), we find

$$ \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)b_{\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2p}}}\right]\leqslant\frac{C_{2p}}{N^{2p}}(\alpha_{d})^{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{G}^{2p}}}\right\rvert\leqslant C_{2p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d^{k}\alpha_{d}}{N\sqrt{d}}}}\right)^{2p}, $$

which suffices. ∎

## 8 Self-consistent equations II: Proofs of Propositions 3.3 and 3.4

The goal of this section is to prove Propositions 3.3 and 3.4. The latter follows from the former fairly quickly.

#### Lemma 8.1.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle 1\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\prec 1, \displaystyle 1\prec\im(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))\prec 1. $$

#### Proof.

The estimate (8.1) follows immediately from Lemma 6.2, which shows $1\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert\prec 1$ , and from Proposition 3.2, which shows $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert 1+s(z)(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert\prec d^{-\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}$ . The upper bound of (8.2) is immediate from that of (8.1). For the lower bound, we note that the imaginary part of $\widetilde{s}$ is almost surely nonnegative: Indeed, from (4.4) we have

$$ \im\widetilde{s}(z)=\frac{1}{M}\Tr(\im(TUG_{N}(z)U^{\ast}T))=\Tr(TU(\im G_{N}(z))U^{\ast}T)\geqslant 0 $$

where we used that $G_{N}(z)$ is a resolvent, so that its imaginary part is positive definite, as well as the general result that $B^{\ast}AB=(A^{1/2}B)^{\ast}(A^{1/2}B)$ is positive semidefinite if $A$ is (square and) positive definite and $B$ is any (possibly rectangular) matrix. ∎

#### Proposition 8.2.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 8.2.

Define

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mu}^{(1)} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=-T_{\mu}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G_{jj}+(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right)\sum_{\nu}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mu}^{(2)} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mu}^{(3)} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mu}^{(4)} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{N}T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G_{\mu\mu}^{(j)}-G_{\mu\mu}}}\right), $$

so that, by the resolvent identity $G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu}=-T_{\mu}\sum_{j}G_{jj}\sum_{\nu}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}$ from (4.5), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mu} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=\mathcal{E}^{(1)}_{\mu}+\mathcal{E}^{(2)}_{\mu}+\mathcal{E}^{(3)}_{\mu}+\mathcal{E}^{(4)}_{\mu}=-T_{\mu}\sum_{j}G_{jj}\sum_{\nu}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}-\frac{T_{\mu}G_{\mu\mu}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}=G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu}-\frac{T_{\mu}G_{\mu\mu}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)} \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\frac{T_{\mu}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right)(G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu})+\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}=\frac{(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{\mu})(G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu})+T_{\mu}^{2}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}. $$

Thus

$$ G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu}-\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{\mu}}}}\right)\mathcal{E}_{\mu}, $$

so if we define

$$ \mathcal{E}_{k}^{(a)}\vcentcolon=\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathcal{E}_{\mu}^{(a)},\qquad a=1,2,3,4, $$

then

$$ \displaystyle\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu}-\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{\mu}}\mathcal{E}_{\mu}}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\sum_{a=1}^{4}\frac{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{\mu}}\mathcal{E}^{(a)}_{k}. $$

Thus the problem reduces to showing

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{k}}\mathcal{E}^{(a)}_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}} $$

for $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ and $a\in\llbracket 1,4\rrbracket$ . Lemma 8.1 shows $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\prec 1$ as well as

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{k}}}\right\rvert\geqslant\im(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{k})=\im(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))\succ 1, $$

so $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-T_{k}}}}\right\rvert\prec 1$ , and we only need show

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}^{(a)}_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}} $$

for $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ and $a\in\llbracket 1,4\rrbracket$ . In the following we will often, but not always, use the estimate $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert\prec 1$ , from (8.1). We handle one $a$ at a time:

- • ( $a=1$ ): On the one hand, from (7.1) and (8.1) we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}+(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert=\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))+1}}\right\rvert}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert}\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

(8.4) Since the distribution of the left-hand side does not depend on $j$ , we can put a maximum over $j$ on the left-hand side. On the other hand, we claim

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec 1. $$

(8.5) Assume (8.5) momentarily. Since we can put $\max_{j=1}^{N}$ on the left-hand side for the same reasons as above, we use it along with (8.4) to find

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}^{(1)}_{k}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\max_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}+(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\max_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert}}\right)\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

Thus it remains only to check (8.5). We split $\sum_{\nu}$ into the term $\nu=\mu$ and the remainder. For the latter, we recall that (7.8) shows that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k^{\prime}},\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle=s}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{-\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}$ for each $k^{\prime}$ and $s\leqslant\min(k,k^{\prime})$ (except when $k=k^{\prime}$ , in which case $s$ is at most $k-1$ ). By summing this over the various values of $k^{\prime}$ and $s$ , and using the trivial bound $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec 1$ , we obtain

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}, $$

(8.6) which is better than claimed – this is not the main term. When $\nu=\mu$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}(G^{(j)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert+\frac{N}{d^{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}(G^{(j)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert+1, $$

where we used the simple bound $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{k}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu j}^{2}\prec\frac{d^{k}}{N}$ . The remaining term is also straightforward: (6.7) implies $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert U_{\mu j}^{2}(G^{(j)}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{k}}$ , and taking a maximum over $\mu$ finishes the proof of (8.5).

- • ( $a=2$ ): In (8.6) we showed

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

Since the distribution of the left-hand side does not depend on $j$ , we can also put a maximum over $j$ on the left-hand side, and use this to obtain

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}^{(2)}_{k}}}\right\rvert=\frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\max_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}U_{\mu j}U_{\nu j}G^{(j)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

- • ( $a=3$ ): From Lemma 7.2, we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)T_{\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{d^{k}}{N}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sqrt{\frac{d^{k}}{N}}. $$

Since the distribution of the left-hand side does not depend on $j$ , we can also put a maximum over $j$ on the left-hand side, and obtain

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)T_{\mu}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\max_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)T_{\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

Similarly, in (7.9) we showed

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu})}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

and running the same argument about taking the maximum over $j$ yields

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu})}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} $$

(actually we discard the $\sqrt{N/d^{k}}$ in the upper bound here). Then, splitting $G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}=(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}+T_{\mu})-T_{\mu}$ and using these two bounds, we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}^{(3)}_{k}}}\right\rvert=\frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{N}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu j}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

which is better than needed.

- • ( $a=4$ ): In (7.10) we showed that

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}-G_{\mu\mu})}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{N}. $$

As always we can put a maximum over $j$ , then estimate

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}^{(4)}_{k}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{N^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{\mu}(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}}}\right\rvert\sum_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}-G_{\mu\mu})}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{N}\max_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}(G^{(j)}_{\mu\mu}-G_{\mu\mu})}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{N} $$

which is much better than needed.

∎

In the following result, recall that $\ell_{c}$ is the least integer strictly bigger than $\ell$ .

#### Lemma 8.3.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}-\frac{\gamma_{a}}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}+\frac{\gamma_{c}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{(\ell_{c}-\ell)/2}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\frac{1}{d^{(\ell_{c}-\ell)/2}}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer.}\end{cases} $$

#### Proof of Lemma 8.3.

From the definition $T_{k}=c_{k}\sqrt{k!}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}$ , we find

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\frac{T_{k}^{2}}{T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}=\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}c_{k}^{2}(k!)\frac{M_{k}}{d^{k}}\frac{1}{T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}. $$

Furthermore, since $(k!)M_{k}$ counts the number of tuples $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\in[d]^{k}$ which are all distinct, we have $(k!)M_{k}/d^{k}=1+\OO(1/d)$ when $c_{k}\neq 0$ (recall $M_{k}=0$ otherwise); since we showed in (8.3) that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1$ , this gives

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\frac{T_{\mu}^{2}}{T_{\mu}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}-\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\frac{c_{k}^{2}}{T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d}. $$

For $k>\ell$ with strict inequality (i.e., $k\geqslant\ell_{c}$ ), we have $T_{k}\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{k-\ell}{2}}}$ . Since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1$ (from (8.3)) and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1$ (from (8.1)), the definition $\gamma_{c}=\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{L}c_{k}^{2}$ (recall that $\ell_{c}$ is the smallest integer strictly bigger than $\ell$ ) gives

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{L}\frac{c_{k}^{2}}{T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}+\frac{\gamma_{c}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{L}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{c_{k}^{2}}{T_{k}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}+\frac{c_{k}^{2}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right)}}\right\rvert\prec\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{L}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{-\frac{(\ell_{c}-\ell)}{2}}. $$

If $\ell$ is not an integer, then $\lceil\ell\rceil=\ell_{c}$ and the proof is complete. Otherwise, the remaining term is $k=\ell$ , for which we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{\ell}-\gamma_{b}}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert c_{\ell}\sqrt{\ell!}(\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}}-\sqrt{\kappa})}}\right\rvert=\OO\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert}}\right) $$

which is $\oo(1)$ by the assumption (2.3), and thus (since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1$ by the same argument as in (8.3))

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{c_{\ell}^{2}}{T_{\ell}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}-\frac{\gamma_{a}}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert T_{\ell}-\gamma_{b}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 3.3.

This follows immediately from Proposition 8.2 and Lemma 8.3, simply by noting that

$$ q_{\ell}=\min\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\frac{\ell_{c}-\ell}{2},\frac{\min(1,\ell)}{2}}}\right\}. $$

∎

#### Proof of Proposition 3.4.

This is just an exercise in showing that the stochastic domination bound in (3.11) interacts nicely with the arithmetic. We have

$$ \begin{split}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\frac{\gamma_{a}s(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}s(z)}+\gamma_{c}s(z)}}\right\rvert&\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert+\gamma_{a}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{\gamma_{b}+\frac{1}{s(z)}}-\frac{1}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\\
&\quad+\gamma_{c}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)+\frac{1}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)+\frac{\gamma_{a}}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}-\frac{\gamma_{c}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\end{split} $$

By Proposition 3.3, the last term on the right-hand side is stochastically dominated by $d^{-q_{\ell}}$ , plus $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert$ in the case that $\ell$ is an integer. Now we make some simple estimates before bounding the first three terms, frequently using that the quantities $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert$ , $\im(s(z))$ , $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert$ , and $\im(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))$ are stochastically dominated above and below by $1$ , from Lemmas 6.2 and 8.1, respectively. For example, since $\gamma_{b}$ is real, these give us

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\gamma_{b}+1/s(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\im(1/s(z))}}\right\rvert\succ 1 $$

and

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\im(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert\succ 1, $$

so that

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{\gamma_{b}+\frac{1}{s(z)}}-\frac{1}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\gamma_{b}+\frac{1}{s(z)}}}\right\rvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert}\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert. $$

Since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert 1+s(z)(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert$ and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)+\frac{1}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert 1+s(z)(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert$ , we bound the first three terms on the right-hand side of (8.8) by

$$ (1+\gamma_{a}+\gamma_{c})\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert 1+s(z)(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}\leqslant\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}, $$

where we applied Proposition 3.2 in the penultimate step, completing the proof of (3.12). ∎

## 9 Error analysis

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 2.5, which replaces the given matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ with a friendlier matrix $B$ which has the same global spectral behavior.

We start by importing the following estimate of [LY22].

#### Lemma 9.1.

[LY22, Lemma 18] If $H_{1},H_{2}$ are $N\times N$ Hermitian matrices with Stieltjes transforms $s_{1},s_{2}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{1}(z)-s_{2}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{\|H_{1}-H_{2}\|_{\textup{Frob}}}{\sqrt{N}\eta^{2}}, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{1}(z)-s_{2}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C\rank(H_{1}-H_{2})}{N\eta}, $$

where $C$ is an absolute constant.

We will apply this to compare the given matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ with the matrix $B$ defined in (2.6). We will need the intermediate error matrices $\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}$ and $B^{\textup{full}}$ , whose definitions we give below, along with recalling the definitions of $A$ , $\widetilde{A}$ , and $B$ for the reader’s convenience. We recall that, throughout, $f$ is a finite-degree polynomial. All matrices are real-symmetric, $N\times N$ , and defined entrywise:

$$ \displaystyle A_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right) \displaystyle\widetilde{A}_{ij} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)&\text{if }\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \displaystyle(\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}})_{ij} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=0}^{L}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)^{k}\frac{c_{k}}{d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}&\text{if }\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \displaystyle(B^{\textup{full}})_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=0}^{L}\frac{c_{k}}{d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}, \displaystyle B_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\frac{c_{k}}{d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}, $$

(By convention, if $k=0$ , we set $\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}=1$ . In this section, we find it easier to work with $\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}$ than $\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{k}}$ ; this is why we write the factors $\sqrt{k!}$ where we do.) The notation “full” means that the sum on $k$ in the definitions of $\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}$ and $B^{\textup{full}}$ includes $k=0,\ldots,\lceil\ell\rceil-1$ , which are morally low-rank terms that do not affect the global law. We remove these terms in the step going from $B^{\textup{full}}$ to $B$ .

It turns out that all five of these matrices have the same global law, as we will see by considering the error matrices

$$ E_{A,\widetilde{A}}\vcentcolon=A-\widetilde{A},\qquad E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}\vcentcolon=\widetilde{A}-\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},\qquad E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}\vcentcolon=\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}-B^{\textup{full}},\qquad E_{B^{\textup{full}},B}\vcentcolon=B^{\textup{full}}-B. $$

The first three of these matrices each have small Frobenius norm. The last is treated differently, since it contains a low-rank part (this can create spikes but does not affect the global law) which may not have small Frobenius norm, but after subtracting this low-rank part the remainder has small Frobenius norm. We remark that “small” means only $\|\cdot\|_{\textup{Frob}}\ll\sqrt{N}$ ; this kind of estimate does not suffice to compare operator norms of $A$ , $\widetilde{A}$ and so on (indeed, [LY22, pp. 25-26] gives an example where $\|\widetilde{A}\|_{\textup{op}}=\OO_{\prec}(1)$ but $\|A\|_{\textup{op}}\to\infty$ due to spike eigenvalues), but it does suffice to say that all the matrices $A$ , $\widetilde{A}$ , etc. have the same global law.

#### Proposition 9.2.

We have the entrywise bounds

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(E_{A,\widetilde{A}})_{ij}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{Nd}},\qquad\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}})_{ij}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{Nd}},\qquad\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}})_{ij}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{Nd}}, $$

and hence (immediately, since $E_{A,\widetilde{A}}$ , $E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}$ , and $E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}$ each have zero diagonal and equidistributed off-diagonal elements)

$$ \|E_{A,\widetilde{A}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}\prec\sqrt{\frac{N}{d}},\qquad\|E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}\prec\sqrt{\frac{N}{d}},\qquad\|E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}\prec\sqrt{\frac{N}{d}}. $$

#### Proposition 9.3.

The matrix $E_{B^{\textup{full}},B}$ can be decomposed into a low-rank part and a small-Frobenius-norm part

$$ E_{B^{\textup{full}},B}=E_{\textup{lr}}+E_{\textup{Frob}}, $$

where there exists a deterministic sequence $(r_{N})_{N=1}^{\infty}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\rank(E_{\textup{lr}}) \displaystyle\leqslant r_{N}\quad\text{almost surely}, \displaystyle r_{N} \displaystyle=\OO(d^{\lceil\ell\rceil-1}), \displaystyle\|E_{\textup{Frob}}\|_{\textup{Frob}} \displaystyle\prec d^{(\lceil\ell\rceil-1)/2}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 2.5, modulo Propositions 9.2 and 9.3.

Since $B^{\textup{full}}-(B+E_{\textup{lr}})=E_{B^{\textup{full}},B}-E_{\textup{lr}}=E_{\textup{Frob}}$ , Lemma 9.1 gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{B}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}(z)}}\right\rvert+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}(z)-s_{B^{\textup{full}}}(z)}}\right\rvert+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{B^{\textup{full}}}(z)-s_{B+E_{\textup{lr}}}(z)}}\right\rvert+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{B+E_{\textup{lr}}}(z)-s_{B}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{\|E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}}{\sqrt{N}\eta^{2}}+\frac{\|E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}}{\sqrt{N}\eta^{2}}+\frac{\|E_{\textup{Frob}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}}{\sqrt{N}\eta^{2}}+\frac{Cr_{N}}{N\eta}. $$

By Propositions 9.2 and 9.3, the right-hand side is stochastically dominated by $d^{(\lceil\ell\rceil-\ell-1)/2}=d^{-r_{\ell}}$ (the worst term is the third), which tends to zero. As a very weak consequence of this, for any $\varepsilon,D>0$ we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{B}(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant\varepsilon)\leqslant C_{\varepsilon,D}d^{-D} $$

which suffices for almost-sure convergence by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. The comparison of $s_{A}$ to $s_{B}$ is similar. ∎

In the remaining sections, we prove Propositions 9.2 and 9.3.

### 9.1 Common estimates

In the proof, we will deal with generic i.i.d. vectors $X$ and $Y$ , only later selecting $X=X_{i}$ and $Y=X_{j}$ , and we will frequently work on the good event

$$ \mathcal{G}_{XY}=\{\|X\|\neq 0\neq\|Y\|\} $$

which has high probability, as we will see.

#### Lemma 9.4.

If $X\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ has i.i.d. entries, centered with unit variance, then

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\|X\|^{2}-d}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{d}, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\|X\|-\sqrt{d}}}\right\rvert\prec 1, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}-1}}\right\rvert\mathbf{1}\{\|X\|\neq 0\}\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}-1}}\right\rvert\mathbf{1}\{\|X\|\neq 0\}\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\|X\|^{2}-d=\sum_{i=1}^{d}(X_{i}^{2}-1)$ is a sum of centered independent variables with all finite moments, the estimate (9.5) is standard; see, e.g., [EY17, (7.57)]. This gives (9.6) which in turn gives (9.7) and (9.8). ∎

#### Lemma 9.5.

Let $\mu_{X},\mu_{Y}$ be centered probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments, and let $(X_{a})_{a=1}^{d},(Y_{a})_{a=1}^{d}$ be independent vectors with all entries i.i.d. samples from $\mu_{X}$ and $\mu_{Y}$ , respectively. Set

$$ \widetilde{X}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}X&\text{if }\|X\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\widetilde{Y}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}Y&\text{if }\|Y\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

Then for each $g\in\mathbb{N}$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}}\ldots X_{a_{g}}Y_{a_{1}}\ldots Y_{a_{g}}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{g/2} $$

and

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{g}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{g}}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{g/2} $$

#### Proof.

Set $F_{d}\vcentcolon=\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}}\ldots X_{a_{g}}Y_{a_{1}}\ldots Y_{a_{g}}$ . For $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[(F_{d})^{2p}]=\sum_{a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}\cdots\sum_{a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{b=1}^{2p}X_{a^{(b)}_{1}}\ldots X_{a^{(b)}_{g}}Y_{a^{(b)}_{1}}\ldots Y_{a^{(b)}_{g}}}}\right]}_{=\vcentcolon G(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g})}. $$

Since all the entries of $X$ and $Y$ are centered and independent, and $X$ and $Y$ are independent of one another, $G(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g})$ if any of its arguments appears only one time. This forces index coincidences, specifically of the form

$$ \#\{a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g}\}\leqslant pg $$

when $G(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g})\neq 0$ , instead of the naive $2pg$ . Thus

$$ \#\{(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g}):G(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g})\neq 0\}\leqslant C_{p,g}d^{pg}, $$

since one can first select at most $pg$ elements of $\llbracket 1,d\rrbracket$ to be the values of the set $\{a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g}\}$ , and once these values are selected, choosing which values to assign to which $a$ ’s only adds a multiplicative factor $C_{p,g}$ . Furthermore, since the $X$ and $Y$ entries have all finite moments, Hölder’s inequality gives us

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G(a^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(1)}_{g},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(2p)}_{g})}}\right\rvert\leqslant C_{p,g}, $$

and thus

$$ \mathbb{E}[(F_{d})^{2p}]\leqslant C_{p,g}d^{pg} $$

which suffices for (9.9). For (9.10), we set $\widetilde{F_{d}}=\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{g}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{g}}$ . If $\|X\|=0$ or $\|Y\|=0$ then (9.10) is trivial, so it suffices to restrict to the good event $\mathcal{G}_{XY}$ from (9.4); on this event, we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\widetilde{F_{d}}}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert F_{d}}}\right\rvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}}}\right)^{g}}}\right\rvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}}}\right)^{g}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert F_{d}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{g/2}, $$

where the first inequality follows from Lemma 9.4 and the second from the first half of this proof. ∎

### 9.2 Estimates for $E_{A,\widetilde{A}}$

#### Lemma 9.6.

Let $\mu$ be a centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments, and let $(X_{a})_{a=1}^{d},(Y_{a})_{a=1}^{d}$ be independent vectors with all entries i.i.d. samples from $\mu$ . Set

$$ \widetilde{X}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}X&\text{if }\|X\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\widetilde{Y}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}Y&\text{if }\|Y\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Then for each $k$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

#### Proof.

The good set $\mathcal{G}_{XY}=\{\|X\|\neq 0\neq\|Y\|\}$ from (9.4) has much higher probability than required by stochastic domination, since if $\mathbb{P}(X_{a}=0)=p<1$ then we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{XY}^{c})=p^{2d} $$

which tends to zero exponentially quickly in $d$ . Thus we can restrict to $\mathcal{G}_{XY}$ when showing (9.11). On this event, from Lemma 9.4 we have

$$ \frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}=1+\delta_{X},\qquad\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}=1+\delta_{Y} $$

with error terms $\delta_{X},\delta_{Y}$ satisfying $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\delta_{X}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\delta_{Y}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ . Thus

$$ \frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}=\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}=\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}(1+\delta_{X})(1+\delta_{Y})=\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}+\underbrace{(\delta_{X}+\delta_{Y}+\delta_{X}\delta_{Y})\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}_{=:\varepsilon_{XY}}, $$

with an error term satisfying $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\varepsilon_{XY}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ . This already completes the proof if $k=0,1$ . For $k>1$ , we will Taylor expand; in order to do this, given $\eta>0$ we introduce the good event

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\eta}=\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\varepsilon_{XY}}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{\frac{\eta}{4}-\frac{1}{2}}\}\cap\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{\frac{\eta}{4(k-1)}+\frac{1}{2}}}}\right\}. $$

Since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{XY}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a}X_{a}Y_{a}}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{d}$ , we know that for every $D>0$ there exists $C_{D}$ and $d_{0}(\eta,D)$ such that, for $d\geqslant d_{0}(\eta,D)$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}^{c})\leqslant C_{D}d^{-D}. $$

At the same time, since $H^{\prime}_{k}$ is a degree- $(k-1)$ polynomial, there exists $C_{k}$ such that for every $\alpha>0$ we have $\sup_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert x}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{\alpha}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H^{\prime}_{k}(x)}}\right\rvert\leqslant C_{k}d^{(k-1)\alpha}$ . Thus, on $\mathcal{G}_{\eta}$ , a first-order Taylor expansion gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}+\varepsilon_{XY}}}\right)-H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\varepsilon_{XY}}}\right\rvert\sup_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert x}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{\frac{\eta}{2(k-1)}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H^{\prime}_{k}(x)}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{\frac{\eta}{2}-\frac{1}{2}} $$

and therefore

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}X_{a}Y_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right\rvert\geqslant d^{\eta-1/2}}}\right)\leqslant\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{\eta}^{c}). $$

Combined with (9.12), this completes the proof. ∎

### 9.3 Estimates for $E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}$

#### Lemma 9.7.

Let $\mu$ be a centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments, and let $(X_{a})_{a=1}^{d},(Y_{a})_{a=1}^{d}$ be independent vectors with all entries i.i.d. samples from $\mu$ . Set

$$ \widetilde{X}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}X&\text{if }\|X\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\widetilde{Y}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}Y&\text{if }\|Y\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Then for each $k$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

(Here $H_{k}$ is the $k$ th monic Hermite polynomial, which satisfies $H_{k}=\sqrt{k!}h_{k}$ ; we use this for this lemma only so that we do not need to carry $\sqrt{k!}$ ’s everywhere.)

#### Proof.

We restrict to the good event $\mathcal{G}_{XY}=\{\|X\|\neq 0\neq\|Y\|\}$ in the same way as before. On this event, we first compute

$$ \sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}=\sum_{a=1}^{d}((\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1)+1)((\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-1)+1)=\sum_{a=1}^{d}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1)(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-1)+d, $$

since $\sum_{a}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1)=\sum_{a}(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-1)=0$ , so that

$$ \frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}}{d}-1=\frac{\sum_{a}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1)(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-1)}{d}=\vcentcolon\Delta. $$

We will need the estimate $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\Delta}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ . This does not follow from Lemma 9.5, because the variables $\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1$ are not independent and centered, nor are they the normalizations of such variables. To handle this, we rewrite

$$ \displaystyle\Delta \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{a}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-1)(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-1)}{d}=\frac{\sum_{a}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}+\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}-1)(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}}+\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}}-1)}{d} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{a}(\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}-\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}})(\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}-\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}})}{d}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}-1}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}}-1}}\right) \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}}}}\right)\frac{\sum_{a}(X_{a}^{2}-1)(Y_{a}^{2}-1)}{d}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X\|^{2}}-1}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|Y\|^{2}}-1}}\right). $$

Since the variables $X_{a}^{2}-1$ are centered with order-one variance, Lemma 9.5 does apply to them; the estimate (9.9) gives $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a}(X_{a}^{2}-1)(Y_{a}^{2}-1)}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{d}$ . Combining this with several applications of Lemma 9.4, we find

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\Delta}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

Now we prove (9.13) by induction on $k$ , using the three-term recurrence formula

$$ H_{k+1}(x)=xH_{k}(x)-kH_{k-1}(x). $$

- • $\mathbf{k=0,1}$ : These are trivial, since the left-hand side of (9.13) is deterministically zero.

- • $\mathbf{k=2}$ : Since $H_{2}(x)=x^{2}-1$ , we have $\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert H_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{b}}}\right\rvert$ $\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{b}-1-\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{b}}}\right\rvert$ $\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{2}}{d}-1}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\Delta}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}.$

- • $\mathbf{k\geqslant 3}$ : We claim that

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}-\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{\frac{k-2}{2}}. $$

(9.15) Assume this claim momentarily. By induction, we have $\displaystyle H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}+\mathcal{E}_{k},$ $\displaystyle H_{k-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{(k-1)/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}+\mathcal{E}_{k-1}$ with error terms satisfying $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{k-1}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ . From the three-term recurrence for Hermite polynomials, we obtain $\displaystyle H_{k+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)=$ $\displaystyle\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{b}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{b}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)H_{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-kH_{k-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{b}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{b}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}+\mathcal{E}_{k}}}\right)$ $\displaystyle-k\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{(k-1)/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}+\mathcal{E}_{k-1}}}\right).$ Consider the product

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{b}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{b}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}}}\right). $$

(9.16) When we multiply the sums together, either the index $b$ is distinct from the indices $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\}$ , or it is not. If $b$ is distinct, this contributes to the main term; if $b$ is not distinct, we end up with a term of the form $\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}$ . Since the indices $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\}$ are themselves distinct, $b$ can only match with one of them, and this can happen in $k$ ways; thus the expression in (9.16) is equal to $\displaystyle\frac{1}{d^{(k+1)/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k+1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k+1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k+1}}+\frac{k}{d^{(k+1)/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}.$ Combining this with the estimate $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(\sum_{b}\widetilde{X}_{b}\widetilde{Y}_{b}/\sqrt{d})\mathcal{E}_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{k}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ , from Lemma 9.9; the estimate $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert k\mathcal{E}_{k-1}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{d}$ , of course; and (9.15), we obtain

$$ H_{k+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sum_{a}\widetilde{X}_{a}\widetilde{Y}_{a}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)=\frac{1}{d^{(k+1)/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k+1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k+1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k+1}}+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right) $$

as desired. Now we prove (9.15). Applying the same type of expansions as discussed just after (9.16), we find $\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}-\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{b=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{b}^{2}\widetilde{Y}_{b}^{2}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}}}\right)-\frac{k-1}{d}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}$ $\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}$ $\displaystyle=\Delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}}}\right)-\frac{k-1}{d}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}.$ By the estimate (9.14) and Lemma 9.5, the first term on the right-hand side is stochastically dominated by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}d^{\frac{k-1}{2}}=d^{\frac{k-2}{2}}$ in absolute value. To handle the second term on the right-hand side, we will make expansions like $\displaystyle\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{b=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{b}^{3}\widetilde{Y}_{b}^{3}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{a_{2},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}}}\right)$ $\displaystyle-(k-2)\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-2}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{4}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-2}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{4}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}},$ then expand from fourth powers into fifth powers, and so on, until the process terminates when all that remains is $\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{p}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{p}$ for some power $p$ (and an irrelevant prefactor $C_{k}$ ). To track this, we introduce the following bookkeeping notation: Defining $\displaystyle\alpha_{k,p}$ $\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k+2-p}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{p}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k+2-p}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{p}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k+2-p}}$ $\displaystyle\beta_{k,p}$ $\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{b=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{b}^{p}\widetilde{Y}_{b}^{p}}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{a_{2},\ldots,a_{k+2-p}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k+2-p}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k+2-p}}}}\right)$ expansions like those above show, with $x_{n}$ the falling factorial $x_{n}=x(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-n+1)$ , $\displaystyle\alpha_{k,p}$ $\displaystyle=\beta_{k,p}-(k+1-p)\alpha_{k,p+1}=\beta_{k,p}-(k+1-p)(\beta_{k,p+1}-(k-p)\alpha_{k,p+2})$ $\displaystyle=\beta_{k,p}-(k+1-p)\beta_{k,p+1}+(k+1-p)_{2}(\beta_{k,p+2}-(k-1+p)\alpha_{k,p+3})$ $\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{j=0}^{k+1}(-1)^{j}(k+1-p)_{j}\beta_{k,p+j}}}\right)+(k+1-p)_{k+2}\alpha_{k,p+k+2}.$ It is easy to compute $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{p}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{p}}}\right\rvert\prec d$ for any fixed $p$ ; in particular

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\alpha_{k,p+k+2}}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a=1}^{d}\widetilde{X}_{a}^{p+k+2}\widetilde{Y}_{a}^{p+k+2}}}\right\rvert\prec d, $$

and combining this with (9.10) we obtain

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\beta_{k,p}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{1+\frac{k+1-p}{2}} $$

(since the indexing in the definition of $\beta$ starts with $a_{2}$ ). Thus

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\alpha_{k,p}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{1+\frac{k+1-p}{2}} $$

as long as $k+1-p\geqslant 0$ . In particular,

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{k-1}{d}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{X}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k-1}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}^{3}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{2}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k-1}}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\alpha_{k,3}}}\right\rvert\prec d^{\frac{k-2}{2}} $$

which completes the proof of (9.15).

∎

### 9.4 Estimates for $E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}$

#### Lemma 9.8.

Let $\mu$ be a centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments, and let $(X_{a})_{a=1}^{d},(Y_{a})_{a=1}^{d}$ be independent vectors with all entries i.i.d. samples from $\mu$ . Set

$$ \widetilde{X}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X\|}X&\text{if }\|X\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\widetilde{Y}=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|Y\|}Y&\text{if }\|Y\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Then for each $k$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}-\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}}\ldots X_{a_{k}}Y_{a_{1}}\ldots Y_{a_{k}}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

#### Proof.

We restrict to the good event $\mathcal{G}_{XY}=\{\|X\|\neq 0\neq\|Y\|\}$ in the usual way. From (9.9) we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}\widetilde{X}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{X}_{a_{k}}\widetilde{Y}_{a_{1}}\ldots\widetilde{Y}_{a_{k}}-\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}}\ldots X_{a_{k}}Y_{a_{1}}\ldots Y_{a_{k}}}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X\|\|Y\|}}}\right)^{k}-1}}\right\rvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}}\ldots X_{a_{k}}Y_{a_{1}}\ldots Y_{a_{k}}}}\right\rvert\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X\|\|Y\|}}}\right)^{k}-1}}\right\rvert. $$

But

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}-1}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{j}\|}-1}}\right\rvert+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}-1}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)^{k}-1}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)^{j}-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)^{j-1}}}\right\rvert=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}-1}}\right\rvert\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)^{j} \displaystyle\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{d}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}-1}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, $$

which finishes the proof. ∎

### 9.5 Proof of Propositions 9.2 and 9.3

#### Proof of Proposition 9.2.

The decomposition $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}h_{k}(x)$ induces decompositions

$$ A=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}A_{k},\qquad\widetilde{A}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}\widetilde{A}_{k},\qquad\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}(\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}})_{k},\qquad B^{\textup{full}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}(B^{\textup{full}})_{k}, $$

which in turn induce decompositions

$$ E_{A,\widetilde{A}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}E_{A,\widetilde{A},k},\qquad E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},k},\qquad E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}},k}. $$

Since there is a finite number of terms in the sum, it suffices to prove the desired estimates one $k$ at a time. In the usual way, we can restrict to the good event $\{\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|\}$ , in which case we can apply the preceding lemmas by choosing $X=X_{i}$ and $Y=X_{j}$ : The estimate $|(E_{A,\widetilde{A},k})_{ij}|\prec 1/\sqrt{Nd}$ follows from Lemma 9.6; the estimate $|(E_{\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},k})_{ij}|\prec 1/\sqrt{Nd}$ for follows from Lemma 9.7; the estimate $|(E_{\widetilde{B}^{\textup{full}},B^{\textup{full}},k})_{ij}|\prec 1/\sqrt{Nd}$ follows from Lemma 9.8. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 9.3.

In the decomposition $B^{\textup{full}}=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}(B^{\textup{full}})_{k}$ , it suffices to show that $(B^{\textup{full}})_{k}$ admits a low-rank-plus-small-Frobenius-norm decomposition for each $k=0,\ldots,\lceil\ell\rceil-1$ . Fix such $k$ . The decomposition merely adds in the “missing diagonal”: Dropping $k$ from the notation, $E_{\textup{lr}}=E_{\textup{lr},k}$ and $E_{\textup{Frob}}=E_{\textup{Frob},k}$ are defined entrywise by

$$ \displaystyle(E_{\textup{lr}})_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j} \displaystyle(E_{\textup{Frob}})_{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sqrt{N}d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}^{2}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}^{2}. $$

The matrix $E_{\textup{lr}}$ is a sum of $d^{k}$ rank-one matrices of the form $M_{ij}=X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}$ (actually slightly fewer than $d^{k}$ , since the sum only counts $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\}$ distinct), hence has rank at most $d^{k}\leqslant d^{\lceil\ell\rceil-1}$ .

The matrix $E_{\textup{Frob}}$ is diagonal, and its entries are bounded above by

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}d^{k/2}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d}X_{a_{1}i}^{2}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}^{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}d^{k/2}}\|X\|^{2k}\prec\sqrt{\frac{d^{k}}{N}}=\OO\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(d^{(\lceil\ell\rceil-1-\ell)/2}}}\right). $$

Hence $\|E_{\textup{Frob}}\|_{\textup{Frob}}\prec d^{(\lceil\ell\rceil-1)/2}$ , completing the proof. ∎

## Appendix A General nonlinearities by approximation: Proof of Theorem 2.7

In this appendix, we prove Theorem 2.7 about general nonlinearities, via approximation by polynomials. The structure mimics the proof of [LY22, Theorem 2]. For the whole section, $\mu$ will be a centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments, and $X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ will be i.i.d. random vectors each of whose entries is an i.i.d. sample from $\mu$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 2.7.

Consider the inner product on functions with respect to Gaussian weight,

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle f,g}}\right\rangle\vcentcolon=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[f(Z)g(Z)], $$

and corresponding norm $\|f\|^{2}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle f,f}}\right\rangle$ . If $f$ satisfies Assumption 1, it is easy to show that $\|f\|^{2}=\sigma^{2}$ .

Fix some $\varepsilon$ . The theorem involves some $z$ in the complex upper half plane; recall that we write $\eta>0$ for its imaginary part. Since $\sum_{k}c_{k}^{2}$ converges, there exists some integer $L\geqslant\ell+1$ such that

$$ \sigma^{2}-(\eta^{4}\varepsilon^{2}/64)\leqslant\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}c_{k}^{2}\leqslant\sigma^{2}. $$

For this $L$ , we define the approximating polynomial

$$ f_{\textup{app}}(x)\vcentcolon=\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}c_{k}h_{k}(x)+\widehat{c_{L}}h_{L}(x) $$

with the adjustment $\widehat{c_{L}}\vcentcolon=(\sigma^{2}-\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}c_{k}^{2})^{1/2}$ , which is made so that $\gamma_{c}=\hat{\gamma_{c}}$ , where the former is defined by (2.5) with respect to $f_{\textup{app}}$ , and the latter is defined by (2.10) with respect to $f$ . Notice that $f_{\textup{app}}$ always satisfies Assumption 1.

We also define the error-like function

$$ e_{f,L}(x)=f(x)-\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}h_{k}(x). $$

Since the Hermite polynomials are orthogonal, we have

$$ \|f-f_{\textup{app}}\|^{2}=\|(c_{L}-\widehat{c_{L}})h_{L}(x)+e_{f,L}\|^{2}=(c_{L}-\widehat{c_{L}})^{2}+(\sigma^{2}-\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}^{2})\leqslant 2c_{L}^{2}+2\widehat{c_{L}}^{2}+\sigma^{2}-\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}^{2}=c_{L}^{2}+2\widehat{c_{L}}^{2}+\sigma^{2}-\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}c_{k}^{2}. $$

By (A.1) we have $\widehat{c_{L}}^{2}\leqslant\eta^{4}\varepsilon^{2}/64$ and $c_{L}^{2}\leqslant\eta^{4}\varepsilon^{2}/64$ ; thus we have

$$ \|f-\widehat{f}\|^{2}\leqslant\eta^{4}\varepsilon^{2}/16. $$

Now let $A_{\textup{app}}$ be the unnormalized matrix (1.1) but for $f_{\textup{app}}$ , with corresponding Stieltjes transform $s_{A_{\textup{app}}}$ . Similarly, let $\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}$ be the normalized matrix (1.2) but for $f_{\textup{app}}$ , with corresponding Stieltjes transform $s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}$ . On the one hand, from Theorem 2.1 we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A_{\textup{app}}}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

On the other hand, from Lemma A.1 below, we have

$$ \displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-s_{A_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert}}\right) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\|f-f_{\textup{app}}\|+\oo\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}}}\right)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{4}+\oo\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}}}\right)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right)\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right), $$

where the last inequality holds for $d$ large enough depending on $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$ . Thus

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{\ell/2}}}}\right), $$

meaning that for any $\varepsilon$ and $D$ we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert>\varepsilon)\leqslant C_{\varepsilon,D}d^{-D} $$

for $d$ large enough. By fixing $D$ and applying the Borel-Cantelli lemma, this suffices to show the almost-sure convergence of $s_{A}(z)$ to $\mathfrak{m}(z)$ . ∎

#### Lemma A.1.

Fix two functions $f,f_{\textup{app}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ that each satisfy Assumption 1, and a centered probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance and all finite moments. Write $A$ for the matrix (1.1), constructed with $f$ , where the i.i.d. vectors $(X_{i})_{i=1}^{N}$ have i.i.d. entries drawn from $\mu$ , with corresponding Stieltjes transform $s_{A}(z)$ . Write $A_{\textup{app}}$ for the analogue with $f$ replaced by $f_{\textup{app}}$ , with Stieltjes transform $s_{A_{\textup{app}}}(z)$ . Write also $\widetilde{A}$ for the corresponding normalized model (1.2), constructed with $f$ , and $\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}$ for the analogue constructed with $f_{\textup{app}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-s_{A_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[(f(Z)-f_{\textup{app}}(Z))^{2}]}}\right)^{1/2}+\oo\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}}}\right)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right), \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[(f(Z)-f_{\textup{app}}(Z))^{2}]}}\right)^{1/2}+\oo\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}}}\right)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right), $$

#### Proof.

Lemma 19 of [LY22] shows

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-s_{A_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{E}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-f_{\textup{app}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right)^{2}}}\right]}}\right)^{1/2}+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right). $$

Applying Lemma A.2 below to the function $g(x)=f(x)-f_{\textup{app}}(x)$ yields (A.2). The proof of (A.3) is a little more involved for technical reasons, since

$$ \widetilde{A}_{ij}=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)\mathds{1}\{\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|\} $$

but as written Lemma 19 of [LY22] only allows a direct comparison of matrices of the form

$$ (\widetilde{A}_{f})_{ij}=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{j}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|\}}}\right) $$

(by taking what they call $\mathbf{x}_{i}$ to be what we call $X_{i}/\|X_{i}\|$ if well-defined, or the zero vector otherwise), for various choices of $f$ . That is, on the exponentially unlikely occasions where $\|X_{i}\|=0$ , the corresponding row and column are set to zero in $\widetilde{A}$ but $f(0)/\sqrt{N}$ in $\widetilde{A}_{f}$ . By applying Lemma 19 of [LY22] and Lemma A.2 as in the unnormalized case, we obtain

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}_{f}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{A}_{f_{\textup{app}}}}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[(f(Z)-f_{\textup{app}}(Z))^{2}]}}\right)^{1/2}+\oo\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}}}\right)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\eta\sqrt{N}}}}\right). $$

It remains to compare $s_{\widetilde{A}}$ and $s_{\widetilde{A}_{f}}$ , as well as $s_{\widetilde{A}_{f_{\textup{app}}}}$ and $s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}$ , which we will do with the rank estimate (9.2). Bounding the rank of a matrix by its number of nonzero rows, this gives

$$ \displaystyle\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{A}_{f}}(z)}}\right\rvert,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}_{f_{\textup{app}}}}(z)-s_{\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}}(z)}}\right\rvert}}\right) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C\max(\rank(\widetilde{A}-\widetilde{A}_{f}),\rank(\widetilde{A}_{f_{\textup{app}}}-\widetilde{A}_{\textup{app}}))}{N\eta} \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C\#\{i:\|X_{i}\|=0\}}{N\eta}\prec\frac{1}{N\eta}, $$

where the last estimate holds since $\mathbb{P}(\|X_{i}\|=0)$ is exponentially small, so that $\#\{i:\|X_{i}\|=0\}\prec 1$ . Absorbing this into $\OO_{\prec}((\eta\sqrt{N})^{-1})$ completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma A.2.

Fix $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ that satisfies Assumption 1. If $\mu$ has all finite moments, then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[g^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)}}\right]\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathbb{E}_{Z}[g^{2}(Z)], \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[g^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{1}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{2}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{1}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{2}\|\}}}\right)}}\right]\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathbb{E}_{Z}[g^{2}(Z)]. $$

#### Proof.

Write $\mu_{d}$ for the law of $\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}$ , and $\widetilde{\mu_{d}}$ for the law of $\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{1}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{2}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{1}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{2}\|\}$ – neither of which necessarily has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure – as well as $\mu_{G}$ for standard Gaussian measure. By the usual central limit theorem, $\mu_{G}$ is the $d\to\infty$ weak limit of the measures $\mu_{d}$ . It is straightforward to show that $\frac{d}{\|X_{1}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{1}\|\neq 0\}$ and $\frac{d}{\|X_{2}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{2}\|\neq 0\}$ each converge in probability to one, so that $\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{1},X_{2}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{1}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{2}\|}\mathds{1}\{\|X_{1}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{2}\|\}$ also converges to a Gaussian variable, meaning that $\mu_{G}$ is also the $d\to\infty$ weak limit of the measures $\widetilde{\mu_{d}}$ .

Fix any constant $M\geqslant\max(1,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\alpha_{1}}}\right\rvert,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\alpha_{K}}}\right\rvert)$ . Write $g_{M}$ for the function which agrees with $g$ on $[-M,M]$ , vanishes outside $[-(M+1),M+1]$ , linearly interpolates on $[M,M+1]$ between $g(M)$ and $0$ , and linearly interpolates on $[-(M+1),-M]$ between $0$ and $g(-M)$ , and define $e_{M}$ by

$$ g^{2}(x)=g_{M}^{2}(x)+e_{M}(x). $$

The result will follow if we can show

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{d\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}g_{M}^{2}(x)(\mu_{d}-\mu_{G})(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\lim_{d\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}g_{M}^{2}(x)(\widetilde{\mu_{d}}-\mu_{G})(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x) \displaystyle=0, $$

for any fixed $M$ , as well as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{M\to\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\int_{\mathbb{R}}e_{M}(x)\mu_{G}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{d\to\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\int_{\mathbb{R}}e_{M}(x)\mu_{d}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{d\to\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\int_{\mathbb{R}}e_{M}(x)\widetilde{\mu_{d}}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle=0. $$

We start with the proof of (A.6) and (A.7). Notice that, since $g(x)$ is the difference of the nonlinear function $f(x)$ and a finite degree polynomial, and $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous with a polynomial growth rate, $g^{2}(x)$ is also piecewise continous with a polynomial growth rate, and $g_{M}^{2}(x)$ is piecewise continuous (with “no growth rate” since it vanishes outside $[-(M+1),M+1]$ . The possible discontinuities of $g^{2}(x)$ and $g_{M}^{2}(x)$ occur at $\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{K}\}$ .

Write $h(x)=g_{M}^{2}(x)$ . For any $\varepsilon\in(0,\min_{1\leqslant i<K}\{\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}\}/2)$ , construct a “smoothed” version $h_{\varepsilon}(x)$ such that $h_{\varepsilon}(x)=h(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\bigcup_{1\leqslant i\leqslant K}[\alpha_{i}-\varepsilon,\alpha_{i}+\varepsilon]$ ; on the interval $[\alpha_{i}-\varepsilon,\alpha_{i}+\varepsilon]$ , for $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,K\}$ , the function $h_{\varepsilon}(x)$ is a linear interpolation between $h(\alpha_{i}-\varepsilon)$ and $h(\alpha_{i+1}+\varepsilon)$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\int h(x)(\mu_{d}-\mu_{G})(dx)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\int h_{\varepsilon}(x)(\mu_{d}-\mu_{G})(dx)}}\right\rvert+\int\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert h(x)-h_{\varepsilon}(x)}}\right\rvert\mu_{d}(dx)+\int\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert h(x)-h_{\varepsilon}(x)}}\right\rvert\mu_{G}(dx). $$

Since $h_{\varepsilon}(x)$ is a continuous function with compact support, the first term on the right-hand sides converges to $0$ as $d\to\infty$ due to the CLT. To control the second and third terms on the right-hand side, we note that

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert h(x)-h_{\varepsilon}(x)}}\right\rvert\leqslant C_{M}\sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant K}\mathbf{1}_{[\alpha_{i}-\varepsilon,\alpha_{i}+\varepsilon]}(x), $$

where $C_{M}$ is some finite constant that can depend on $M$ . Since $\mu_{G}$ has a bounded density function,

$$ \int\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert h(x)-h_{\varepsilon}(x)}}\right\rvert\mu_{G}(dx)\leqslant C_{M}\sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant K}\int\mathbf{1}_{[\alpha_{i}-\varepsilon,\alpha_{i}+\varepsilon]}(x)\mu_{G}(dx)\leqslant 2KC_{M}\varepsilon. $$

Similarly,
