# Quantum diffusion and delocalization in one-dimensional band matrices via the flow method

**Authors:** Sofiia Dubova ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Harvard Univeristy Kevin Yang††footnotemark:

## Abstract

We study a class of Gaussian random band matrices of dimension $N\times N$ and band-width $W$ . We show that delocalization holds for bulk eigenvectors and that quantum diffusion holds for the resolvent, all under the assumption that $W\gg N^{8/11}$ . This improves the best-known result of [8, 9, 40]. Our analysis is based on a flow method, and a refinement of it may lead to an improvement on the condition $W\gg N^{8/11}$ .

## 1 Introduction

In [36], Wigner introduced the random matrix universality class to be a model for highly correlated quantum systems. Although the Wigner ensemble is a mean-field model, it is conjectured to also describe the behaviors (e.g. spectral data) of many other models. A prototypical class of Wigner matrices is the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE), whose entries are standard complex Gaussians independent up to the Hermitian constraint.

A historically important non-mean-field model that is conjecturally related to the random matrix universality class is the Anderson model on lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ . This model is the operator $\Delta+\lambda V$ , where $\Delta$ is the discrete Laplacian, where $\lambda>0$ , and where $V$ is a random diagonal matrix with i.i.d. entries. It is believed [4] that for large $\lambda$ , eigenvalues of $\Delta+\lambda V$ form a Poisson point process, and eigenvectors have a finite localization (i.e. support) length. For small $\lambda$ , eigenvalue and eigenvector statistics of $\Delta+\lambda V$ are believed to agree with random matrix statistics, e.g. delocalization of eigenvectors. There has been a lot of work showing localization for large $\lambda$ [1, 10, 11, 14, 16, 23, 24, 25, 26]. However, delocalization has remained an outstanding problem with some results on the Bethe lattice [2, 3].

Another important non-mean-field example, which is conjectured to exhibit a similar transition between random matrix and Poisson statistics, is the random band matrix [7]. This is the model of interest in this paper. It is a Hermitian matrix $H$ of dimension $N\times N$ . Its entries $H_{xy}$ are i.i.d. complex random variables up to the Hermitian constraint, and they vanish when the distance (with respect to periodic boundary conditions on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ ) between the indices $x,y$ is larger than a fixed band width parameter $W$ . (The matrix $H$ is also normalized so that the matrix $S$ of variances $S_{xy}=\mathbb{E}|H_{xy}|^{2}$ is a doubly stochastic matrix.)

When $W\gg 1$ in the large- $N$ limit, the global eigenvalue density of $H$ converges to the Wigner semicircle law [6]. However, based on Thouless’ conductance fluctuation theory and scaling arguments [33], numerical simulations [12], and non-rigorous supersymmetric heuristics [18], local eigenvalue statistics and eigenvector statistics are conjectured to exhibit the following transition [7] in the bulk (i.e. for eigenvalues with real part $|E|<2$ independent of $N$ ):

- • If $W\gg N^{1/2}$ , then bulk eigenvalues have GUE statistics, and eigenvectors are delocalized, i.e. there is no length-scale $\ell\ll N$ to which eigenvectors are localized.

- • If $W\ll N^{1/2}$ , then bulk eigenvalues form a Poisson process, and eigenvectors are localized.

Thus, random band matrices and the Anderson model are believed to be similar when $\lambda\sim W^{-1}$ . We note that a similar transition exists at the edge, i.e. for eigenvalues of order $N^{-2/3}$ from the spectral edge $2$ of the semicircle. In this case, GUE statistics occur for $W\gg N^{5/6}$ and Poisson statistics occur for $W\ll N^{5/6}$ ; this was shown by Sodin [31], as was a detailed description of spectral statistics at the transition point $W\sim N^{5/6}$ .

A long series of works established GUE statistics under improving assumptions on the band width. The works [19, 21] showed that the percentage of localized eigenvectors in the bulk is $\mathrm{o}(1)$ , first for $W\gg N^{6/7}$ , then for $W\gg N^{4/5}$ . This was improved to a stronger form of delocalization and GUE eigenvalue statistics in [8, 9, 40] for $W\gg N^{3/4}$ . In addition, there has been work on bounds on the localization length [8, 9, 27, 40]. We also mention [30], which shows delocalization for Gaussian band matrices with a special variance profile $S_{xy}$ . These use the supersymmetric method, and they work up to $W\gg N^{6/7}$ . (Extensions to more general matrices without the Gaussian assumption were given in [5], which require $W\geq cN$ .) The supersymmetric method has also been able to show a transition in the two-point correlations of bulk eigenvalues at $W\sim N^{1/2}$ [29], though it is unclear if these methods extend to delocalization versus localization of eigenvectors. On the other side of the transition, localization for all the eigenvectors was shown in [28, 27, 13], first for $W\ll N^{1/8}$ , then for $W\ll N^{1/7}$ in specific Gaussian models, and most recently for $W\ll N^{1/4}$ .

The goal of this paper is to show delocalization of bulk eigenvectors for a large class of Gaussian random band matrices with very general variance profiles assuming $W\gg N^{8/11}$ . This improves on the best-known result of $W\gg N^{3/4}$ [8, 9, 40]. We also prove a phenomenon known as quantum diffusion; this derives the resolvent of a diffusion operator from the resolvent of $H$ . Showing delocalization through quantum diffusion, which has the benefit of being “natural” in the sense explained after Theorem 2, goes back at least to [20].

Our analysis is built on the flow method. In this method, the spectral parameter $z$ for the resolvent of $H$ follows a constant-speed characteristic in the upper-half plane. Its imaginary part starts at an order $1$ value, and it ends at a small-scale $\eta$ of interest. Simultaneously, the entries of $H$ are realized as Brownian motions. The upshot to this method is the introduction of dynamical ideas. It was used to prove a local semicircle law for a class of Wigner matrices [34, 35], but the application to band matrices seems to be new to this work.

Finally, we mention progress on random band matrices in higher dimension $d$ (in which the matrix size is $N=L^{d}$ , and the predicted thresholds are in terms of $W$ and $L$ ). For $d\geq 2$ , some lower bounds on the localization length were obtained [19, 20]. In [37, 38, 39], the authors showed a weak form of delocalization (see Corollary 5) for bulk eigenvectors in dimension $d\geq 8$ , as well as GUE eigenvalue statistics in dimension $d\geq 7$ . The former work assumes only (essentially) the optimal constraint that $W\gg L^{\varepsilon}$ ; the latter assumes instead that $W\gg L^{95/(d+95)}$ (which, for large dimension $d$ , looks like $W\gg L^{\varepsilon}$ ).

The next section states precisely our model and main results as well as an outline for the rest of the paper.

### 1.1 Acknowledgements

We thank Horng-Tzer Yau for helpful discussions. K.Y. was supported in part by NSF DMS-2203075.

## 2 Main results

We now introduce the matrix model precisely. First, let $\mathbb{T}_{N}=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ be the discrete torus of length $N$ . We identify it with $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and we will give it the periodic distance $|x-y|_{N}:=\min([x-y],[y-x])$ for any $x,y\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ , where $[\cdot]$ means taking the mod- $N$ equivalence class in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ .

Next, let $f$ be a symmetric and compactly supported probability density on $\mathbb{R}$ . We let $S=(S_{xy};x,y=1,\ldots,N)$ be a doubly stochastic matrix whose entries are given by

$$ \displaystyle S_{xy}:=Z_{N,W}^{-1}f\left(\frac{|x-y|_{N}}{W}\right). $$

Here, $Z_{N,W}$ is a normalizing constant satisfying $Z_{N,W}\asymp W$ , where $\asymp$ means bounded above and below up to fixed, positive factors. We also assume that $S$ admits a matrix square root $S^{1/2}$ satisfying the same properties for a possibly different but still symmetric and compactly supported probability density $f$ . (This is an entirely technical assumption that can probably be removed, though it is already quite general. Since our main attention is in the size of $W$ relative to $N$ , we do not pursue this.)

The matrix ensemble of interest in this paper is denoted by $H=(H_{xy};x,y=1,\ldots,N)$ . It is Hermitian, and for any $x\leq y$ , $H_{xy}$ is a complex Gaussian random variable satisfying $\mathbb{E}H_{xy}=0$ and $\mathbb{E}|H_{xy}|^{2}=S_{xy}$ .

Next, we introduce the Stieltjes transform of the Wigner semicircle law below:

$$ \displaystyle m(z):=\int_{-2}^{2}\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}}{x-z}dx=\frac{-z+\sqrt{z^{2}-4}}{2}, $$

where the second identity follows from the standard fact (see (3.13) in [22]) that $m(z)$ is the unique solution to the following self-consistent equation:

$$ \displaystyle z=-m(z)^{-1}-m(z),\quad\mathrm{Im}(z),\mathrm{Im}m(z)>0. $$

Throughout this paper, we follow standard notation and write $z=E+i\eta$ with $E\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\eta>0$ .

To conclude this subsection, we now introduce frequently used notation for inequalities. We use standard big-O notation. We often write $a\lesssim b$ if $a=\mathrm{O}(b)$ (and similarly $a\gtrsim b$ if $b=\mathrm{O}(a)$ ). We also introduce the following standard notion of stochastic domination in random matrix theory.

#### Definition 1.

Consider two sequences of random variables, denoted by $X=\left\{X_{N}(s):N\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+},s\in S_{N}\right\}$ and $Y=\left\{Y_{N}(s):N\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+},s\in S_{N}\right\}$ , that are parametrized by $s$ in some index set $S_{N}$ . We say that $X$ is stochastically dominated by $Y$ uniformly in $s$ and write $X\prec Y$ or $X=\mathcal{O}(Y)$ if for any $\varepsilon,D>0$ we have

$$ \sup_{s\in S_{N}}{\mathbb{P}}\left(X_{N}(s)>N^{\varepsilon}Y_{N}(s)\right)<N^{-D} $$

for large enough $N$ .

### 2.1 Quantum diffusion

Our first main theorem is an analysis of the following $T$ -matrix and its comparison to the diffusion profile $\Theta$ :

$$ \displaystyle T(z)_{ab} \displaystyle:=T_{ab}:=\sum_{x,y}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}|G_{xy}|^{2}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{yb}; \displaystyle\Theta(z) \displaystyle:=\Theta:=\frac{|m(z)|^{2}S}{1-|m(z)|^{2}S}. $$

We clarify that in the formula for $T(z)_{ab}$ , the value $S^{1/2}_{\alpha\beta}$ refers to the $(\alpha,\beta)$ entry of the matrix square root.

#### Theorem 2.

First, assume that $|E|<2$ is fixed. Assume that there exists a fixed $\upsilon>0$ so that $\eta\asymp W^{2}N^{-2}$ and $W\geq N^{8/11+\upsilon}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{x,y}|T_{xy}-\Theta_{xy}|\prec W^{-\frac{7}{4}}\eta^{-\frac{3}{2}}. $$

#### Remark 3.

The assumptions in Theorem 2 imply that $\eta\geq W^{-3/4+\upsilon}$ for some $\upsilon>0$ .

Roughly speaking, Theorem 2 establishes $T\approx\Theta$ . (In particular, the error bound in Theorem 2 is much smaller than the maximal entry size of $\Theta$ . Indeed, by classical resolvent bounds for diffusions, as in Proposition 2.8 in [21] or Lemma 23, the maximal entry of $\Theta$ is order $W^{-1}\eta^{-1/2}$ . Now, use that $\eta\gg W^{-3/4}$ to get $W^{-7/4}\eta^{-3/2}\ll W^{-1}\eta^{-1/2}$ .) This is often called quantum diffusion for the following reason. Classical asymptotics (see Lemma 3.5 in [21] and Lemma 6.2 in [22]) show that $1-|m(z)|^{2}\asymp\eta$ in the bulk ( $|E|<2$ ). Thus, one can rewrite $\Theta$ as

$$ \displaystyle\Theta\sim\frac{S}{1-|m(z)|^{2}+|m(z)|^{2}(S-\mathrm{Id})}\sim\frac{S}{\alpha\eta+(S-\mathrm{Id})}, $$

where $\alpha\asymp 1$ . The matrix $S$ is the transition operator for a random walk on the torus $\mathbb{T}_{N}\simeq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ . It has jump length $W$ and diffusivity proportional to $W^{2}$ . Thus, $S-\mathrm{Id}$ is the generator for such a random walk, which provides $\Theta$ the interpretation as the resolvent of the generator for a random walk on $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . Moreover, the spectral gap for a random walk on $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ with steps of variance $W^{2}$ is of order $W^{2}N^{-2}$ . The assumption $\eta\asymp W^{2}N^{-2}$ therefore means that Theorem 2 shows diffusion until the relaxation time $\eta^{-1}\asymp N^{2}W^{-2}$ of the random walk (which is often called the Thouless time [17, 32, 33]).

As mentioned above, Theorem 2 is the main result that leads to proofs of the other theorems in this paper. A conceptual benefit to proving delocalization using Theorem 2 is that $\Theta$ naturally explains the conjectured threshold $W\gg N^{1/2}$ . Indeed, $S-\mathrm{Id}$ has a spectral gap of $W^{2}N^{-2}$ , so it is natural to take $\eta\asymp W^{2}N^{-2}$ . On the other hand, we want $\eta\gg N^{-1}$ in the bulk, since $N^{-1}$ is the typical eigenvalue gap size, which leads to $W^{2}N^{-2}\gg N^{-1}$ , i.e. $W\gg N^{1/2}$ . The roadblock to proving quantum diffusion all the way to $W\gg N^{1/2}$ seems to be technical. We explain this (and a possible angle to overcome this difficulty) in Section 5.

### 2.2 Local law and eigenvector delocalization

We now present the following local law, whose proof ultimately follows by Theorem 2 and other gymnastics that are relatively standard (as explained in Section 3).

#### Theorem 4.

Retain the setting of Theorem 2. We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{x,y}|G_{xy}-m(z)\delta_{xy}|^{2}\prec W^{-1}\eta^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

As a consequence of Theorem 4, we deduce what [21] calls the “complete delocalization of (bulk) eigenvectors”. To state it, we first introduce some notation. Fix any index $x$ and any integer $\ell\geq 1$ . We let $P_{x,\ell}$ be the projection onto the complement of the radius- $\ell$ ball around $x$ , so that $P_{x,\ell}(y):=\mathbf{1}[|x-y|\geq\ell]$ for any indices $x,y$ . Next, for any eigenvalue $\lambda_{\alpha}$ of $H$ , we choose a unit-norm eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}$ with this eigenvalue. Given any $\kappa>0$ we let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon,\ell,\kappa}:=\left\{\alpha:\lambda_{\alpha}\in[-E+\kappa,E-\kappa]:\sum_{x}|\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}(x)\|P_{x,\ell}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}\|\leq\varepsilon\right\} $$

be the labeling set for bulk eigenvectors that are localized to scale $\ell$ up to a small error $\varepsilon>0$ . (As in Remark 7.2 of [21], this includes the set of bulk eigenvectors that are exponentially localized to scale $\ell$ .) The result below shows that this set has a small density.

#### Corollary 5.

Retain the setting of Theorem 2. For any $\ell\ll N$ and any $\varepsilon,\kappa>0$ fixed, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon,\ell,\kappa}|}{N}\lesssim\sqrt{\varepsilon}+\mathcal{O}(N^{-c}), $$

where $c>0$ is a fixed constant.

#### Proof.

The proof is exactly the content of Proposition 7.1 in [21], which we now verify applies to the current situation. We first note that their condition $\eta\geq W^{-1+\gamma}$ for some $\gamma>0$ is satisfied by our assumptions on $\eta$ in Theorem 4; see Remark 3. Next, we observe that by (2.2), we have $|G_{xy}-m(z)\delta_{xy}|^{2}\prec W^{-1}\eta^{-1/2}\lesssim N^{-1}\eta^{-1}$ ; the last bound follows by $\eta\asymp W^{2}N^{-2}$ . Finally, since we assume that $\eta\asymp W^{2}N^{-2}$ and $N\ll W^{11/8}$ , we have $N^{-1}\eta^{-1}\asymp NW^{-2}\ll W^{-5/8}$ . Thus, the assumptions in Proposition 7.1 of [21], namely the lower bound on $\eta$ , the a priori bound on $|G_{xy}|^{2}$ , and the “admissible estimate” on $|G_{xy}-m(z)\delta_{xy}|^{2}$ (as defined in Definition 3.7 of [21]), are all satisfied. But Proposition 7.1 in [21] implies the desired estimate directly, so the proof is complete. ∎

### 2.3 Outline for the rest of the paper

Section 3 sets up the flow method and shows Theorems 2 and 4 modulo a key estimate (Proposition 11). Section 4 shows this estimate via graphical expansions. Section 5 explains refinements of our analysis that may lead to an improvement on the assumption $W\gg N^{8/11}$ . Section A gives auxiliary matrix estimates.

## 3 The SDE flow

Let $B_{t,ij}$ be independent standard complex Brownian motions for all $i,j=1,\ldots,N$ . Consider the process

$$ \displaystyle dH_{t,ij}=\sqrt{S_{ij}}dB_{t,ij},\quad H_{0}=0. $$

Next, for any $z=E+i\eta$ with $E\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\eta>0$ , define the path

$$ \displaystyle t\mapsto w_{t}:=\frac{-1}{m(z)}-tm(z)=z+(1-t)m(z), $$

where $m(z)$ is the Stieltjes transform of the semicircle distribution at $z$ (so that the second identity follows by the self-consistent equation for $m(z)$ ). Note that $w_{1}=z$ and $w_{0}=-m(z)^{-1}=z+m(z)$ . Now, consider the resolvent of $H_{t}$ at the points $w_{t}$ and the associated $T$ -matrix:

$$ \displaystyle G_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=(H_{t}-w_{t})^{-1}. \displaystyle T_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=S^{\frac{1}{2}}F_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}},\quad\mathrm{where}\ F_{t}(z)_{ij}:=|G_{t}(z)_{ij}|^{2}. $$

An elementary application of Ito’s lemma gives the following SDEs.

#### Lemma 6.

We have $G_{0}=m(z)$ , and we have the SDE

$$ \displaystyle dG_{t}(z)=-G_{t}(z)dH_{t}G_{t}(z)+G_{t}(z)\{\mathcal{S}[G_{t}(z)]-m(z)\}G_{t}(z)dt, $$

where $\mathcal{S}:M_{N}(\mathbb{C})\to M_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ is the linear operator defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}[X]_{ij}:=\delta_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^{N}S_{ik}X_{kk}. $$

We also have the SDE

$$ \displaystyle dT_{t}(z) \displaystyle=T_{t}(z)^{2}dt-S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}+S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt, \displaystyle dM_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\overline{G}_{t}(z)\odot\{G_{t}(z)dH_{t}G_{t}(z)\}+\overline{G_{t}(z)dH_{t}G_{t}(z)}\odot G_{t}(z), \displaystyle\Omega_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\overline{G}_{t}(z)\odot\{G_{t}(z)\{\mathcal{S}[G_{t}(z)]-m(z)\}G_{t}(z)\}+\overline{G_{t}(z)\{\mathcal{S}[G_{t}(z)]-m(z)\}G_{t}(z)}\odot G_{t}(z). $$

where $\odot$ denotes entry-wise multiplication of matrices.

#### Proof.

Fix any indices $\alpha,\beta,a,b$ . By resolvent perturbation, we have

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{H_{t,\alpha\beta}}G_{t}(z)_{ab} \displaystyle=-G_{t}(z)_{a\alpha}G_{t}(z)_{\beta b} \displaystyle\partial_{H_{t,\beta\alpha}}\partial_{H_{t,\alpha\beta}}G_{t}(z) \displaystyle=G_{t}(z)_{a\beta}G_{t}(z)_{\alpha\alpha}G_{t}(z)_{\beta b}+G_{t}(z)_{a\alpha}G_{t}(z)_{\beta\beta}G_{t}(z)_{\alpha b} \displaystyle\partial_{t}G_{t}(z)_{ab} \displaystyle=G_{t}(z)^{2}_{ab}\partial_{t}w_{t}=-m(z)G_{t}(z)^{2}_{ab}, $$

where in the last line, $G_{t}(z)^{2}_{ab}$ is the $(a,b)$ entry of the squared matrix $G_{t}(z)^{2}$ . The first SDE now follows by the Ito formula. Next, we have

$$ \displaystyle dF_{t}(z)_{ij} \displaystyle=d|G_{t}(z)_{ij}|^{2}=G_{t}(z)_{ij}d\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{ij}+\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{ij}dG_{t}(z)_{ij}+d[G_{t}(z)_{ij},\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{ij}] \displaystyle=-dM_{t}(z)+\Omega_{t}(z)dt+d[G_{t}(z)_{ij},\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{ij}], $$

where the last line follows by plugging in the $G_{t}(z)$ SDE. On the other hand, we have

$$ \displaystyle d[G_{t}(z)_{ij},\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{ij}] \displaystyle=d\left[\sum_{\alpha,\beta}G_{t}(z)_{i\alpha}dH_{t,\alpha\beta}G_{t}(z)_{\beta j},\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{i\alpha}d\overline{H}_{t,\alpha\beta}\overline{G}_{t}(z)_{\beta j}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}S_{\alpha\beta}|G_{t}(z)_{i\alpha}|^{2}|G_{t}(z)_{\beta j}|^{2}dt=[F_{t}(z)SF_{t}(z)]_{ij}dt. $$

If we now multiply the above by $S^{1/2}$ on the left and right, we ultimately deduce

$$ \displaystyle dT_{t}(z)=S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}+S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt+S^{\frac{1}{2}}F_{t}(z)SF_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt. $$

The last term is just $T_{t}(z)^{2}dt$ , so the proof is complete. ∎

Our goal is to analyze the $T_{t}(z)$ equation. Define the time-dependent diffusion profile to be

$$ \displaystyle\Theta_{t}=\frac{|m(z)|^{2}S}{1-t|m(z)|^{2}S}. $$

Straightforward differentiation shows that $d\Theta_{t}=\Theta_{t}^{2}dt$ , and direct inspection shows $T_{0}(z)=\Theta_{0}=|m(z)|^{2}S$ . Now, define $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z):=T_{t}(z)-\Theta_{t}$ . Our goal is to show that $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ is small. We start by computing its evolution equation.

#### Lemma 7.

Retain the notation of Lemma 6. We have $\mathcal{E}_{0}(z)=0$ and

$$ \displaystyle d\mathcal{E}_{t}(z) \displaystyle=(\Theta_{t}\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)\Theta_{t})dt+\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)^{2}dt-S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}+S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt. $$

We also have the integral equation $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)=\mathcal{E}^{M}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{D}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{S}_{t}(z)$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{M}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=-\int_{0}^{t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{D}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}ds, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{S}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}ds. $$

#### Proof.

Recall that $d\Theta_{t}=\Theta_{t}^{2}dt$ . Combining this with Lemma 6 gives

$$ \displaystyle d\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)=T_{t}(z)^{2}dt-\Theta_{t}^{2}dt-S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}+S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt. $$

To get the first SDE, it suffices to note that $T_{t}(z)^{2}-\Theta_{t}^{2}=\Theta_{t}\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)\Theta_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)^{2}$ . To show that the integral equation holds, it is enough to use pathwise uniqueness of solutions to SDEs and to verify that $\mathcal{E}^{M}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{D}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{S}_{t}(z)$ satisfies the same SDE as $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ . For the latter, we note that

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\} \displaystyle=\partial_{t}\frac{1-s|m(z)|^{2}S}{1-t|m(z)|^{2}S}=\Theta_{t}\frac{1-s|m(z)|^{2}S}{1-t|m(z)|^{2}S}=\Theta_{t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}, $$

at which point verifying the SDE for $\mathcal{E}^{M}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{D}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{S}_{t}(z)$ amounts to just calculus. ∎

### 3.1 Stopping time construction

The RHS of the $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ equation in Lemma 7 has nonlinear powers of $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ itself, so we will need a stopping time argument to show small-ness of these nonlinear powers. Fix $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}>0$ small but independent of $N$ , and fix any large $D=\mathrm{O}(1)$ . We define the stopping times

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1} \displaystyle:=\inf\left\{s\geq 0:\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{ab}|\geq W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}\wedge 1, \displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{stop},2} \displaystyle:=\inf\left\{s\geq 0:\max_{a,b}\frac{|G_{s}(z)_{ab}-\delta_{ab}m(z)|^{2}}{(S^{1/2}T_{s}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}+S^{1/2}_{ab}+W^{-D}}\geq W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}\right\}\wedge 1, \displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{stop}} \displaystyle:=\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{stop},2}. $$

Since the typical size of $\max_{ab}(\Theta_{t})_{ab}$ is $W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ , the first stopping time $\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}$ is giving us the small-ness factor $W^{-3/4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ , which indicates the importance of the assumption $\eta\gg W^{-3/4}$ in this paper (since $\mathrm{Im}w_{t}$ is decreasing in $t$ and $\mathrm{Im}w_{1}=\mathrm{Im}z=\eta$ ). We also note that the exponent $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10$ is not itself particularly important, as any small multiple of $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}$ would be sufficient.

The key technical result leading the proof of Theorems 2 and 4 is the following.

#### Theorem 8.

We have $\mathbb{P}[\tau_{\mathrm{stop},i}\neq 1]\lesssim_{D}N^{-D}$ for any $i=1,2$ and $D>0$ .

Our strategy for proving Theorem 8 is to construct a “stopped” version of the $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ dynamics. To be more precise, let $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}$ denote the solution to

$$ \displaystyle d\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z) \displaystyle=(\Theta_{t}\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)\Theta_{t})dt+\mathbf{1}_{t\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)^{2}dt \displaystyle-\mathbf{1}_{t\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathbf{1}_{t\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}dt $$

Now, by the Duhamel formula as in the proof of Lemma 7, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)=\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{S},\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}dM_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}ds, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z) \displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}ds. $$

Since $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ is a stopping time with respect to the Brownian filtration, by uniqueness of strong solutions to finite-dimensional Ito SDEs, we know that $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)=\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ for all $t\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ . With this in mind, our goal is to now control each term in the previous display uniformly over all $t\in[0,1]$ with high probability, and the bounds we obtain will be better than the ones defining $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ . In particular, this will show that the stopping time $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ is self-propagating, in which case Theorem 8 will follow since $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}>0$ with probability $1$ .

We start with the term $\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)$ ; we give a deterministic bound for this.

#### Lemma 9.

There exists $\delta>0$ so that $|\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}|\lesssim W^{-\delta}W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ for all $t\in[0,1]$ .

#### Proof.

We first claim the following estimates:

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}_{xy}+\sup_{y}\sum_{x}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}_{xy}=1+\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|). $$

Since the matrix $\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}$ is symmetric, it suffices to control only one of the two terms on the LHS; we choose the first. It suffices to show that $\sum_{y}(t-s)(\Theta_{t})_{xy}=\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|)$ , since $\sum_{y}\mathrm{Id}_{xy}=1$ . Recall that $w_{s}=-m(z)^{-1}-sm(z)$ , so that $\mathrm{Im}w_{s}=\mathrm{Im}w_{t}+(t-s)\mathrm{Im}m(z)$ . Since $|\mathrm{Im}m(z)|$ is bounded uniformly away from $0$ in the bulk (see Lemma 6.2 in [22]), we deduce that $|t-s|=\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|)$ . Thus, to prove (3.7), it suffices to prove that $\sum_{y}(\Theta_{t})_{xy}=\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1})$ (this can be found in Lemma 23).

By (3.7) and matrix multiplication, for any indices $a,b$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\left[1+\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|)\right]^{2}\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}_{ab}|ds \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}_{ab}|ds+\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{2}\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}_{ab}|ds. $$

By matrix multiplication, definition of $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ , and $N\leq W^{11/8-\upsilon}$ , we have the bound below for any $s\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)^{2}_{ab}| \displaystyle\leq N\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{ab}|^{2}\leq W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}NW^{-\frac{3}{2}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-2}W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1} \displaystyle\leq W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}. $$

We combine the previous two displays to get

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{t}W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}ds+\int_{0}^{t}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}ds. $$

We now change variables $\sigma=\mathrm{Im}w_{s}$ . The Jacobian factor is $\mathrm{Im}m(z)\asymp 1$ (see Lemma 6.2 in [22]). Moreover, for any $s\in[0,t]$ , we have $\mathrm{Im}w_{s}=\mathrm{Im}w_{t}+(t-s)\mathrm{Im}m(z)\geq\mathrm{Im}w_{t}$ (which implies $\mathrm{Im}w_{s}=\eta+(1-s)\mathrm{Im}m(z)\leq\eta+\mathrm{Im}m(z)=\mathrm{Im}w_{0}\lesssim 1$ by taking $t=1$ ); we explained this in the paragraph after (3.7). Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{E}^{S,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}\sigma^{-3}d\sigma+\int_{|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}\sigma^{-1}d\sigma \displaystyle\lesssim W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}+W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{17}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}\log|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{3}{8}-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}\log|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Because $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}$ is small and $\upsilon>0$ is fixed, and since $|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|\geq\eta\geq W^{-3/4}$ , the first factor on the RHS, namely $W^{2\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-3/8-\upsilon}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}\log|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ , is $\mathrm{o}(1)$ , and the claim follows. ∎

We now tackle the stochastic integral $\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{z}(t)$ . For this, we will prove a pointwise moment bound and use a crude continuity estimate in time to bootstrap to a uniform estimate over $t\in[0,1]$ with high probability. Ultimately, we arrive at the following outcome.

#### Lemma 10.

Recall $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}>0$ from the definition of $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ . We have the stochastic domination estimate

$$ \displaystyle\max_{t\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}|}{W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\prec W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}. $$

#### Proof.

Recall $dM_{t}(z)$ from Lemma 6; using this, we write

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z) \displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}(z)\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}(z)\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)}\odot G_{s}(z)\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\} \displaystyle=:\mathcal{E}^{M,1}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{M,2}_{t}(z). $$

We will control $\mathcal{E}^{M,1}_{t}(z)$ ; bounds for $\mathcal{E}^{M,2}_{t}(z)$ follow by the same argument. We further split

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{M,1}_{t}(z) \displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{2}\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Theta_{t} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Theta_{t} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]S^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle=:\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{M,12}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{M,13}_{t}(z)+\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z). $$

We now claim that for any indices $a,b$ , we have the deterministic estimate

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-\frac{3}{2}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}\cdot W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1},\quad j=1,2,3,4, $$

where the square brackets on the RHS mean quadratic variation. This, along with standard martingale arguments, will complete the proof, as we explain now. By the BDG inequality, since $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ is a stopping time, for any $p\geq 1$ finite and indices $a,b$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}|^{2p}\leq C_{p}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}]^{p},\quad j=1,2,3,4, $$

where the square brackets on the RHS indicate quadratic variation. Thus, by the Chebyshev inequality, we have $\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}|\geq N^{\delta}[\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}]^{1/2})\leq C_{p}N^{-2p\delta}$ for any $\delta>0$ and $p\geq 1$ . By (3.14), we then get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)_{ab}|}{W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\prec W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}. $$

A union bound allows us to put a maximum over all indices $a,b$ and over all $t\in[0,1]\cap W^{-D}\mathbb{Z}$ for any $D>0$ fixed. Next, we control entries of $G_{s}(z)$ using its Frobenius norm, for example. Since the operator norm of $G_{s}(z)$ is $\mathrm{O}(|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1})$ , we get the crude bound $|G_{s}(z)_{ij}|\lesssim N|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}\lesssim W^{4}$ (recall that $\mathrm{Im}w_{s}\geq\mathrm{Im}w_{1}=\eta\gg W^{-3/4}$ and $N\ll W^{11/8}$ ). This controls the stochastic integrand in $\mathcal{E}^{M,1j}_{t}(z)$ by $W^{C}$ for some $C=\mathrm{O}(1)$ , so we can then use a standard Hölder continuity argument for stochastic integrals to upgrade the supremum over $t\in[0,1]\cap W^{-D}\mathbb{Z}$ to a supremum over $t\in[0,1]$ (assuming $D>0$ is large enough but independent of $W$ ). The desired bound (3.8) then follows, so we are left to prove (3.14).

Throughout this argument, for convenience, we will denote $G_{xy}:=G_{s}(z)_{xy}$ for any indices $x,y$ . We start with $j=1$ . In this case, we directly compute as follows (note that $\Theta_{t},S^{1/2}$ commute):

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{4}\sum_{x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime},u,v}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{yb}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{y^{\prime}b}ds. $$

For any $u$ -index, we define the following matrices with indices parameterized by $y,y^{\prime}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Upsilon^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{v}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{yb}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{y^{\prime}b}, \displaystyle\Omega^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}}. $$

In this notation, we have

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{4}\sum_{u}\sum_{y}(\Omega^{u}\Upsilon^{u,\ast})_{yy}ds. $$

We now note that $\Omega^{u}$ is a positive-semidefinite matrix; this can be readily verified by the observation that $\Omega^{u}$ has the form $G^{\ast}\mathcal{Q}GG^{\ast}\mathcal{Q}G$ , where $\mathcal{Q}$ is a diagonal matrix with entries $\mathcal{Q}_{ij}=\delta_{ij}(\Theta_{t}S^{1/2})_{ai}$ . By the von Neumann trace inequality, we can therefore bound the sum over $y$ by $\|\Upsilon^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sum_{y}\Omega^{u}_{yy}$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}]\leq\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{4}\sum_{u}\|\Upsilon^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sum_{y}\Omega^{u}_{yy}ds. $$

First, we estimate as follows, in which $S^{u}$ is the diagonal matrix $S^{u}_{ij}=\delta_{ij}S_{ui}=\mathrm{O}(W^{-1})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|\Upsilon^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\|G^{\ast}S^{u}G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-2}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}. $$

Next, if we let $|G|^{2}=GG^{\ast}$ and $|G|^{4}=|G|^{2}|G|^{2}$ , then we claim that the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{u,y}\Omega^{u}_{yy} \displaystyle=\sum_{u,y,x,x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\sum_{u,x,x^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}}G_{xu}|G|^{2}_{x^{\prime}x}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u} \displaystyle=\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}}|G|^{2}_{xx^{\prime}}|G|^{2}_{x^{\prime}x} \displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}|^{2}|G|^{2}_{xx^{\prime}}|G|^{2}_{x^{\prime}x}+2\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax^{\prime}}|^{2}|G|^{2}_{xx^{\prime}}|G|^{2}_{x^{\prime}x} \displaystyle=4\sum_{x}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}|^{2}|G|^{4}_{xx}\lesssim|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}\max_{k}\mathrm{Im}G_{kk}\sum_{x}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ax}|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{3}{2}}, $$

The first three lines follow by matrix multiplication. The fourth line follows by Schwarz; for this, note that since $|G|^{2}$ is Hermitian, we have that $|G|^{2}_{xx^{\prime}}|G|^{2}_{x^{\prime}x}=||G|^{2}_{xx^{\prime}}|^{2}$ is non-negative. The fifth line follows by matrix multiplication and $|G|^{4}_{xx}\leq|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}\max_{k}\mathrm{Im}G_{kk}$ (i.e. Ward). The last inequality uses $s\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ in the quadratic variation, so that $|G_{kk}|$ -terms are all $\mathrm{O}(W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}})$ . In the last inequality, we also use the bounds $\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t})_{\alpha\beta}|\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_{\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{1/2})_{\alpha\beta}|\lesssim|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ (see Lemma 23). By the previous three displays, and recalling from the proof of Lemma 9 that $(t-s)\lesssim|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}]\lesssim\int_{0}^{t}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{3}{2}}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}ds. $$

Again, as in the proof of Lemma 9, we can change variables $\sigma=|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|$ to get

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}]\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{3}{2}}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\int_{\mathrm{Im}w_{t}}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}\sigma^{-1}\lesssim W^{-4+\delta+\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{5}{2}}, $$

where the last bound follows since $\log|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\lesssim\log\eta^{-1}\lesssim W^{\delta}$ for any $\delta>0$ and $\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\lesssim W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ and $|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|=\mathrm{O}(1)$ . (For these latter two bounds, see Lemma 23 and note that $\mathrm{Im}w_{t}=\eta+(1-t)\mathrm{Im}m(z)\lesssim 1$ .) If $\delta,\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}$ are small enough, the previous display immediately gives (3.7) for $j=1$ .

We now move to $j=3$ . The idea again is the same. First, we compute

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,13}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{2}\sum_{x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime},u,v}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{yb}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{y^{\prime}b}ds. $$

We now consider the following matrices for any $u$ , which are indexed by $y,y^{\prime}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Upsilon^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{v}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{yb}(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{y^{\prime}b}, \displaystyle\Xi^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax^{\prime}}. $$

The matrix $\Upsilon^{u}$ is the same as in our analysis for $j=1$ , and $\Xi^{u}$ is the same as $\Omega^{u}$ but dropping the $\Theta_{t}$ matrices therein. With this notation, as in our estimates for $[\mathcal{E}^{M,11}_{t}(z)_{ab}]$ (see (3.15), (3.16), and (3.17)), we have the following (note that $\Xi^{u}$ is also positive-semidefinite):

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,13}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{2}\sum_{u}\|\Upsilon^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sum_{y}\Xi^{u}_{yy}ds \displaystyle\leq W^{-1}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}(t-s)^{2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-2}\sum_{u,y}\Xi^{u}_{yy}ds. $$

To control the remaining summation over $u,y$ , we follow exactly the calculation from (3.18)-(3.23). The only difference is that all $\Theta_{t}S^{1/2}$ -matrices are replaced by $S^{1/2}$ . In particular, we can copy (3.18)-(3.22) verbatim, and then we can use that $S^{1/2}_{ab}=\mathrm{O}(W^{-1})$ and $\sum_{b}S^{1/2}_{ab}=\mathrm{O}(1)$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{u,y}\Xi^{u}_{yy} \displaystyle\lesssim|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}\max_{k}\mathrm{Im}G_{kk}\sum_{x}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}|^{2}\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}. $$

Combining the last two displays and using the change-of-variables $\sigma=\mathrm{Im}w_{s}$ (as in (3.24) and (3.25)) gives

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,13}_{t}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-2}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-5}ds \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-2}\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\int_{\mathrm{Im}w_{t}}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}\sigma^{-3}d\sigma \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-2}W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}, $$

where the last line again uses $\max_{\alpha,\beta}|(\Theta_{t}S^{1/2})_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\lesssim W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ (see Lemma 23). If we take $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}>0$ small enough, then the last line of the above display is $\ll W^{-3/2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}$ since $\mathrm{Im}w_{t}\geq\eta\gg W^{-3/4}$ (see Remark 3). Thus, (3.14) for $j=3$ follows. The case $j=2$ follows by the exact same argument if we swap $u$ with $v$ indices, and if we swap $(x,x^{\prime})$ with $(y,y^{\prime})$ indices, and if we swap $a$ with $b$ indices.

Thus, we are left with $j=4$ . We will get two bounds on $[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}]$ and interpolate them. For the first bound, we will follow the same strategy as we used for $j=1,2,3$ . To start, we compute

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\sum_{x,x^{\prime},y,y^{\prime},u,v}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{yb}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{y^{\prime}b}ds. $$

Now, define the following matrices for any $u$ , which are indexed by $y,y^{\prime}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{v}S_{uv}G_{vy}\overline{G}_{vy^{\prime}}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{yb}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{y^{\prime}b}, \displaystyle\Xi^{u}_{yy^{\prime}} \displaystyle:=\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{xy}G_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ax^{\prime}}. $$

In this notation, we have

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\sum_{u,y}(\Xi^{u}\Gamma^{u,\ast})_{yy}ds. $$

Again, we note that $\Xi^{u}$ is positive semi-definite. This implies that $\sum_{y}(\Xi^{u}\Gamma^{u,\ast})_{yy}\leq\|\Gamma^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sum_{y}\Xi^{u}_{yy}$ . Next, analogous to (3.17), we note that $\|\Gamma^{u}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\max_{\alpha,\beta}|S^{1/2}_{\alpha\beta}|^{2}\|G^{\ast}S^{u}G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim W^{-3}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-2}$ . If we combine this paragraph with the previous display and (3.27), then we get

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{t}W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-5}ds \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-4}\int_{\mathrm{Im}w_{t}}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}\sigma^{-5}d\sigma\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-4}. $$

The second line follows again by the change-of-variables $\sigma=\mathrm{Im}w_{s}$ as in (3.25). We now get a second bound on $[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}]$ . Recall $\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)$ from (3.13). Because $S^{1/2}$ is an averaging operator, when we compute estimate the bracket $[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}]$ , we can drop the second $S^{1/2}$ -factor in $\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)$ . (In words, the quadratic variation of an average is bounded above by the average of the quadratic variations because of Schwarz.) So,

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\leq\max_{\alpha,\beta}\left[\left\{\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\overline{G}_{s}(z)\odot\{G_{s}(z)dH_{s}G_{s}(z)\}\right]\right\}_{\alpha\beta}\right] \displaystyle=\max_{\alpha,\beta}\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\sum_{x,x^{\prime},u,v}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\alpha x}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\alpha x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{x\beta}G_{x^{\prime}\beta}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}S_{uv}|G_{v\beta}|^{2}ds. $$

Before time $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ , we can bound $|T_{s}(z)_{xy}|\lesssim|(\Theta_{s})_{xy}|+|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{xy}|\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1/2}$ . Before time $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ , this bound on $|T_{s}(z)_{xy}|$ also gives $\sum_{v}S_{uv}|G_{v\beta}|^{2}\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}S_{u\beta}+W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}[S^{1/2}T_{s}(z)S^{1/2}]_{u\beta}\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}S_{u\beta}+W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1/2}\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1/2}$ since $\mathrm{Im}w_{s}=\mathrm{O}(1)$ . Using this and the previous display, we claim

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\lesssim\max_{\alpha,\beta}\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime},u}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\alpha x}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\alpha x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{x\beta}G_{x^{\prime}\beta}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}ds \displaystyle=\max_{\alpha,\beta}\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}GG^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta}ds, $$

where $S^{1/2,\alpha}_{ij}=\delta_{ij}S^{1/2}_{\alpha i}$ . The second line is a direct matrix multiplication calculation. To show the first line, we note that for any $u$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{x,x^{\prime}}S^{1/2}_{\alpha x}S^{1/2}_{\alpha x^{\prime}}\overline{G}_{x\beta}G_{x^{\prime}\beta}G_{xu}\overline{G}_{x^{\prime}u}=(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}GG^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{uu} $$

which is non-negative since it is a diagonal entry of a covariance matrix. Therefore, in (3.30), we can bound the $\sum_{v}S_{uv}|G_{v\beta}|^{2}$ -term as described after (3.30) without the need to introduce absolute values. Thus, (3.31) follows. We now control the $(\ldots)_{\beta\beta}$ -term in (3.31). By Ward and general operator bounds, we have

$$ \displaystyle(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}GG^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta} \displaystyle=|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}\mathrm{Im}GS^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta} \displaystyle\lesssim|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}\|\sqrt{S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}}\mathrm{Im}G\sqrt{S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-2}(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta}, $$

where $\sqrt{S^{1/2,\alpha}}$ is the matrix square root of $S^{1/2,\alpha}$ . The last line follows by a direct bound on the entries of the diagonal matrix $\sqrt{S^{1/2,\alpha}}$ of $\mathrm{O}(W^{-1/2})$ , as well as the operator norm bound $\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}$ . Next, observe that

$$ \displaystyle(G^{\ast}S^{\frac{1}{2},\alpha}G)_{\beta\beta} \displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\alpha\gamma}|G_{\gamma\beta}|^{2}\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where the second bound is explained immediately after (3.30). If we combine the previous two displays with (3.31), we get

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{t}W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-3}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-3}ds \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\mathrm{Im}w_{t}}^{\mathrm{Im}w_{0}}W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-3}\sigma^{-3}d\sigma\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-3}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}. $$

Again, the last line is by change-of-variables $\sigma=\mathrm{Im}w_{s}$ . We now interpolate the bounds (3.29) and (3.34):

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{E}^{M,14}_{t}(z)_{ab}] \displaystyle\lesssim\sqrt{W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{10}}W^{-4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-4}}\sqrt{W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-3}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-\frac{7}{2}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-3} \displaystyle=W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{5}}W^{-\frac{3}{2}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-2}\cdot W^{-2}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1} $$

This is exactly (3.14) for $j=4$ , so we are done. ∎

The final ingredient is to control the drift $\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)$ . This is more complicated, as it requires integration-by-parts expansions of the integrand. (These expansions, fortunately, are concrete, and only two expansions are needed.) We state the estimate below, and then we defer its proof to a future section.

#### Proposition 11.

We have the stochastic domination estimate

$$ \displaystyle\max_{t\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}|}{W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\prec 1. $$

### 3.2 Basic Green’s function estimates

We now focus on estimates to propagate $\tau_{\mathrm{stop},2}$ . First, we obtain an off-diagonal estimate assuming a weak a priori on-diagonal estimate.

#### Lemma 12.

Fix any $t\in[0,1]$ . Suppose that $\max_{x}|G_{t}(z)_{xx}|\prec 1$ and $\max_{x\neq y}|G_{t}(z)_{xy}|\prec W^{-\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a\neq b}\frac{|G_{t}(z)_{ab}|^{2}}{(S^{1/2}T_{t}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}+S^{1/2}_{ab}}\prec 1. $$

#### Proof.

First, some notation. For any index $\alpha$ , we let $G_{t}(z)^{(\alpha)}:=(H_{t}^{(\alpha)}-w_{t})^{-1}$ , where $H_{t}^{(\alpha)}$ is the minor of $H_{t}$ obtained by removing the $\alpha$ -row and $\alpha$ -column. Also, for convenience, we will denote $G^{(\alpha)}_{xy}:=G_{t}(z)^{(\alpha)}_{xy}$ . We record the following observations from the proof of Lemma 3.7 in [40]:

$$ \displaystyle|G_{xy}|^{2}\prec|G_{xx}|^{2}\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G^{(x)}_{wy}|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim|G_{xx}|^{2}\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xy}|G_{wy}|^{2}+|G_{xy}|^{2}\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wx}|^{2} \displaystyle\prec\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2}+W^{-2\delta}|G_{xy}|^{2}, $$

where the last bound follows by the assumptions $|G_{xx}|\prec 1$ and $\sup_{w\neq x}|G_{wx}|^{2}\prec W^{-\delta}$ . (In principle, every factor of and $S$ -entry above should have a factor of $t$ , since the entries of $H_{t}$ have variance $t$ . But for the sake of an upper bound, we can drop all factors of $t$ .) By the same token, but for $G^{\ast}$ instead of $G$ , for any $w\neq y$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|G_{wy}|^{2} \displaystyle=|G^{\ast}_{yw}|^{2}\prec|G^{\ast}_{yy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}S_{yu}|G^{\ast,(y)}_{uw}|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim|G^{\ast}_{yy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}S_{yu}|G^{\ast}_{uw}|^{2}+|G^{\ast}_{yw}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}S_{yu}|G^{\ast}_{uy}|^{2} \displaystyle=|G_{yy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}|G_{wu}|^{2}S_{uy}+|G_{wy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}|G_{yu}|^{2}S_{uy}. $$

If we now multiply by $S_{xw}$ and sum over all indices $w$ that are not equal to $x$ , then we get the following, where the first line follows by first isolating $w=y$ , where the second line follows by applying the previous display and re-inserting $w=y$ (which does not violate the upper bound being true since the summands are non-negative), and where the rest uses the a priori bounds from the statement of Lemma 12:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2} \displaystyle\prec S_{xy}|G_{yy}|^{2}+\sum_{w\neq x,y}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim S_{xy}|G_{yy}|^{2}+\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{yy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}|G_{wu}|^{2}S_{uy}+\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}|G_{yu}|^{2}S_{uy} \displaystyle\prec S_{xy}|G_{yy}|^{2}+\sum_{w,u}S_{xw}|G_{wu}|^{2}S_{uy}+\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2}\sum_{u\neq y}|G_{yu}|^{2}S_{uy} \displaystyle\prec S_{xy}+\sum_{w,u}S_{xw}|G_{wu}|^{2}S_{uy}+W^{-2\delta}\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2} \displaystyle=S_{xy}+(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{xy}+W^{-2\delta}\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2}. $$

In the previous display, if we move the last term in the last line to the LHS of the first line, then we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{w\neq x}S_{xw}|G_{wy}|^{2}\prec S_{xy}+(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{xy}. $$

Combining this with the first display of this proof gives

$$ \displaystyle|G_{xy}|^{2}\prec S_{xy}+(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{xy}+W^{-2\delta}|G_{xy}|^{2}, $$

which, by moving the last term onto the LHS, implies $\{S_{xy}+(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{xy}\}^{-1}|G_{xy}|^{2}\prec 1$ . We can now take a union bound over indices to get the desired high probability bound for the maximum over all $x\neq y$ . ∎

Next, we obtain an on-diagonal estimate assuming off-diagonal estimates and weak on-diagonal estimates.

#### Lemma 13.

Suppose that we have the following two a priori estimates for some $\delta>0$ :

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a,b}|G_{t}(z)_{ab}-m(z)\delta_{ab}| \displaystyle\leq W^{-\delta} \displaystyle\max_{a\neq b}|G_{t}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\prec\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{x}|G_{t}(z)_{xx}-m(z)|^{2}\prec\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|+W^{-1}. $$

#### Proof.

We first record an observation from the proof of Lemma 5.3 in [21]. By (5.11) therein and the two displays following it, we have

$$ \displaystyle|G_{xx}-m|^{2}\prec\left|\sum_{k\neq x}\left(|H_{xk}|^{2}-S_{xk}\right)G_{kk}^{(x)}\right|^{2}+\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\neq x\\
k\neq\ell\end{subarray}}H_{xk}G_{k\ell}^{(x)}H_{\ell x}\right|^{2}+\Psi^{4}+M^{-1}, $$

where $M\gtrsim W$ according to (2.10) in [21], and where $\Psi=\max_{a,b}|G_{ab}-m\delta_{ab}|$ as in the statement of Lemma 5.3 in [21]. Now, we use resolvent identities (see Lemma 3.3 in [40]) to get

$$ \displaystyle|G^{(x)}_{k\ell}| \displaystyle\leq|G_{k\ell}|+\frac{|G_{kx}||G_{x\ell}|}{|G_{xx}|},\quad\forall k,\ell. $$

By the a priori assumption $\max_{a,b}|G_{ab}-m\delta_{ab}|\leq W^{-\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$ , along with $|G_{xx}|\gtrsim|G_{xx}-m(z)|+|m(z)|\succ|m(z)|\asymp 1$ , the previous inequality implies that $|G_{k\ell}^{(x)}|\prec 1$ . (For $|m(z)|\asymp 1$ , it suffices to prove that $\mathrm{Im}m(z)\asymp 1$ in the bulk, which can be found in Lemma 6.2 in [22].) Thus, following the proof of Lemma 5.3 in [21], we have the stochastic domination bound

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{k\neq x}\left(|H_{xk}|^{2}-S_{xk}\right)G_{kk}^{(x)}\right|^{2}\prec W^{-1}. $$

The proof of Lemma 5.3 in [21] also gives the following stochastic domination bound:

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\neq x\\
k\neq\ell\end{subarray}}H_{xk}G_{k\ell}^{(x)}H_{\ell x}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\prec\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\neq x\\
k\neq\ell\end{subarray}}S_{xk}|G_{k\ell}^{(x)}|^{2}S_{\ell x} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\neq x\\
k\neq\ell\end{subarray}}S_{xk}|G_{k\ell}|^{2}S_{\ell x}+|G_{xx}|^{-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,\ell\neq x\\
k\neq\ell\end{subarray}}S_{xk}|G_{kx}|^{2}|G_{x\ell}|^{2}S_{\ell x} \displaystyle\lesssim\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|, $$

where the last line uses the a priori off-diagonal estimate for $G_{ab}$ -entries, the lower bound $|G_{xx}|\gtrsim|m|-|G_{xx}-m|$ , the estimate $|m|\asymp 1$ , and the a priori bound $|G_{xx}-m|\leq W^{-\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$ . If we combine the previous two displays with the first display of this proof, then we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle\max_{x}|G_{xx}-m|^{2} \displaystyle\prec\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|G_{ab}-m\delta_{ab}|^{4}+W^{-1} \displaystyle\prec\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|+W^{-\delta}\max_{x}|G_{xx}-m|^{2}+W^{-1}, $$

where the last bound holds by $\max_{a,b}|G_{ab}-m\delta_{ab}|^{4}\lesssim\max_{a\neq b}|G_{ab}|^{4}+W^{-\delta}\max_{x}|G_{xx}-m|^{2}$ and the a priori estimates $\max_{a\neq b}|G_{ab}|\lesssim\max_{a,b}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}TS^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}|+\max_{a,b}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}|$ and $\max_{a,b}|G_{ab}-m\delta_{ab}|\lesssim W^{-\delta}$ . Moving $W^{-\delta}\max_{x}|G_{xx}-m|^{2}$ to the LHS in the previous display gives the desired result. ∎

Notice that $|G_{t}(z)\delta_{ab}-m(z)\delta_{ab}|=0$ at $t=0$ by construction of the matrix flow. In particular, the a priori estimates needed in the previous lemmas are true at $t=0$ trivially, and thus true for short times $t=N^{-C}$ for some large but finite $C>0$ by a deterministic Lipschitz bound on the Green’s function and the $w_{t}$ -flow. Therefore, similar to Corollary 5.4 in [21], we can use a continuity argument and the previous two lemmas to derive the following (in which the $W^{-C}$ term comes from bounding the short-time difference of $G_{t}(z)$ via its Lipschitz norm as discussed above).

#### Corollary 14.

First, let $\mathcal{E}$ be the event where

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a,b}(S^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{t}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{ab}\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}},\quad\forall t\in[0,1]. $$

(Observe that $W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}\ll W^{-5/8}$ by Remark 3.) We have the following estimate for any $C>0$ large but independent of $W$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{1}(\mathcal{E})\max_{t\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|G_{t}(z)_{ab}-m(z)\delta_{ab}|}{(S^{1/2}T_{t}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}+S^{1/2}_{ab}+W^{-C}}\prec 1. $$

### 3.3 Proof of Theorems 8, 2, and 4

#### Proof of Theorem 8.

By union bound, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}\neq 1] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[\{\tau_{\mathrm{stop,2}}\neq 1\}\cap\{\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}=1\}]+\mathbb{P}[\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}=\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}<1]. $$

Note that $\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ is continuous in $t$ with probability $1$ . Thus, on the event in the second probability on the RHS above, we know $|\mathcal{E}_{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}(z)_{ab}|\geq W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-3/4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ for some $a,b$ indices. On the other hand, as we noted prior to Lemma 9, we also know that $\mathcal{E}_{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}(z)=\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{stop}}_{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}}(z)$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}=\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}<1] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\max_{t\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|\mathcal{E}^{M,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)_{ab}|}{W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\geq W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}\right]. $$

By Lemmas 9 and 10 and Proposition 11, we know that the RHS of the previous display is $\leq C_{D}N^{-D}$ for any $D>0$ . Combining this with the previous two displays, it now suffices to show $\mathbb{P}[\{\tau_{\mathrm{stop,2}}\neq 1\}\cap\{\tau_{\mathrm{stop},1}=1\}]\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ , i.e. that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{s\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|G_{s}(z)_{ab}-\delta_{ab}m(z)|^{2}}{(S^{1/2}T_{s}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}+S^{1/2}_{ab}+W^{-D}}\prec 1, $$

assuming that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{t\in[0,1]}\max_{a,b}\frac{|\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)_{ab}|}{W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\lesssim 1. $$

The a priori estimate above implies $T_{t}(z)_{ab}\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ since $T_{t}(z)=\Theta_{t}+\mathcal{E}_{t}(z)$ , and $|(\Theta_{t})_{ab}|\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ (see Lemma 23). Since $S^{1/2}$ is an averaging operator, we also get that $(S^{1/2}T_{t}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}\lesssim W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1/2}$ for all $a,b$ and for all $t\in[0,1]$ . The desired estimate now follows by Corollary 14. ∎

#### Proof of Theorems 2 and 4.

By Theorem 8 and definition of $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ (see (3.5), in which $\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}>0$ is any fixed, small parameter), we know that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a,b}|\mathcal{E}_{1}(z)_{ab}| \displaystyle\prec W^{-\frac{7}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{1}|^{-\frac{3}{2}} \displaystyle\max_{a,b}|G_{1}(z)_{ab}-m(z)\delta_{ab}|^{2} \displaystyle\prec\max_{a,b}(S^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{1}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}))_{ab}+\max_{a,b}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{ab}. $$

Recall $\mathrm{Im}w_{1}=\eta$ and $T_{1}(z)=\Theta_{1}+\mathcal{E}_{1}(z)$ ; since $T_{1}=T$ and $\Theta_{1}=\Theta$ (see the display before Theorem 2), Theorem 2 follows. Using this and Lemma 23 (to bound entries of $\Theta$ ), we deduce $\max_{a,b}T_{1}(z)_{ab}\prec W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{1}|^{-1/2}=W^{-1}\eta^{-1/2}$ . Since $S^{1/2}$ is an averaging operator, we also get $\max_{a,b}(S^{1/2}T_{1}(z)S^{1/2})_{ab}\prec W^{-1}\eta^{-1/2}$ . Since $S^{1/2}_{ab}\lesssim W^{-1}$ , Theorem 4 now follows. ∎

## 4 Bounds on the drift term $\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)$

In this section we prove Proposition 11. The analysis of the drift term $\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)$ requires requires expanding the integrands using Gaussian integration by parts. We use underline notation for the fluctuation term arising from the integration by parts.

#### Definition 15.

Consider a differentiable function $f:{\mathbb{C}}^{N^{2}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}$ and a time $s\in[0,1]$ . Given an expression $H_{s,\alpha\beta}f(G_{s}(z))$ , for some $\alpha,\beta\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ , we define the renormalization of this expression as

$$ \underline{H_{s,\alpha\beta}f(G_{s}(z))}=H_{s,\alpha\beta}f(G_{s}(z))-sS_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{H_{s,\beta\alpha}}f(G_{s}(z)). $$

The renormalization operation extends linearly to the linear combinations of the terms $H_{s,\alpha\beta}f(G_{s}(z))$ .

In the following lemma we provide the two operations on the resolvent expressions that will be needed.

#### Lemma 16.

Consider a differentiable function $f:{\mathbb{C}}^{N^{2}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}$ and fix a time $s\in[0,1]$ . Define a deterministic matrix $B_{s}=(I-sm(z)^{2}S)^{-1}$ and let $m:=m(z)$ . Then we have two identities.

- • (Loop expansion) For any $v\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ , we have $\displaystyle(G_{s}(z)_{vv}-m)f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle=sm\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{N}B_{v\alpha}S_{\alpha\beta}(G_{s}(z)_{\alpha\alpha}-m)(G_{s}(z)_{\beta\beta}-m)f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle-sm\sum_{\alpha\beta=1}^{N}B_{v\alpha}S_{\alpha\beta}G_{s}(z)_{\beta\alpha}\partial_{H_{s,\beta\alpha}}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle-m\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N}B_{v\alpha}\underline{(H_{s}G_{s}(z))_{\alpha\alpha}f(G_{s}(z))}.$

- • (Regular vertex expansion) For any $x,y,u\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ $\displaystyle G_{s}(z)_{xu}G_{s}(z)_{uy}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle=mB_{uy}G_{s}(z)_{xy}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle+sm\sum_{\alpha\beta=1}^{N}B_{u\alpha}S_{\alpha\beta}G_{s}(z)_{x\alpha}(G_{s}(z)_{\beta\beta}-m)G_{s}(z)_{\alpha y}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle+sm\sum_{\alpha\beta=1}^{N}B_{u\alpha}S_{\alpha\beta}G_{s}(z)_{x\beta}(G_{s}(z)_{\alpha\alpha}-m)G_{s}(z)_{\beta y}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle-sm\sum_{\alpha\beta=1}^{N}B_{u\alpha}S_{\alpha\beta}G_{s}(z)_{x\alpha}G_{s}(z)_{\beta y}\partial_{H_{s,\beta\alpha}}f(G_{s}(z))$ $\displaystyle-m\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N}B_{u\alpha}\underline{G_{s}(z)_{x\alpha}(H_{s}G_{s}(z))_{\alpha y}f(G_{s}(z))}.$

#### Proof.

The loop expansion was obtained in Lemma 3.5 of [38], and the regular vertex expansion – in Lemma 3.14 of [38] in case $s=1$ . Using those results for a band matrix with variance profile $sS$ , extends the expansions to any fixed $s\in[0,1]$ . Note also that, while [38] considers the high-dimensional band matrices, the results of lemmas 3.5 and 3.14 are identities and their proofs are independent of dimension. ∎

For a clearer presentation, we now introduce diagrammatic notation.

#### Definition 17.

Given a standard oriented graph, we will assign it the following structures.

- • Vertices in the graph will be given a label (e.g. $\alpha\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ ).

- • For a vertex $\alpha$ , the symbol $\Delta$ denotes a factor of $G_{s}(z)_{\alpha\alpha}-m(z)$ .

- • A solid edge from vertex $\alpha$ to vertex $\beta$ represents a factor of either $G_{s}(z)_{\alpha\beta}$ or $\overline{G}_{s}(z)_{\alpha\beta}$ . The former will be given to blue edges, and the latter will be assigned to red edges.

- • A waved edge from vertex $\alpha$ to vertex $\beta$ , if given a neutral black color, indicates a factor of $S_{\alpha\beta}$ . A waved edge that is blue corresponds to a factor $(B_{s})_{\alpha\beta}$ from Lemma 16.

- • An edge that is denoted by a double line corresponds to a factor of $\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{1/2}$ .

- • If a vertex denoted by $\alpha$ has degree at least $2$ or a hollow $\Delta$ , then we will sum over all $\alpha\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ .

Let us illustrate this with an example. Recall $\mathcal{E}^{D,\mathrm{stop}}_{t}(z)$ from (3.6), and take its integrand at time $s$ . Upon recalling $\Omega_{s}(z)$ therein from Lemma 6, we have that

$$ \displaystyle[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}\Omega_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}]_{ab} \displaystyle=\sum_{x,u,v,y}[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{ax}\overline{G}_{s}(z)_{xy}G_{s}(z)_{xu}S_{uv}[G_{s}(z)_{vv}-m(z)]G_{s}(z)_{uy}[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{yb} \displaystyle+\sum_{x,u,v,y}[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{ax}G_{s}(z)_{xy}\overline{G}_{s}(z)_{xu}S_{uv}[\overline{G}_{s}(z)_{vv}-\overline{m(z)}]\overline{G}_{s}(z)_{uy}[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{yb} $$

is equal to the sum of the graph below and its complex conjugate.

$$ a x u y b v $$

We now use Lemma 16 to unfold the graph in (4.2) further. We note that for any $\alpha,\beta$ indices, resolvent perturbation gives us $\partial_{H_{\beta\alpha}}G_{xy}=-G_{x\beta}G_{\alpha y}$ and $\partial_{H_{\beta\alpha}}\overline{G}_{xy}=-\overline{G}_{x\alpha}\overline{G}_{\beta y}$ , where $G$ is the resolvent of $H$ . Thus, by Lemma 16 applied to the vertex $v$ in (4.2) and $f(G_{s}(z))$ equal to the rest of the graph, the above graph admits the following decomposition.

#### Lemma 18.

Fix any $s\in[0,1]$ and any indices $a,b$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle=\mathcal{G}_{1,s}(z)_{ab}+sm(z)\mathcal{G}_{2,s}(z)_{ab}+sm(z)\mathcal{G}_{3,s}(z)_{ab}+sm(z)\mathcal{G}_{4,s}(z)_{ab}+\mathcal{F}_{0,s}(z)_{ab}. $$

The term $\mathcal{F}_{0,s}(z)$ is the fluctuation below:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{0,s}(z)_{ab} \displaystyle=-m(z)\sum_{x,u,v,y,\alpha}B_{v\alpha}\underline{(H_{s}G_{s}(z))_{\alpha\alpha}f(G_{s}(z))}, \displaystyle f(G) \displaystyle:=[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{ax}G_{xy}\overline{G}_{xu}S_{uv}\overline{G}_{uy}[\{\mathrm{Id}+(t-s)\Theta_{t}\}S^{\frac{1}{2}}]_{yb} $$

Moreover, $\mathcal{G}_{1,s}(z)_{ab},\ldots,\mathcal{G}_{4,s}(z)_{ab}$ are given by the following graphs:

$$ \mathcal{G}_{1,s}(z)_{ab}= a x u y b \alpha \beta v $$

$$ \mathcal{G}_{2,s}(z)_{ab}= a x u y b \alpha \beta v $$

$$ \mathcal{G}_{3,s}(z)_{ab}= a x u y b \alpha \beta v $$

$$ \mathcal{G}_{4,s}(z)_{ab}= a x u y b \alpha \beta v $$

We will now apply the regular vertex expansion from Lemma 16 to each of the graphs $\mathcal{G}_{j,s}(z)$ for $j=1,2,3,4$ from Lemma 18. In particular, each said graph has a vertex $u$ with one incoming and one outgoing blue edge; this is where we expand. The expression we obtain is given in the following lemma. (In what follows, we describe the relevant graphs with words. We illustrate them as pictures when we analyze them in the proofs of Lemmas 20, 21, and 22.)

#### Lemma 19.

Fix $s\in[0,1]$ , indices $a,b\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ and $i\in\llbracket 1,4\rrbracket$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{i,s}(z)_{ab}=m(z)\mathcal{G}_{i0,s}(z)_{ab}+sm(z)\sum_{j=1}^{2}\mathcal{G}_{ij,s}(z)_{ab}-sm(z)\mathcal{G}_{i3,s}(z)_{ab}-m(z)\mathcal{F}_{i,s}(z)_{ab}, $$

where the fluctuation term $\mathcal{F}_{i,s}(z)_{ab}$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}_{i,s}(z)_{ab}$ by replacing the outgoing blue $G_{s}(z)$ -edge from vertex $u$ by $H_{s}G_{s}(z)$ and renormalizing, i.e. applying the underline operation. The main term $\mathcal{G}_{i0,s}(z)_{ab}$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}_{i,s}(z)_{ab}$ by removing the two blue edges $G_{s}(z)_{\xi u}$ and $G_{s}(z)_{u\zeta}$ going through $u$ and replacing them with $G_{\xi\zeta}$ and $B_{u\zeta}$ . The other three main terms introduce two new vertices $\gamma,\delta$ where $\gamma$ is connected to $u$ by a blue waved edge, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are connected by a black waved edge. The the two blue edges $G_{s}(z)_{\xi u}$ and $G_{s}(z)_{u\zeta}$ going through $u$ are removed. The new $G$ -edges are added as follows.

- • In the term $\mathcal{G}_{i1,s}(z)_{ab}$ , add $G_{s}(z)_{\xi\gamma}$ , $G_{s}(z)_{\gamma\zeta}$ and a blue hollow $\Delta$ at the vertex $\delta$ .

- • In the term $\mathcal{G}_{i2,s}(z)_{ab}$ , add $G_{s}(z)_{\xi\delta}$ , $G_{s}(z)_{\delta\zeta}$ and a blue hollow $\Delta$ at the vertex $\gamma$ .

- • In the term $\mathcal{G}_{i3,s}(z)_{ab}$ , add $G_{s}(z)_{\xi\gamma}$ , $G_{s}(z)_{\delta\zeta}$ . Additionally, in this term we apply a derivative $\partial_{H_{s,\gamma,\delta}}$ to all other blue or red edges. This results in a sum of three more graphs, where each remaining $G$ -edge is split in two and reattached to vertices $\gamma$ and $\delta$ .

We now give two lemmas. The first controls the graphs $\mathcal{G}_{ij,s}(z)_{ab}$ for $j=0,1,2$ , and the second controls $\mathcal{G}_{i3,s}(z)_{ab}$ .

#### Lemma 20.

Recall $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ from (3.5), and recall that $N\ll W^{11/8}$ . We have the deterministic estimate

$$ \displaystyle\max_{a,b}\max_{i=1,\ldots,4}\max_{j=0,1,2}\left|\int_{0}^{\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}\wedge t}\mathcal{G}_{ij,s}(z)_{ab}ds\right| \displaystyle\lesssim W^{-\frac{3}{4}}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-1}\cdot W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{t}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

We start with a few preliminaries. Recall that $T_{s}(z)=\Theta_{s}+\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)$ , and recall $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ from (3.5). With this, for any $s\in[0,\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}]$ , we have the following, where the last line below is a consequence of the fact that $S^{1/2}$ is an averaging operator:

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{x}\sum_{y}|G_{s}(z)_{xy}|\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}\sup_{x}\sum_{y}|(S^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{s}(z)S^{\frac{1}{2}})_{xy}|^{\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}\sup_{x}\sum_{y}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{xy}|^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\left\{\sum_{\gamma,\delta}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{x\gamma}(\Theta_{s})_{\gamma\delta}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\delta y}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\left\{\sum_{\gamma,\delta}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{x\gamma}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{\gamma\delta}|S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\delta y}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}W^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\lesssim W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\left\{\sum_{\gamma,\delta}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{x\gamma}(\Theta_{s})_{\gamma\delta}S^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\delta y}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}N\max_{\gamma,\delta}|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{\gamma\delta}|^{\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}}{20}}W^{\frac{1}{2}} $$

We now use $(S^{1/2}\Theta_{s}S^{1/2})_{xy}\lesssim W^{-1+\delta}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1/2}\exp\{-{K}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{1/2}W^{-1-\varepsilon}|x-y|_{N}\}+\exp\{-W^{\varepsilon}\}$ , where we recall that $|\cdot|_{N}$ is the periodic distance on $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ . This holds for any $\varepsilon,\delta,K>0$ fixed (see Lemma 24). We also use that for any $s\leq\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ , we have $|\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)_{\gamma\delta}|\lesssim W^{\delta_{\mathrm{stop}}/10}W^{-3/4}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1}W^{-1}|\mathrm{Im}w_{s}|^{-1/2}$ . Plugging these into the above implies the following (for a possibly different but still small $\varepsilon>0$ ):

where the last line follows by Lemma 23 and a priori bounds for $\mathcal{E}_{s}(z)$ before $\tau_{\mathrm{stop}}$ . We now prove (4.4) for $j=0$ . The graphs at hand are
