## 1 Introduction

Eigenvector statistics of random matrix ensembles have been extensively studied in random matrix theory. In the case of Hermitian random matrices, which can be viewed as Hamiltonians of disordered quantum systems, the Quantum Unique Ergodicity (QUE) conjecture [34] asserts that their eigenvectors tend to be distributed uniformly on a sphere. For Gaussian orthogonal and Gaussian unitary ensembles this statement is trivially correct due to their invariance under multiplication by orthogonal and unitary matrices respectively. A great deal of work has been done to show that the behavior of the eigenvectors of (generalized) Wigner ensemble is consistent with QUE: delocalization of eigenvectors [21], asymptotic normality and independence of finitely many deterministic projections of eigenvectors [9, 30], the size and normality of other eigenvector statistics [14, 16, 6, 5]. Similar results have been established for other Hermitian ensembles in [10, 8, 1].

In the case of non-Hermitian i.i.d. ensembles, less is known. The delocalization of the eigenvectors has been established in [32, 33, 3, 4, 27, 28]. Some work has been done on the size and distribution of the overlaps $\mathcal{O}_{ij}=\langle u_{j},u_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle$ , where $u_{i},u_{j}$ and $v_{i},v_{j}$ are the right and left eigenvectors of a non-Hermitian i.i.d. matrix $A$ , see e.g. [7, 12, 19]. Overlaps $\mathcal{O}_{ij}$ are of particular interest for the non-Hermitian models as they govern [7, 24] the evolution of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A_{t}$ under the flow $\mathrm{d}A_{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{d}B_{t}$ , where $B_{t}$ is a Brownian motion. In this work we obtain the Gaussianity of the deterministic projections of eigenvectors of $A$ .

The standard process for proving Gaussianity of the eigenvector statistics for a Hermitian ensemble $H$ is the well-known three-step strategy, initially used for the local eigenvalue statistics in [20]:

- 1. Local laws for the resolvent of $H$ ;

- 2. Gaussianity of the eigenvector statistics of a Gaussian divisible ensemble $H_{t}=H+\sqrt{t}B$ , where $B$ is GOE;

- 3. Comparison of the eigenvector statistics of the initial ensemble $H$ and $H_{t}$ .

The key component of this argument is the second step, which is done using the Eigenvector Moment Flow (EMF), first developed in [9]. EMF is derived from the evolution of eigenvectors under the flow $\mathrm{d}H_{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{d}B_{t}$ , where $B_{t}$ is a standard Hermitian Brownian motion. The non-Hermitian analogue of this eigenvector evolution is a lot more complicated, see e.g. [7, 24].

In this paper we take a different approach to the second step of the three-step strategy. Our method is inspired by the supersymmetric approach recently used to prove the universality of local eigenvalue statistics of complex i.i.d. non-Hermitian matrices in the bulk in [29] and extended to the real case in [18, 31]. This method allows us to compute the moment generating functions of the eigenvector statistics of the Gaussian divisible ensemble $A+\sqrt{t}B$ directly through asymptotic analysis of the exact integral formulas for these functions at the time-scale $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ .

Some of the details behind the third step for non-Hermitian matrices are also different from what is done the Hermitian case [25]. As in [29], this comparison is done through Girko’s formula, and this requires translating eigenvector statistics into eigenvalue statistics in some sense. More is explained towards the end of the introduction.

Now we state the main result of this paper.

#### Theorem 1.

Let $A$ be an $N\times N$ complex random matrix with i.i.d. entries satisfying $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}=0$ , $\mathbb{E}\left|A_{ij}\right|^{2}=N^{-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}\left|A_{ij}\right|^{p}\leq C_{p}N^{-p/2}$ . Fix $\epsilon,\tau>0$ , $m_{R},m_{L}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , set $m=m_{R}+m_{L}$ . Consider deterministic points in the complex plane $\left\{z^{0}_{j}=z^{0}_{j}(N)\right\}_{j=1}^{m}\subset\mathbb{C}$ such that $\left|z^{0}_{j}\right|<1-\tau$ for any $1\leq j\leq m$ and $\left|z^{0}_{j}-z^{0}_{k}\right|\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ for any distinct $1\leq j,k\leq m$ . Let $(\lambda_{j},u_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue and the corresponding right eigenvector of $A$ for $1\leq j\leq m_{R}$ and $(\lambda_{j},v_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue and the corresponding left eigenvector of $A$ for $m_{R}+1\leq j\leq m$ . Let $\left\{T_{j}=T_{j}(N)\right\}_{j=1}^{m}$ be a family of deterministic bounded rank matrices with bounded norm. Then for any test function $F\in C_{c}^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{C}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\right)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),\|T_{1}u_{1}\|^{2},\ldots,\|T_{m}v_{m}\|^{2}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2}\right), $$

where $Z=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{N})$ consists of independent Gaussian random variables $Z_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|T_{j}\|_{F}^{2})$ which are independent of $A$ .

Theorem 1 implies convergence in distribution of $\|T_{1}u_{1}\|^{2},\ldots,\|T_{m}v_{m}\|^{2}$ to squares of independent Gaussians. The point of including $\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z_{1}^{0}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z_{m}^{0})$ is to pin down the corresponding eigenvalues near $z_{1}^{0},\ldots,z_{m}^{0}$ . Based on the universality result for local eigenvalue statistics in Theorem 1.2 of [29] (and its proof), we anticipate that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2}\right) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}\mathbb{E}F(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m},Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2})\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})\mathrm{d}w_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}w_{m}, $$

where the expectation in the second line is with respect to $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})=\det\left[\frac{1}{\pi}e^{-\frac{1}{2}(|w_{j}|^{2}+|w_{\ell}|^{2})+w_{j}\overline{w}_{\ell}}\right]_{j,\ell=1}^{m}. $$

(We can assume that $z_{j}^{0}$ converge as $N\to\infty$ by taking a subsequence and observe that the limiting $m$ -point correlation function $\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}$ in Theorem 1.2 of [29] is independent of said limits of $z_{j}^{0}$ .) This should follow exactly from the proof of Theorem 1.2 in [29], but we have stated Theorem 1 in the above way since this argument is not written down.

As mentioned above, the proof of Theorem 1 follows the three-step strategy. The first step is carried out in [3, 17, 15, 12], where the authors establish the local laws for the resolvent of the Hermitization of $A$ :

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}-i\eta&A-z\\
A^{\ast}-\bar{z}&-i\eta\end{pmatrix}^{-1}. $$

In particular, the results we use in our proof are the averaged and isotropic local laws as well as the two-resolvent averaged local laws with possibly different shifts $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ . The second step is covered in Sections 2-6. Here we adapt the method of [29] to access left and right eigenvectors. The first technical aspect of this step is analyzing the resolvents $[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}+Y]^{-1}$ and $[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}+Y]^{-1}$ , where $Y$ is finite rank, Hermitian, and possibly negative. The method of [29] depends crucially on various positivity properties and estimates for the resolvents when $Y=0$ . We must ensure these properties are stable under perturbation by $Y$ ; this is why we require isotropic local laws in addition to the estimates used in [29]. Moreover, when studying multiple eigenvalues, we must also analyze these resolvents after projecting to the orthogonal complement of the span of finitely many eigenvectors. Isotropic local laws for deterministic vectors alone no longer suffice. We must also remove the projection using various perturbations and the concentration estimates in Section 6 of [29] (this is the content of Section 6).

The third step, the comparison between the eigenvector statistics of a general i.i.d. matrix and a Gaussian divisible matrix, is done in Sections 7 and 8. This argument follows the same framework as the eigenvector comparison argument of [25] for the Hermitian matrices. The key novelty of our proof is the approximation of the eigenvector statistics with certain functions of $G^{z}$ in Lemma 21 and Girko’s formula [23]. This approximation relies on the level repulsion estimate for the singular values of $A-z$ in Proposition 23 that we derive using Theorem 2.10 of [19] and Theorem 3.2 of [11]. The rest of the argument is a standard Green function comparison, see e.g. [26].

We denote the standard basis vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ by $\mathbf{e}_{j,m}$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ . Whenever the dimension of the space is clear from the context we omit it and write $\mathbf{e}_{j}=\mathbf{e}_{j,m}$ . We write $\llbracket a,b\rrbracket=\mathbb{Z}\cap[a,b]$ . Given a matrix $X$ , normalized trace of $X$ is $\left\langle X\right\rangle=N^{-1}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}X$ .

## 2 Gaussian divisible matrices

In this section we state the main results for Gaussian divisible matrices. For any $A\in M_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ we define its Hermitization by

$$ \mathcal{H}_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}0&A-z\\
A^{\ast}-\bar{z}&0\end{pmatrix},\,z\in\mathbb{C}. $$

The resolvent of this Hermitization $G_{z}(\eta)=\left(\mathcal{H}_{z}-i\eta\right)^{-1}$ can be written as

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}i\eta\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)(A-z)\\
(A^{\ast}-\bar{z})\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle H_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}. $$

We will now condition on some assumptions on $A$ ; we explain shortly why they hold with probability $1-O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ . Consider $\epsilon_{0}>0$ . We assume that for any $\eta,\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\in[N^{-\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}},10]$ , $\eta^{\ast}=\max\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ and $z,z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z|,|z_{1}|,|z_{2}|<1-\tau$ for some fixed $\tau>0$ , there exist constants $c=c(\epsilon_{0})>0$ and $C=C(\epsilon_{0})>0$ such that

#### A1:

We have

$$ \displaystyle c\eta^{-1}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-1}, \displaystyle c\eta^{-2}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-2}, \displaystyle\left|\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)^{2}(A-z)\right\rangle\right|\leq C\eta^{-1}, \displaystyle c\eta^{-3}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)^{2}\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-3}. $$

For

$$ B_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes I_{N}\text{ or }\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes I_{N} $$

we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle G_{z}(\eta_{1})B_{1}G_{z}(\eta_{2})B_{2}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq C. $$

#### A2:

We have

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}, \displaystyle\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}, \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq\frac{c}{\eta^{\ast}\left(\eta^{\ast}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\right)}. $$

We fix $m$ families of finite rank deterministic matrices $T_{j}$ , where $j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ and $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ . Then matrices $T_{j}T_{j}^{\ast}$ have spectral decomposition

$$ \displaystyle T_{j}T_{j}^{\ast}=\sum_{k=1}^{l_{j}}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}, $$

where $q_{j,k}$ are positive constants and $\{\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\}_{k}$ are deterministic orthonormal vectors for each $j$ . We make the following assumption on $A$ in relation to matrices $T_{j}$ .

#### A3:

For any $\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2}\in\left\{\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}},\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}}\pm\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{2}},\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}}\pm i\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{2}}\right\}_{j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket,k_{1},k_{2}\in\llbracket 1,l_{j}\rrbracket}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}H_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2}\right|\leq C\eta^{-\frac{3}{2}}N^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \displaystyle\left|\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2}\right|\leq C\eta^{-\frac{3}{2}}N^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Let us explain why assumptions A1, A2, A3 hold for i.i.d. matrices $A$ with probability $1-O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ fixed. All of A1 is explained in Section 7 of [29]; see after Lemma 7.1 in [29]. For A2, see (8.3)-(8.5). For A3, see Proposition 29.

Now, following [29], for any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z|<1$ and $t>0$ , we define $\eta_{z,t}>0$ such that $t\langle H_{z}(\eta_{z,t})\rangle=1$ . By (A1.1), we know $ct\leq\eta_{z,t}\leq Ct$ for finite constants $C,c>0$ for all $|z|<1-\tau$ and $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ . (The existence and uniqueness of such $\eta_{z,t}$ for $|z|<1$ and $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ holds by Theorem 1.1 in [29].)

#### Theorem 2.

Suppose $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ for some $\epsilon_{0}>0$ fixed. Let $m_{R},m_{L}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ . For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},u_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and for any $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},v_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ . Assume that there exists $\upsilon>0$ such that $|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}|\geq N^{-1/2+\upsilon}$ for any distinct $j,k\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ and for any distinct $j,k\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ . Let $\{T_{j}\}_{j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket}$ be deterministic, finite-rank matrices. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $\mathfrak{q}>0$ depending only on $T_{1},\ldots,T_{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ such that for all $q_{1},\ldots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}<\mathfrak{q}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}v_{j}\|^{2}] \displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

Above, $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}$ denotes expectation conditioning on $\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ .

The choice $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon}$ can perhaps be improved to $t=N^{-\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}$ , or even $t=N^{-1+\epsilon}$ ; see the end of Section 1 in [29]. For this reason, often in the proof we use only the lower bounds $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ .

Theorem 2 gives joint normality in the large $N$ limit of finitely many components of finitely many left and right eigenvectors (subject to a separation condition on eigenvalues for eigenvectors on the same side, right or left). This is the content of the following result.

#### Corollary 3.

The random vector $(N\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2},N\|T_{k}v_{k}\|^{2})_{j,k}$ converges in distribution to $(Z_{j}^{2},Z_{k}^{2})_{j,k}$ , where $Z_{j}\sim N(0,\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2})$ are independent (here, $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ is the Frobenius norm for square matrices).

#### Proof.

By Theorem 2, it suffices to show that for the above choices of $T_{j}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1}=[1-tq_{j}\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}]^{-1}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})] $$

for small enough $q_{j}>0$ and for some $\kappa>0$ . To this end, we claim

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right] \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-q_{j}q_{j,k}\|\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\|^{2}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right] \displaystyle=[1-tq_{j}\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}]^{-1}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})], $$

where vectors $\mathbf{w}_{j,k}$ and scalars $q_{j,k}$ are defined by (2.1). The second line holds by (A3.1) and $t=\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle$ . It suffices to show the first line. To this end, for any $j$ , define the vectors

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{j,k}=q_{j,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{1/2}\mathbf{w}_{j,k} $$

and let $\{\mathbf{y}_{j,k}\}$ be the collection of orthogonal vectors obtained by Gram-Schmidt applied to $\{\mathbf{x}_{j,k}\}_{k}$ without dividing by the norm. In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\det\left[1-tq_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\right]^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}]^{-1}. $$

By (A1.1) and (A3.1), we know $\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,m}=O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})$ if $k\neq m$ and $C^{-1}t^{-1}\leq|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}|^{2}\leq Ct^{-1}$ for some $C>0$ . It follows by Gram-Schmidt that $\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}=\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}[1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1}. $$

By (A3.1) and $t\geq N^{-1/3+\epsilon_{0}}$ and $t\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle=1$ , we know for some $\kappa>0$ that

$$ \displaystyle tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k} \displaystyle=tq_{j}q_{j,k}\left[\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})\right] \displaystyle=q_{j}q_{j,k}\left[1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})\right]=q_{j}q_{j,k}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})]. $$

In particular, since $q_{j},q_{j,k}\neq 0$ and $|q_{j}|$ is small, this implies that

$$ \displaystyle[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1} \displaystyle=[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}]^{-1}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

The first main step to prove Theorem 2 is the case where $m_{R}+m_{L}=1$ . The second is the case $q_{1},\ldots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}\leq q$ , where we have a priori bounds of the form $\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}]\leq 1$ .

#### Proposition 4.

Suppose $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ for some $\epsilon_{0}>0$ fixed. Let $(\lambda_{1},u)$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and let $T$ be a fixed deterministic finite rank matrix. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $q_{T}>0$ such that for all $q<q_{T}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{1}}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]=\frac{1}{\det[1-tqH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})T^{\ast}T]}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

Let $(\lambda_{2},v)$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and let $T$ be a fixed deterministic finite rank matrix. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $q_{T}>0$ such that for all $q<q_{T}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{2}}\exp[Nq\|Tv\|^{2}]=\frac{1}{\det[1-tq\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{2}}(\eta_{\lambda_{2},t})T^{\ast}T]}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

#### Proposition 5.

Retain the setting of Theorem 2. Then (2.2) holds for all $q_{1},\dots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}\leq 0$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 2.

Proposition 4 implies the term inside the expectation in (2.2) (for small enough $q_{j}$ ) is tight as $N\to\infty$ , and its expectation converges along subsequences to that of its subsequential limits. Proposition 5 identifies these subsequential limits. ∎

## 3 Change of variables

In this section, we prepare the necessary change of variables for multiple left/right eigenvectors. For any positive integer $j$ consider a manifold

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{j}=\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{S}^{N-j}\times\mathbb{C}^{N-j}. $$

We define Householder transformations $R_{j}:\mathbb{S}^{N-j}\to\mathbf{U}(N-j+1)$ via

$$ \displaystyle R_{j}(u) \displaystyle=I_{N-j+1}-2\frac{(\mathbf{e}_{1}-u)(\mathbf{e}_{1}-u)^{\ast}}{\|\mathbf{e}_{1}-u\|^{2}}. $$

Now, define the maps

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{R},\Phi_{j}^{L}:\Omega_{j}\times M_{N-j}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{N-j+1}(\mathbb{C}) $$

given by the data

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{R}(\lambda_{j},u^{(j-1)},w_{j},M^{(j)}) \displaystyle=R_{j}(u^{(j-1)})\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{j}&w_{j}^{\ast}\\
0&M^{(j)}\end{pmatrix}R_{j}(u^{(j-1)}), \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{L}(\lambda_{j},v^{(j-1)},w_{j},M^{(j)}) \displaystyle=R_{j}(v^{(j-1)})\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{j}&0\\
w_{j}&M^{(j)}\end{pmatrix}R_{j}(v^{(j-1)}). $$

Finally, consider a map

$$ \Phi:\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\Omega_{j}\times M_{N-m_{R}-m_{L}}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{N}(\mathbb{C}) $$

given by the composition of several $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ and $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ maps

$$ \Phi=\Phi_{1}^{R}\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{2}^{R}\right)\circ\ldots\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}}^{R}\right)\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}+1}^{L}\right)\circ\ldots\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}+m_{L}}^{L}\right). $$

For brevity we denote the total number of steps by $m=m_{R}+m_{L}$ .

#### Lemma 6.

The Jacobian of $\Phi$ is given by the following:

$$ \displaystyle J(\Phi)=|\Delta(\bm{\lambda})|^{2}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(m)}]|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\Phi$ is the composition of several $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ and $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ maps, we have the chain rule

$$ J(\Phi)=\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}J(\Phi_{j}^{R})\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}J(\Phi_{j}^{L}). $$

We now claim that

$$ \displaystyle J(\Phi_{j}^{R})=J(\Phi_{j}^{L})=\left|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(j)}]\right| $$

for $j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ . For the maps $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ , this holds by Lemma 3.1 of [29]. For the maps $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ , we use Lemma 3.1 in [29] (this lemma holds for left eigenvectors as well, since one can always replace $M^{(j-1)}$ , for which we apply Lemma 3.1 of [29], by its adjoint). It remains to note

$$ \left|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(j)}]\right|=\left(\prod_{k=j+1}^{m}\left|\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{j}\right|\right)\left|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(m)}]\right|. $$

∎

We now apply this transformation to the ensemble $M_{t}=A+t^{\frac{1}{2}}B$ . Since $B$ is Gaussian, the distribution of $M_{t}$ is given by the following density with respect to flat measure on $M_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , the space of $N\times N$ complex matrices:

$$ \displaystyle\rho(M_{t})\mathrm{d}M_{t}=\left(\frac{N}{\pi t}\right)^{N^{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[(M_{t}-A)^{\ast}(M_{t}-A)]\right\}\mathrm{d}M_{t}. $$

Now, by following the computations in Section 4 of [29] and combining them with Lemma 6, we have the following formula, which uses notation $A^{(j)}$ and $b_{j}$ that we define afterwards:

$$ \displaystyle\rho(M_{t})\mathrm{d}M_{t} \displaystyle=|\Delta(\bm{\lambda})|^{2}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(m)}]|^{2} \displaystyle\times\left(\frac{N}{\pi t}\right)^{N^{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[(M_{t}^{(m)}-A^{(m)})^{\ast}(M_{t}^{(m)}-A^{(m)})]\right\} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})u^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}v^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|w_{j}-b_{j}\|^{2}\right\}\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|w_{j}-c_{j}\|^{2}\right\} \displaystyle\times\mathrm{d}\bm{\lambda}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}w_{j}\mathrm{d}M_{t}^{(m)} \displaystyle=:\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{\lambda}}(u,\ldots,u^{(m_{R}-1)},v^{(m_{R})},\ldots,v^{(m-1)},w_{1},\ldots,w_{m},M_{t}^{(m)}) \displaystyle\times\mathrm{d}\bm{\lambda}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}w_{j}\mathrm{d}M_{t}^{(m)} $$

Here, $M_{t}^{(m)}$ is the same as $M^{(m)}$ from above after applying the change-of-variables procedure to $M_{t}$ . The vectors $b_{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{N-j}$ and the matrices $A^{(j)}\in M_{N-j}(\mathbb{C})$ are defined by the identities

$$ \displaystyle R_{j}(u^{(j-1)})A^{(j-1)}R_{j}(u^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}a_{j}&b_{j}^{\ast}\\
c_{j}&A^{(j)}\end{pmatrix}. $$

We clarify that (3.1) holds with the additional adjoint in the third line because the $(m_{R}+1)$ -st through $m$ -th steps are obtained by following Section 4 of [29] but for the adjoint of $A^{(j)}$ instead of $A^{(j)}$ itself. This is because we perform the change-of-variables with respect to the left eigenvector; see the proof of Lemma 6. In the rest of the paper we will be computing expectations of functions of $u^{(j)}$ , $v^{(j)}$ , $w_{j}$ conditionally on $\bm{\lambda}$ . Thus we can integrate out $M^{(m)}$ by following Section 5 of [29] verbatim. Ultimately, we have the following in which $C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}$ depends only on $N,t,\bm{\lambda_{1}}$ (and it may vary from line to line):

$$ \displaystyle\int_{M_{N-2}(\mathbb{C})}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[\lambda_{j}-M_{t}^{(m)}]|^{2}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[(M_{t}^{(m)}-A^{(m)})^{\ast}(M_{t}^{(m)}-A^{(m)})]\right\}\mathrm{d}M_{t}^{(m)} \displaystyle=C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{m}\left[1+O(N^{-\delta})\right]. $$

Here, $V_{j}=I_{2}\otimes u^{(j-1)}$ for $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ and $V_{j}=I_{2}\otimes v^{(j-1)}$ for $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket$ , and $\delta>0$ is fixed. Also, $G_{z}^{(k)}(\eta)$ is the same as $G_{z}(\eta)$ but for the matrix $A^{(k)}$ instead of $A$ . We can also integrate out $w_{j}$ variables because they are Gaussian. In particular, the marginal of $\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{\lambda}}$ after integrating out $w_{j}$ variables and $M_{t}^{(m)}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{\lambda}}(u,\ldots,u^{(m_{R}-1)},v^{(m_{R})},\ldots,v^{(m-1)}) \displaystyle=C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{m} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})u^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}v^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}. $$

Additionally, we introduce the following measures on $\mathbb{S}^{N-j}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{j}(u^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle=K_{j}(\lambda_{j},A^{(j-1)})^{-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})u^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)},\,j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket, \displaystyle\nu_{j}(v^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle=K_{j}(\lambda_{j},A^{(j-1)})^{-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}v^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)},\,j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle K_{j}(\lambda_{j},A^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-j}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})u^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)},\,j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket, \displaystyle K_{j}(\lambda_{j},A^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-j}}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}v^{(j-1)}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)},\,j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket. $$

From Lemma 4.1 of [29], we have

$$ \displaystyle K_{j}(\lambda_{j},A^{(j-1)})=C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{k=1}^{j-1}\left|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]\right|^{-1}(1+O(N^{-\delta})). $$

The measures of the variables $w_{j}$ are Gaussian on $\mathbb{C}^{N-j}$ and given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\omega_{j}(w_{j}) \displaystyle=\left(\frac{N}{\pi t}\right)^{N-j}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|w_{j}-b_{j}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}w_{j}, \displaystyle j \displaystyle\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\omega_{j}(w_{j}) \displaystyle=\left(\frac{N}{\pi t}\right)^{N-j}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{t}\|w_{j}-c_{j}\|^{2}\right\}\mathrm{d}w_{j}, \displaystyle j \displaystyle\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket. $$

The the marginal of $\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{\lambda}}$ after integrating out $M_{t}^{(m)}$ (but not $w_{j}$ variables) is

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\rho}_{\bm{\lambda}}(u,\ldots,u^{(m_{R}-1)},v^{(m_{R})},\ldots,v^{(m-1)},w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}w_{j} \displaystyle=C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\left|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]\right|^{j} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j}(u^{(j-1)})\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j}(v^{(j-1)})\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\omega_{j}(w_{j})\left[1+O(N^{-\delta})\right]. $$

## 4 Proof of Proposition 4

We prove (2.3), since (2.4) follows by the same argument (just replace $A$ by $A^{\ast}$ to make left eigenvectors into right eigenvectors; in particular, this is why (2.4) has $\tilde{H}$ instead of $H$ ). Now, to compute $\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]$ , we use (3.2) and integrate out everything except $u$ (equivalently, set $m=m_{R}=1$ in our application of (3.2)). This gives the formula

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{1}}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]\approx\det[H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{Nq\|Tu\|^{2}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}\|(A-\lambda_{1})u\|^{2}}|\det[V_{1}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})V_{1}]|\mathrm{d}u \displaystyle=e^{\frac{N}{t}\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}}\det[H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]u}|\det[V_{1}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1}})V_{1}]|\mathrm{d}u \displaystyle=:e^{\frac{N}{t}\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}}\det[H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}K_{q}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}|\det[V_{1}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})V_{1}]|\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u), $$

where $\approx$ means true up to a factor of $1+O(N^{-\delta})$ for $\delta>0$ , and where

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]u}\mathrm{d}u, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u) \displaystyle:=K_{q}^{-1}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]u}\mathrm{d}u. $$

Before we can further analyze $K_{q}$ and the other remaining terms, we need a preliminary estimate. For convenience, let us the use the notation $H_{\lambda,q}(\eta):=[(A-\lambda)^{\ast}(A-\lambda)+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1}$ . Note that $H_{\lambda,0,T}(\eta):=H_{\lambda}(\eta)$ . Let us also use the following more general notation, since it will be important for the proof of Proposition 5. For any $j\geq 0$ , recall $A^{(j)}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta) \displaystyle:=[(A^{(j)}-\lambda)^{\ast}(A^{(j)}-\lambda)+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{\lambda,q,T}^{(j)}(\eta) \displaystyle:=[(A^{(j)}-\lambda)(A^{(j)}-\lambda)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1} $$

We also define $H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta):=H_{\lambda,0,T}^{(j)}(\eta)$ and $\tilde{H}_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta):=H_{\lambda,0,T}^{(j)}(\eta)$ . Here, we always assume that $T$ has the same dimension as $A^{(j)}$ , and that $T$ is finite rank.

#### Lemma 7.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ . There exists $q_{T}>0$ such that if $q<q_{T}$ , then for some finite-rank, positive semi-definite Hermitian matrix $Y$ with operator norm $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})=H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}[I+qY]H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Moreover, we have $\langle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})\rangle=\langle H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})\rangle+O(N^{-1})$ . The same is true for $\tilde{H}$ in place of $H$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the claim for $H$ and not $\tilde{H}$ ; for $\tilde{H}$ , again, the same argument applies (just replace $A$ by $A^{\ast}$ ). Also, We first assume $j=0$ ; we comment on general $j$ at the end. Recall $C^{-1}t\leq\eta_{\lambda,t}\leq Ct$ for some $C>0$ . By the Woodbury matrix identity, we have

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})+H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}[t^{-1}q^{-1}-TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}]^{-1}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t}). $$

By (A1.1) and (A3.1), since $T^{\ast}T$ is a finite rank projection with $O(1)$ operator norm, we have $\|TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(t^{-1})$ . Hence, we can choose $q_{T}>0$ such that if $q<q_{T}$ , then the term in square brackets on the RHS is a Hermitian operator that is bounded below by $Cq^{-1}t^{-1}$ . In particular, the second term on the RHS of the above identity has the form $tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})$ with $X$ Hermitian, bounded, and positive, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})+tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\{I+tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

To prove the first estimate, it suffices to show that the second term inside the curly brackets without the factor $q$ has operator norm $O(1)$ . This term is a finite rank, positive operator, so we can bound its operator norm by its trace. This gives

$$ \displaystyle\|tH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle=t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}X \displaystyle\leq t\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}. $$

Again, we use (A1.1) and (A3.1) to get $t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(1)$ . Now use $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ to get the first estimate. For the comparison of normalized traces, we have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle={\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}X \displaystyle=O(1){\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(t^{-1}); $$

the last line holds by $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , by (A1.1), and (A3.1), and by $\eta_{\lambda,t}^{-1}=O(t^{-1})$ . Multiply by $O(N^{-1}t)$ to conclude. For general $j\neq 0$ , the same argument works. Indeed, all we need are

$$ \displaystyle\|TH_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(t^{-1})\quad\mathrm{and}\quad{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(t^{-1}). $$

The former follows from the latter. The latter follows by interlacing (and the corresponding estimate without the $(j)$ superscript). ∎

We proceed to analyze $K_{q}$ . By Lemma 7, we know $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ for a finite, positive constant $C$ . In particular, by Lemma 6.1 in [29], we have

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle=C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p. $$

The two-sided bound $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is used in the proof of Lemma 6.1 of [29] only to guarantee that $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is strictly positive. We now use it to justify the following approximation (see immediately after the proof of Lemma 6.1 in [29]):

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p. $$

By the trace estimate in Lemma 7, we can continue as follows (below, $\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}=O(1)$ ):

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p[1-t\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle]}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\exp\left\{i\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}p\right\}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{N^{1/2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}^{2}}{2N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle}\right\}. $$

The last line follows by Gaussian Fourier transform. The bounds $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ and $\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},q})^{2}\rangle\geq C^{-1}\eta_{\lambda_{1},q}^{-3}$ and $\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}=O(1)$ show that the exponential in the last line is $\approx 1$ . Now, note that if $q\geq 0$ , then $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\geq 0$ , and that if $q\leq 0$ , the reverse inequality holds. This follows by Lemma 7. In particular, $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is always positive or negative semi-definite; it cannot have both positive and negative eigenvalues. Using this, we have the following, where the last line follows by $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ and Lemma 7:

$$ \displaystyle|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}-\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}|\lesssim|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle-\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle|^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\lesssim(\|H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}})|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle| \displaystyle\lesssim\|H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}}||\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle|\lesssim N^{-1}t^{-2}. $$

Because $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ , we also have $\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}\gtrsim\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}\gtrsim t^{-3/2}$ . We deduce from this and the previous display that $\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}\approx\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}$ since $t\ll 1$ . Ultimately, since $\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle$ depends only on $N,t$ (recall that $\lambda_{1}$ is fixed), we have

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle=C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p\approx C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]. $$

We now control the $\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u)$ integration. First, we record the following from Section 6 of [29]:

$$ \displaystyle|\det[V_{1}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})V_{1}]| \displaystyle=\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}(u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u)(u^{\ast}\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u)+|u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})(A-\lambda_{1})u|^{2}. $$

We claim the following concentration estimates:

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(|\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u-t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle|\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}, \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(|\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u-t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle|\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t^{3/2}}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}, \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(|\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})(A-\lambda_{1})u-t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})(A-\lambda_{1})\rangle|\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}. $$

For $q=0$ , these estimates are exactly the content of Lemma 6.2 in [29]. Assuming these estimates hold, we can finish the proof of Proposition 4 by following the calculation after the proof of Lemma 6.3 in [29] (in said calculation, we set $j=1$ , so that Lemma 6.3 in [29] is unnecessary). In particular, this would give

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}|\det[V_{1}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})V_{1}]|\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u) \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}. $$

We can combine the previous display with our computation (4.2) of $K_{q}$ and (4.1) to get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{1}}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]\approx C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}\det[H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]=C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}\det[1-tqH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})T^{\ast}T]^{-1}, $$

where the last identity follows from an elementary resolvent identity. To finish the proof of Proposition 4, it suffices to note that the constant $C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}$ on the far RHS is equal to $1+O(N^{-\kappa})$ for some $\kappa>0$ . This can be verified by plugging in $q=0$ in the above identity.

We now show (4.3)-(4.5). We give details for (4.3); it amounts to adjustments in the proof of Lemma 6.2 in [29]. The other two estimates follow by the same adjustments. We first prove

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u-t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}. $$

The bound (4.3) would then follow by proving the same but replacing $H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ by its negative:

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(-\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u+t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}. $$

As in Lemma 6.2 in [29], this holds by the same argument as the proof of (4.6), so we focus on (4.6). By following the proof of Lemma 6.2 in [29], we eventually apply Markov to the LHS of (4.6). In particular, let $Y$ be a Hermitian, semi-definite matrix. (Any matrix is a linear combination of such matrices $Y$ .) We must control the following for $r>0$ :

$$ \displaystyle m_{Y}(r) \displaystyle=e^{-\frac{rt}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})Y]}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{ru^{\ast}Yu}\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u) \displaystyle=e^{-\frac{rt}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})Y]}e^{\frac{N}{t}\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}}K_{q}^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T-\frac{rt}{N}Y]u}\mathrm{d}u. $$

For the choice of $Y$ which produces (4.6), as in the proof of Lemma 6.2 in [29], we pick $r=N^{-1/2}\log N$ . It turns out by inspection of the proof of Lemma 6.2 in [29] that we always have $r\leq N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2}\log N$ , so the following argument will use only this. Our choices of $Y$ will also always satisfy $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ . As in our computation of $K_{q}$ from earlier, we use Lemma 2.3 in [29] to get

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T-\frac{rt}{N}Y]u}\mathrm{d}u \displaystyle=C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q,r}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p, $$

where $H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}):=[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T-N^{-1}rtY]^{-1}$ . (Technically, for this to apply, we need $H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})>0$ in order to perform a Gaussian integration. This holds by Lemma 7 and the trivial bound $N^{-1}t\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(N^{-1}t)$ .) In fact, this gives $H_{\lambda_{1},q,r}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\gtrsim H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ . In particular, we can again approximate the determinant in the $\mathrm{d}p$ integration by a Gaussian density. It also allows us to restrict to the region $|p|\leq N^{-1/2}t^{3/2}\log N$ . Ultimately,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-ipN\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}p^{2}N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-ipN\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}p^{2}N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p. $$

(The last line follows since $\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle=\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle+O(N^{-1}t^{-2})$ by resolvent perturbation, the bound $N^{-1}t\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(N^{-1}t)$ , and $\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\lesssim\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\lesssim t^{-1}$ ; see Lemma 7. Multiply by $p=O(N^{-1/2}t^{3/2}\log N)$ to get an error inside the exponential of $O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})$ . A similar perturbation shows $p^{2}N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q,Y}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle=p^{2}N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle+O(N^{-\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$ , hence the last line follows.) On the other hand, we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q,r}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})] \displaystyle=\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\det[I-N^{-1}rtH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{1/2}YH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{1/2}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\exp\left\{-{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\log\left[1-N^{-1}rtH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{1/2}YH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{1/2}\right]\right\}. $$

Ultimately, we have

$$ \displaystyle m_{Y}(r) \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}K_{q}^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-ipN\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-\frac{1}{2}p^{2}N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\times\exp\left\{-{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})N^{-1}rtY]-{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\log\left(1-N^{-1}rt[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{-\frac{1}{2}}]\right)\right\}. $$

By our asymptotics for $K_{q}$ from earlier, we deduce

$$ \displaystyle m_{Y}(r) \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}\exp\left\{-{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})N^{-1}rtY]-{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\log\left(1-N^{-1}rt[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{-\frac{1}{2}}]\right)\right\}. $$

The exponential on the RHS is equal to $1$ when we set $r=0$ ; this means $C_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}\approx 1$ . At this point, we can now follow the proof of Lemma 6.2 and use elementary log-inequalities to get

$$ \displaystyle m_{Y}(r) \displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left\{\frac{{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{-\frac{1}{2}}]^{2}}{1-\|N^{-1}rtH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\right\}. $$

We must now control the terms inside the exponential. This is done for $q=0$ in the proof of Lemma 6.2. To inherit the estimates for all $q<q_{T}$ (with $q_{T}>0$ small enough), it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\|\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\lesssim\|\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\lesssim{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})Y\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{\frac{1}{2}} $$

for $\tilde{H}_{\lambda,q}(\eta):=[(A-\lambda)(A-\lambda)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]$ . Both follow by semi-definiteness of $Y$ and $\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq C\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ ; this can be shown by using the exact same proof of Lemma 7 (but with $A-\lambda$ replaced by its adjoint). The bound (4.6) follows, and the proof is finished. ∎

## 5 Proof of Proposition 5

For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ consider the composition of first $j$ Householder transforms

$$ \displaystyle U_{j} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{j}\left(I_{k-1}\oplus R_{k}(u^{(k-1)})\right), \displaystyle\,j \displaystyle\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket; \displaystyle U_{j} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{m_{R}}\left(I_{k-1}\oplus R_{k}(u^{(k-1)})\right)\prod_{k=m_{R}+1}^{j}\left(I_{k-1}\oplus R_{k}(v^{(k-1)})\right), \displaystyle\,j \displaystyle\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket. $$

We start by expressing the finite-rank projections of left and right eigenvectors $u_{j}$ , $v_{j}$ through the integration variables $u^{(j-1)},v^{(j-1)}$ . This is the content of the following lemma.

#### Lemma 8.

Set $\epsilon_{1}=\min\{\epsilon_{0},\upsilon\}$ . Then for $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ we have

$$ \displaystyle|T_{j}|u_{j}=|T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}+\mathcal{O}_{\mu}\left(N^{-\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{1}}\right). $$

For $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket$ we have

$$ \displaystyle|T_{j}|v_{j}=|T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
v^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}+\mathcal{O}_{\mu}\left(N^{-\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{1}}\right). $$

The error terms here are bounded in the sense of stochastic domination, defined below, with respect to the measure $\mu$ , where

$$ \mathrm{d}\mu=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\omega_{j}. $$

#### Definition 9 (Stochastic domination).

Suppose

$$ X=\left\{X_{N}(s):N\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+},s\in S_{N}\right\}\text{ and }Y=\left\{Y_{N}(s):N\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+},s\in S_{N}\right\} $$

are sequences of random variables, possibly parametrized by $s$ . We say that $X$ is stochastically dominated by $Y$ uniformly in $s$ with respect to measure $\mu$ and write $X\prec_{\mu}Y$ or $X=\mathcal{O}_{\mu}(Y)$ if for any $\varepsilon,D>0$ we have

$$ \sup_{S_{N}}{\mathbb{P}}_{\mu}\left(X_{N}(s)>N^{\varepsilon}Y_{N}(s)\right)<N^{-D} $$

for large enough $N$ .

We prove Lemma 8 in section 6, where we collect all technical high probability estimates with respect to the measure $\mu$ . In view of Lemma 8, consider the event $\mathcal{E}:=\cap_{j=1}^{m}\mathcal{E}_{j}$ , where for some $\kappa>0$ small,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{j} \displaystyle:=\left\{\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}=\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}+O(N^{-1-\kappa})\right\}\quad\mathrm{if}\ j\leq m_{R}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{j} \displaystyle:=\left\{\|T_{j}v_{j}\|^{2}=\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
v^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}+O(N^{-1-\kappa})\right\}\quad\mathrm{if}\ j\geq m_{R}+1. $$

By Lemma 8 and a union bound, we know that $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}^{C}}=O(N^{-D})$ for large $D>0$ . Since $q_{j}\leq 0$ for all $j$ by assumption, this gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}v_{j}\|^{2}]\right\} \displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
v^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\right\}+O(N^{-D}), $$

where, as before, $\approx$ means true up to a factor of $1+O(N^{-\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$ . Now use (3.2):

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
v^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\right\} \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}\ldots\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{m} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{(j-1),\ast}\left[(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})+\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}^{2}-tq_{j}T_{j}^{(j-1),\ast}T_{j}^{(j-1)}\right]u^{(j-1)}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)} \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}v^{(j-1),\ast}\left[(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}+\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}^{2}-tq_{j}T_{j}^{(j-1),\ast}T_{j}^{(j-1)}\right]v^{(j-1)}}\mathrm{d}v^{(j-1)}. $$

Above, $T_{j}^{(j-1)}$ is the restriction of $T_{j}U_{j-1}$ to the orthogonal complement of $\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{j-1}$ . For $j\leq m_{R}$ , we set

$$ \displaystyle K_{j,q_{j},T_{j}} \displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-j}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{(j-1),\ast}\left[(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})+\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}^{2}-tq_{j}T_{j}^{(j-1),\ast}T_{j}^{(j-1)}\right]u^{(j-1)}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)}, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}(u^{(j-1)}) \displaystyle:=K_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}^{-1}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{(j-1),\ast}\left[(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})^{\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{j})+\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}^{2}-tq_{j}T_{j}^{(j-1),\ast}T_{j}^{(j-1)}\right]u^{(j-1)}}\mathrm{d}u^{(j-1)}, $$

and for $j\geq m_{R}+1$ , we define

With this notation, we can write

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
v^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\right\} \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}K_{j,q_{j},T_{j}} \displaystyle\times\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}\ldots\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{j}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}(u^{(j-1)})\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}(v^{(j-1)}). $$

#### Lemma 10.

There exists an event $\mathcal{E}$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}}=O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ fixed and such that on $\mathcal{E}$ , we have the following for all $j=1,\ldots,m$ :

u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right\|^{2}\right]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp\left[Nq_{j}\left\||T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\

#### Proof of Lemma 11.

In Lemmas 6.2 and 6.3 of [29], it is shown that there is a decomposition $\mathbb{S}^{N-j}=\mathbb{G}_{j}\cup\mathbb{G}_{j}^{C}$ such that the following hold.

- 1. On $\mathbb{G}_{j}$ , we have $|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{j}\approx C_{N,t,j}$ for some $C_{N,t,j}\gtrsim N^{-\upsilon}$ with $\upsilon=O(1)$ .

- 2. We have $\nu_{j,0,T_{j}}(\mathbb{G}_{j}^{C})=O(N^{-D})$ for any large, fixed $D\geq 0$ . This and $|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|=O(t^{-C})$ for some $C=O(1)$ (along with $t\geq N^{-1})$ give the following for any $D\geq 0$ fixed: $\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{G}_{j}^{C}}|\det[V_{j}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})V_{j}]|^{j}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}(u^{(j-1)})\lesssim N^{-D}$

Thus, it suffices to show that for any $q_{j}\leq 0$ independent of $N$ , we have the inequality of measures $\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}\leq N^{C}\mathrm{d}\nu_{j,0,T_{j}}$ for some $C=O(1)$ (note that $\nu_{j,0,T_{j}}$ has no dependence on $T_{j}$ ).
