u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right|^{2}\prec_{\nu_{j\rightarrow k+1}} \displaystyle\frac{t}{N}u^{(k-1),\ast}\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)R_{k}\left(u^{(k-1)}\right)\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&H^{(k)}_{\lambda_{j}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}\right)\end{pmatrix}R_{k}\left(u^{(k-1)}\right)\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)^{\ast}u^{(k-1)}. $$

We use Lemma 2.1 of [29] and Woodbury’s identity again to get

$$ \displaystyle\left|u^{(k-1),\ast}\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)U_{k,j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\prec_{\nu_{j\rightarrow k+1}}\frac{t}{N}u^{(k-1),\ast}\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)H^{(k-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}\right)\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)^{\ast}u^{(k-1)} \displaystyle+\frac{t\left(u^{(k-1),\ast}\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)H^{(k-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}\right)\left(A^{(k-1)}-\lambda_{j}\right)^{\ast}u^{(k-1)}\right)^{2}}{N\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}^{2}u^{(k-1),\ast}\tilde{H}^{(k-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}\right)u^{(k-1)}} \displaystyle\prec_{\nu_{j\rightarrow k}}\frac{t+|\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{j}|^{2}}{Nt}. $$

This concludes the proof. ∎

Now we are ready to prove Lemma 8.

#### Proof of Lemma 8.

First, we note that if $M^{(j)}$ has eigenvalue $\lambda$ with right eigenvector $\tilde{u}_{j}$ and left eigenvector $\tilde{v}_{j}$ , then $M^{(j-1)}$ also has eigenvalue $\lambda$ with right and left eigenvectors given by

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{u}_{j-1} \displaystyle=R_{j}\left(u^{(j-1)}\right)\begin{pmatrix}\frac{w_{j}^{\ast}\tilde{u}_{j}}{\lambda-\lambda_{j}}\\
\tilde{u}_{j}\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle\tilde{v}_{j-1} \displaystyle=R_{j}\left(u^{(j-1)}\right)\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\tilde{v}_{j}\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle j \displaystyle\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket; \displaystyle\tilde{u}_{j-1} \displaystyle=R_{j}\left(v^{(j-1)}\right)\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\tilde{u}_{j}\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle\tilde{v}_{j-1} \displaystyle=R_{j}\left(v^{(j-1)}\right)\begin{pmatrix}\frac{w_{j}^{\ast}\tilde{v}_{j}}{\lambda-\lambda_{j}}\\
\tilde{v}_{j}\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle j \displaystyle\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket. $$

Using this observation, we can express the left and right eigenvectors of $M$ denoted by $u_{1},\ldots,u_{m_{R}}$ , $v_{m_{R}+1},\ldots,v_{m}$ through $u,\ldots,u^{(m_{R}-1)},v^{(m_{R})},\ldots,v^{(m-1)}$ . For instance, take $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ . We consecutively apply the identities (6.23) to compute the right eigenvectors of $M^{(j-2)},\ldots,M^{(1)},M$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{j}$ . In the end, we get

$$ \displaystyle u_{j}=U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}+\sum_{s=1}^{j-1}\sum_{k=1}^{j-s}\sum_{s=i_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots<i_{k+1}=j}a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})U_{s-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(s-1)}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where the scalar coefficients are given by

$$ \displaystyle a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})=\prod_{n=1}^{k}(\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{k+1}})^{-1}w_{i_{n}}^{\ast}U_{i_{n},i_{n+1}-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(i_{n+1}-1)}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Using Lemma 17 to bound the coefficients $a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle\left|a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})\right|^{2}\prec(Nt)^{-k}\prod_{n=1}^{k}(t+|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|^{2})|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{j}|^{-2}, $$

where $i_{k+1}=j$ . We split the set of indices $I=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}$ into two disjoint subsets $I=I_{1}\cup I_{2}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=\{i\in I:\,|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}|>t^{1/2}\}; \displaystyle I_{2} \displaystyle=\{i\in I:\,N^{-1/2+\upsilon}\leq|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}|\leq t^{1/2}\}. $$

Then

$$ \prod_{n=1}^{k}|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{j}|^{-2}\leq t^{-|I_{1}|}N^{|I_{2}|(1-2\upsilon)}. $$

If $|I_{1}|\geq|I_{2}|$ , we bound each term $(t+|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|^{2})$ in the product above by a constant and write $(Nt)^{-k}=(Nt)^{-|I_{1}|-|I_{2}|}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\left|a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})\right|^{2}\prec N^{-|I_{1}|-2\upsilon|I_{2}|}t^{-2|I_{1}|-|I_{2}|}\leq\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{3}}\right)^{|I_{1}|}=N^{-3|I_{1}|\epsilon_{0}}\leq N^{-\epsilon_{0}}. $$

If $|I_{1}|<|I_{2}|$ , we note that for the distance between to eigenvalues to be larger that $2t^{1/2}$ , at least one of them has to be outside of the set $I_{2}$ , thus

$$ \left|\left\{n\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket:\,|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|>2t^{1/2}\right\}\right|\leq 2|I_{1}|. $$

Then for any $n$ outside of this set we can bound $t+|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|^{2}\leq 5t$ , and for any $n$ in this set $t+|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|^{2}\leq C$ . Then the product is bounded by

$$ \prod_{n=1}^{k}(t+|\lambda_{i_{n}}-\lambda_{i_{n+1}}|^{2})\lesssim t^{k-2|I_{1}|}=t^{|I_{2}|-|I_{1}|}. $$

Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\left|a(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k+1})\right|^{2}\prec N^{-|I_{1}|-2\upsilon|I_{2}|}t^{-3|I_{1}|}\leq N^{-\upsilon}. $$

Plugging these coefficient bounds into (6.25), we get

$$ \displaystyle|T_{j}|u_{j} \displaystyle=|T_{j}|U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(j-1)}\end{pmatrix}+\sum_{s=1}^{j-1}\mathcal{O}(N^{-\epsilon_{1}})|T_{j}|U_{s-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(s-1)}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Here $\epsilon_{1}=\min\{\epsilon_{0},\upsilon\}$ . Now we recall that

$$ |T_{j}|=\sum_{s=1}^{l_{j}}q_{j,s}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}. $$

Thus it remains to show that

$$ \left|\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}U_{s-1}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{(s-1)}\end{pmatrix}\right|\prec N^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

This follows by Corollary 16 and the assumption A3. The proof in the left eigenvector case is similar. ∎

## 7 Proof of Theorem 1

Given Theorem 2, the first step is the following moment matching, which is Lemma 3.4 in [22].

#### Lemma 18.

Fix $\beta>0$ and $t=N^{-\beta}$ . There exists a matrix $\tilde{A}$ such that the following hold.

- 1. The entries of $\tilde{A}$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}\tilde{A}_{ij}=0$ and $\mathbb{E}|\tilde{A}_{ij}|^{2}=N^{-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}|\tilde{A}_{ij}|^{p}\leq C_{p}N^{-p/2}$ .

- 2. Consider $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}=(1+t)^{-1/2}(\tilde{A}+t^{1/2}B)$ , where $B$ is sampled from an independent Gaussian ensemble. Set $m_{k}(i,j)=\mathbb{E}A_{ij}^{k}$ and $\tilde{m}_{k}(i,j)=\mathbb{E}(\tilde{M}_{t})_{ij}^{k}$ . Then for all $i,j$ and $k=1,2,3$ and for some $\delta_{t}>0$ , we have $\displaystyle m_{k}(i,j)=\tilde{m}_{k}(i,j)\quad\mathrm{and}\quad m_{4}(i,j)=\tilde{m}_{4}(i,j)+O(N^{-\delta_{t}})$

- 3. The matrices $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ are independent.

(Condition 2 is sometimes referred to as “matching up to three-and-a-half moments”.) Theorem 1 follows by Theorem 2 and the comparison result below for matrices which match up to three-and-a-half moments.

#### Theorem 19.

Take $\tilde{A}$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ from Lemma 18. Fix positive integers $m_{R},m_{L}$ . Fix deterministic $\left\{z_{j}^{0}=z_{j}^{0}(N)\right\}_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\subset\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z_{j}^{0}|<1-\tau$ for each $j$ and for some $\tau>0$ independent of $N$ . Next:

- • For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},u_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $A$ , and for any $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},v_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $A$ .

- • Similarly, let $(\lambda_{j}(t),u_{j}(t))$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $\tilde{M}_{t}$ for $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ , and $(\lambda_{j}(t),v_{j}(t))$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $\tilde{M}_{t}$ for $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ .

- • For any $j$ , let $T_{j}$ be a deterministic, finite-rank matrix.

- • For any $j$ , write $\lambda_{j}=z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}z_{j}$ and $\lambda_{j}(t)=z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}z_{j}(t)$ .

- • Set $\mathbf{z}=(z_{j})_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ and $\mathbf{T}:=(N\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2},N\|T_{k}v_{k}\|^{2})_{j,k}$ . Similarly, set $\mathbf{z}(t)=(z_{j}(t))_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ and $\mathbf{T}(t):=(N\|T_{j}u_{j}(t)\|^{2},N\|T_{k}v_{k}(t)\|^{2})_{j,k}$ .

For any test function $F\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\times\mathbb{R}^{m_{R}+m_{L}})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{T})=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z}(t),\mathbf{T}(t)), $$

where the expectation is over all the randomness in $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ , respectively.

The rest of this section is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 19. The strategy is based on Girko’s formula, and for this reason, we must express eigenvector statistics in terms of eigenvalues. We start with the following construction.

#### Definition 20.

Fix $\delta_{V}>0$ small, and set $\eta_{V}:=N^{-1-\delta_{V}}$ . Fix any finite-rank matrix $T\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ , and define

$$ \displaystyle V(z,T):=N\eta_{V}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}[T^{\ast}T\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta_{V})]=\sum_{k}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}. $$

Above, $\xi_{k}^{z}$ are eigenvalues of the Hermitization $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ , and $\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}$ are the corresponding eigenvalues. We adopt the convention $\xi_{k}^{z}\geq 0$ for all $k\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ , and $\xi_{k}^{z}=-\xi_{-k}^{z}$ for any $k\in\llbracket-N,-1\rrbracket$ . We also impose $\xi_{k}^{z}\leq\xi_{\ell}^{z}$ for $k\leq\ell$ . The sum on the far RHS of the previous display is over all $k\in\llbracket-N,1\rrbracket\cup\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ .

Fix any right eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs $(\lambda_{1},u_{1}),\ldots,(\lambda_{m_{R}},u_{m_{R}})$ and left eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs $(\lambda_{m_{R}+1},v_{m_{R}+1}),\ldots,(\lambda_{m_{R}+m_{L}},v_{m_{R}+m_{L}})$ . Now, fix $j=1,\ldots,m_{R}$ . Since $(A-\lambda_{j})u_{j}=0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\lambda_{j}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u_{j}\end{pmatrix}=0. $$

Similarly, for any $j=m_{R}+1,\ldots,m_{R}+m_{L}$ , since $u_{j}^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{j})=\lambda_{j}u_{j}^{\ast}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\lambda_{j}}\begin{pmatrix}v_{j}\\
0\end{pmatrix}=0. $$

We now provide the following, which essentially compares $V(\lambda_{j},T)$ to the corresponding eigenvector information we are interested in. We explain its utility afterwards.

#### Lemma 21.

We have

$$ \displaystyle V(z,T)=\sum_{k=\pm 1}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}+\mathbf{1}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{V}/2}\right)\mathcal{O}(1)+\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta_{V}/2}). $$

Above, $\mathcal{O}$ is with respect to the randomness of the matrix $A$ . Now, fix any $j=1,\ldots,m_{R}+m_{L}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle V(\lambda_{j},T)=\sum_{k=\pm 1}N\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\lambda_{j}}\|^{2}+\mathbf{1}\left(\xi_{2}^{\lambda_{j}}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{V}/2}\right)\mathcal{O}(1)+\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta_{V}/2}). $$

#### Proof.

To prove the second claim, we set $z=\lambda_{j}$ and use $\xi_{\pm 1}^{\lambda_{j}}=0$ . To prove the first claim, it suffices to show

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\neq\pm 1}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=\mathbf{1}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{V}/2}\right)\mathcal{O}(1)+\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta_{V}/2}). $$

We first write, for some $c>0$ small and independent of $N$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\neq\pm 1}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|\leq c\end{subarray}}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|>c\end{subarray}}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}. $$

Using the trivial bound $\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|=O(1)$ and $\eta_{V}^{2}=N^{-2-2\delta_{V}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|>c\end{subarray}}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}\lesssim N^{-1-2\delta_{V}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|>c\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\lesssim N^{-2\delta_{V}}. $$

Next, for $|\xi_{k}^{z}|<c$ , we can use delocalization (see Proposition 30) and the finite-rank property of $T$ to get $N\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=O(1)$ ; note that delocalization only holds for bulk singular values in Proposition 30. Now, we write

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|\leq c\end{subarray}}\frac{\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}} \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|\leq c\\
|k|\leq N^{\epsilon}\end{subarray}}\frac{\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|\leq c\\
|k|>N^{\epsilon}\end{subarray}}\frac{\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}. $$

The first term on the RHS is bounded deterministically by $N^{\epsilon}$ . For the second term on the RHS, we use rigidity (Proposition 30) to bound it by $\mathcal{O}(N^{-\epsilon})$ . In particular, this gives $|\xi_{k}^{z}|\geq N^{-1}|k|+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1})\geq\frac{1}{2}N^{-1}|k|$ since $|k|>N^{\epsilon}$ , with which we can bound the second term on the RHS. Since $\epsilon>0$ is arbitrary, we get the a priori bound

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\neq\pm 1}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(1). $$

It remains to show that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{1}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\geq N^{-1-\delta_{V}/2}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|\xi_{k}^{z}|\leq c\end{subarray}}\frac{N\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi^{z}_{k})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta_{V}/2}). $$

We again use $N\|T\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(1)$ and (7.1). By the assumption $\xi_{2}^{z}\geq N^{-1-\delta_{V}/2}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|k|\leq N^{\epsilon}\end{subarray}}\frac{\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta_{V}^{2}}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\neq\pm 1\\
|k|\leq N^{\epsilon}\end{subarray}}\frac{\eta_{V}^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}}\leq N^{-\delta_{V}+\epsilon}. $$

Also, we can again use rigidity to show the second term on the RHS of (7.1) is $\mathcal{O}(N^{-\epsilon})$ . Now choose $\epsilon=\delta_{V}/2$ to conclude. ∎

If we choose $T$ appropriately, then our computations before Lemma 21 show that $N\|T\mathbf{u}_{\pm 1}^{\lambda_{j}}\|^{2}=N\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}$ for $j\leq m_{R}$ , and $N\|T\mathbf{u}_{\pm 1}^{\lambda_{j}}\|^{2}=N\|T_{j}v_{j}\|^{2}$ for $j\geq m_{R}+1$ . We expand on this more later when it is more relevant. First, we present the following technical result, which is important to various estimates in the proof of Theorem 19.

#### Lemma 22.

Fix Hermitian $T\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ , and assume $\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ . Fix $\eta\leq N^{-1}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{|z|\leq 1-\tau}|\nabla_{z}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}(\eta)| \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-\frac{3}{2}}\eta^{-2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}), \displaystyle\sup_{|z|\leq 1-\tau}|\nabla_{z}^{2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}(\eta)| \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2}\eta^{-3}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}). $$

The $\mathcal{O}$ is with respect to randomness of $A$ . In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{z}^{m}V(z,T) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1-m/2}\eta_{V}^{-1-m}),\quad m=1,2. $$

#### Proof.

By union bound over a very fine net and elementary resolvent bounds for $G_{z}(\eta)$ , it is enough to prove the proposed bounds for a fixed deterministic $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ . We first write (for some $c>0$ small and independent of $N$ )

$$ \displaystyle G_{z}(\eta):=G+\widehat{G}:=\sum_{\alpha:|\xi_{\alpha}^{z}|\leq c}\frac{\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{\ast}}{\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta}+\sum_{\alpha:|\xi_{\alpha}^{z}|>c}\frac{\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{\ast}}{\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta} $$

Bounds for $|\nabla_{z}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}T\widehat{G}|$ and $|\nabla_{z}^{2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}T\widehat{G}|$ are simple to establish since $\|\widehat{G}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ . Thus, we prove bounds for $|\nabla_{z}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG|$ and $|\nabla_{z}^{2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG|$ . The advantage of this decomposition is the use of delocalization estimates (Proposition 30) for all relevant eigenvectors.

Fix any $Y,Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\{E_{12},E_{21}\}$ , where $E_{12}$ and $E_{21}$ are the $2N\times 2N$ block matrices

$$ \displaystyle E_{12}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{N}\\
0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad E_{21}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
I_{N}&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

By resolvent perturbation identities, it suffices to prove

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}GTGY \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-3/2}\eta^{-2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}),, \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}GTGY_{1}GY_{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-2}\eta^{-3}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}). $$

Now, for any vectors $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$ and any matrix $X$ , we write $X_{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}}:=\mathbf{u}^{\ast}X\mathbf{v}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}GTGY \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\frac{T_{\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}}Y_{\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}}}{(\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\beta}^{z}-i\eta)}. $$

By Proposition 30 applied to $\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}$ , because $T$ is deterministic and Hermitian, we have $|T_{\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}}|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T})$ . By Proposition 31, we also have $|Y_{\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}}|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}+\delta_{|\alpha|=|\beta|}N^{-1}|\alpha|)$ . If we plug these bounds into the previous display and use rigidity of $\xi_{\alpha}^{z}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|{\operatorname{Tr}\,}GTGY| \displaystyle=N^{-1}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}\mathcal{O}\left(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\frac{N^{-\frac{1}{2}}+|\xi_{\alpha}^{z}|\delta_{|\alpha|=|\beta|}}{(\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\beta}^{z}-i\eta)}\right)=\mathcal{O}(N^{-3/2}\eta^{-2}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}). $$

(The last estimate also uses rigidity of $\xi_{\alpha}^{z}$ .) This proves (7.5). To show (7.6), we similarly have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}GTGY_{1}GY_{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\frac{T_{\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}}(Y_{1})_{\mathbf{u}_{\beta}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\gamma}^{z}}(Y_{2})_{\mathbf{u}_{\gamma}^{z}\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{z}}}{(\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\beta}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\gamma}^{z}-i\eta)} \displaystyle=N^{-1}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\sqrt{T^{\ast}T}\mathcal{O}\left(\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\frac{(N^{-\frac{1}{2}}+|\xi_{\alpha}^{z}|\delta_{|\alpha|=|\beta|})(N^{-\frac{1}{2}}+|\xi_{\beta}^{z}|\delta_{|\beta|=|\gamma|})}{(\xi_{\alpha}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\beta}^{z}-i\eta)(\xi_{\gamma}^{z}-i\eta)}\right), $$

at which point we again use rigidity of $\xi^{z}_{\alpha}$ to conclude (7.6). ∎

We now reduce comparison of $N\|T\mathbf{u}_{\pm 1}^{\lambda_{j}}\|^{2}$ to that of $V(\lambda_{j},T)$ via level repulsion.

#### Proposition 23.

Fix any $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ with $\tau>0$ fixed. If $\delta>0$ is small enough, then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\right)\leq N^{-2.1\delta}. $$

We defer the proof of this to the end of this entire section. The coefficient $2.1$ in the exponent is not important; it just needs to be strictly bigger than $2$ .

Note that Proposition 23 is for fixed $|z|<1$ , whereas we will need it for random $z$ . To this end, we use a net argument; we ultimately conclude the following.

#### Lemma 24.

Fix any $z_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z_{0}|\leq 1-\tau$ with $\tau>0$ independent of $N$ . Choose any $R>0$ independent of $N$ , and let $B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2})\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be the ball of radius $RN^{-1/2}$ around $z_{0}$ . If $\delta>0$ is small enough, then there exists $c=c(\delta)>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\lambda\in\mathrm{Spec}(A)\cap B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2}):\ \xi_{2}^{\lambda}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\right)=O(N^{-c}). $$

#### Proof.

Throughout this argument, we set $\eta=N^{-1-\delta_{1}}$ , where $0<\delta_{1}<\delta$ (and $\delta>0$ will be a small parameter chosen shortly). Let $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be a smooth test function such that

$$ \phi(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\geq 1.9\\
0,&x\leq 1.1\end{cases} $$

For convenience, set $B:=B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2})$ . We claim that for some $c>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]\leq N^{-c}, $$

where the expectation is over randomness of the matrix $A$ . To see that this is enough, we first note

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}\geq\frac{2\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{2}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}+\sum_{k=3}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}. $$

Thus, if there is $z\in B$ for which $\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\ll\eta$ , then on this event, we have

$$ \displaystyle\eta\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 2\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{2}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}\geq 1.9. $$

In particular, since this statement is deterministic in $z$ , we have the bounds

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\lambda\in\mathrm{Spec}(A)\cap B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2}):\ \xi_{2}^{\lambda}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 1.9\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right], $$

at which point we conclude. To prove the remaining estimate (7.8), Let $\mathcal{E}\subseteq B$ be such that the distance between any point in $B$ to $\mathcal{E}$ is at most $N^{1/2-\epsilon}\eta$ , and $|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{2\epsilon+2\delta_{1}})$ . Here, $\epsilon>0$ is small. Fix $0<\delta_{2}<\delta_{1}$ such that $2\epsilon+2\delta_{1}-2.1\delta_{2}<0$ . We claim

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 1.1\right) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{P}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}\right) \displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{E}|N^{-2.1\delta_{2}}\lesssim N^{2\epsilon+2\delta_{1}-2.1\delta_{2}}. $$

The first bound follows by union bound and definition of $\phi$ . To show the second bound, we first use the identity in (7.9) to get the upper bound

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle\leq 1+\sum_{k=2}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}. $$

If the LHS of the previous display is $\geq 1.1$ , then $\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}$ (for $N$ large enough). Indeed, if not, then the $k=2$ term in the sum is $O(N^{-\kappa})$ . The same is true for the first $N^{\tau}$ many terms, where $\tau<\kappa$ . Now we use rigidity to handle the remaining terms; see the proof of Lemma 21, for example. The last line follows by Proposition 23. By construction of $\delta_{2}$ , we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]\leq N^{-c}. $$

To extend from $B\cap\mathcal{E}$ to $B$ , take any $z_{1}\in B$ and $z_{2}\in\mathcal{E}$ . By (7.2) for $T=I$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\eta{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z_{1}}(\eta)-\eta{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z_{2}}(\eta)| \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1}|z_{1}-z_{2}|). $$

Now use $|z_{1}-z_{2}|\leq N^{1/2-\epsilon}\eta$ to conclude. ∎

Now, by Lemmas 21 and 24, to conclude the proof of Theorem 19, it suffices to show the following.

#### Proposition 25.

Retain the setting of Theorem 19. Define

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{V} \displaystyle:=(V(\lambda_{j},F_{12}\otimes T_{j}),V(\lambda_{k},F_{21}\otimes T_{k}))_{j,k} \displaystyle\mathbf{V}(t) \displaystyle:=(V(\lambda_{j}(t),F_{12}\otimes T_{j}),V(\lambda_{k}(t),F_{21}\otimes T_{k}))_{j,k}, $$

where $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ and $k\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ , and where $F_{12},F_{21}$ are the $2\times 2$ matrices

$$ \displaystyle F_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad F_{21}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

For any test function $F\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\times\mathbb{R}^{m_{R}+m_{L}})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{V})=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z}(t),\mathbf{V}(t)), $$

where the expectation is over all the randomness in $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ , respectively.

Let us now prove Theorem 19 assuming that Proposition 25 holds.

#### Proof of Theorem 19.

By Lemmas 21 and 24, we get $\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{T})=\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{V})+O(\|F\|_{C^{1}}N^{-\kappa})$ , where $\kappa>0$ . But $\tilde{M}_{t}$ has the same structure as $A$ , so $\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z}(t),\mathbf{T}(t))=\mathbb{E}F(\mathbf{z}(t),\mathbf{V}(t))+O(\|F\|_{C^{1}}N^{-\kappa})$ . Theorem 19 follows immediately by these two estimates and Proposition 25. ∎

### 7.1 Proof of Proposition 25

We approximate general $F\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\times\mathbb{R}^{m_{R}+m_{L}})$ by products of functions $F^{(j)}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{R})$ and provide estimates uniform with respect to some norm on $F^{(j)}$ (this can be done by taking cutoffs of the Fourier transform). In particular, we consider

$$ \displaystyle F(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{V}) \displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}f^{(j)}(\lambda_{k}), \displaystyle f^{(j)}(z) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}NF^{(j)}\left(N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0}),V(z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j})\right)&1\leq j\leq m_{R}\\
NF^{(j)}\left(N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0}),V(z,F_{21}\otimes T_{j})\right)&m_{R}+1\leq j\leq m_{R}+m_{L}\end{cases} $$

and likewise for $F(\mathbf{z}(t),\mathbf{V}(t))$ . Fix $1\leq j\leq m_{R}$ ; the following analysis holds similarly for $m_{R}+1\leq\ell\leq m_{R}+m_{L}$ . For convenience, we define the function $\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z):=F^{(j)}(z,V(z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j}))$ , so that $f^{(j)}(z)=N\tilde{f}^{(j)}(N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0}))$ . We claim that the quantity

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}f^{(j)}(\lambda_{k})-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{D}}f^{(j)}(z)\mathrm{d}^{2}z-I_{\delta_{V}}(A,f^{(j)}), $$

satisfies the bound $\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ for some $\kappa>0$ . Above, $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\leq 1\}$ is the unit disc. Moreover, we introduced

$$ \displaystyle I_{\delta_{V}}(A,f^{(j)}) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}}^{N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

and $m_{z}(i\eta)$ is defined via the self-consistent equation

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{m_{z}(w)}=w+m_{z}(w)-\frac{|z|^{2}}{w+m_{z}(w)},\quad\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(w)]\mathrm{Im}[w]>0. $$

Let us briefly sketch the proof; it is the same argument as Theorem 2.4 in [13]. We start with a priori bounds. Let $\nabla_{1}$ and $\Delta_{1}$ mean gradient and Laplacian, respectively, with respect to the $z$ -variable in the first input into $F^{(j)}$ , and let $\partial_{2}$ mean derivative with respect to the second input into $\tilde{f}^{(j)}$ . Finally, let $\Delta$ be the total Laplacian. We first compute

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z,V(z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j})) \displaystyle=\Delta_{1}\tilde{f}^{(j)}+2N^{-\frac{1}{2}}\nabla_{1}\tilde{f}^{(j)}\cdot(\partial_{2}\tilde{f}^{(j)}\nabla_{z}V(z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j})) \displaystyle+N^{-1}(\partial_{2}\tilde{f}^{(j)})^{2}\|\nabla_{z}V(z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j})\|^{2}+N^{-1}\partial_{2}\tilde{f}^{(j)}\Delta V(z,F_{12}\otimes T_{j}). $$

Since $F^{(j)}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{R})$ , its derivatives are $O(1)$ deterministically. Using this and (7.4), we have

$$ \displaystyle|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z)|=\mathcal{O}(1+N^{-2}\eta_{V}^{-2}+N^{-4}\eta_{V}^{-4}+N^{-3}\eta_{V}^{-3})=\mathcal{O}(N^{4\delta_{V}}), $$

where we recall $\eta_{V}=N^{-1-\delta_{V}}$ with $\delta_{V}>0$ small. On the other hand, since $\delta_{V}>0$ is small, resolvent perturbation also gives the bound $|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z)|=O(N^{4})$ . This last deterministic bound, for example, shows that $|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{10})$ . Next, by (3.2) in [13], which is a deterministic identity that holds even for our random test function $f^{(j)}$ in place of $g$ therein, we must first prove the following estimates:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\log|\det[\mathcal{H}_{z}-iT]|\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-98}\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})})=\mathcal{O}(N^{-94}), \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{100}}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)-\frac{1}{\eta+1}\right)\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-98}\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})})=\mathcal{O}(N^{-94}), $$

The first estimate in each line is by Lemma 3.1 in [13]. To prove the second estimate in each line, we use the compact support property of $f^{(j)}$ along with $\|\Delta f^{(j)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{C})}=O(N^{4})$ . Next, we define the quantities

$$ \displaystyle I_{0}^{\eta_{0}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{0}^{\eta_{0}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, \displaystyle I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

where $\eta_{0}=N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}$ and $\eta_{1}=N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}$ . To conclude $\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ for some $\kappa>0$ , according to proof of Theorem 2.4 in [13], it suffices to prove

$$ \displaystyle|I_{0}^{\eta_{0}}|+|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}| \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})})=\mathcal{O}(N^{4\delta_{V}})\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\mathbb{E}|I_{0}^{\eta_{0}}|+\mathbb{E}|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}|=O(N^{-\kappa}). $$

The first estimate follows from Lemma 3.1 in [13], by $\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})}\lesssim\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{C})}$ (because $\tilde{f}^{(j))}$ is compactly supported) and by our earlier estimate $\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{C})}=\mathcal{O}(N^{4\delta_{V}})$ . To prove the second estimate, we write the following with $L>0$ large but fixed:

$$ \displaystyle I_{0}^{\eta_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda_{k}<N^{-L}}\log\left(1+\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\lambda_{k}^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda_{k}\geq N^{-L}}\log\left(1+\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\lambda_{k}^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\int_{0}^{\eta_{0}}\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}+\mathrm{III}. $$

Using the deterministic bound $|\Delta f^{(j)}(z)|=O(N^{2}|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z)|)=O(N^{6})$ , follow (3.5) and use (2.15), all in [13], to show that if $L>0$ is large enough, then $\mathbb{E}|\mathrm{I}|=O(N^{4}N^{-L})=O(N^{-1})$ . For $\mathrm{II}$ , we use the earlier bound $\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})}=\mathcal{O}(N^{4\delta_{V}})$ to get the following for $\epsilon>0$ small and $D>0$ large:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}|\mathrm{II}| \displaystyle\leq N^{4\delta_{V}+\epsilon}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{|\mathrm{II}|}{\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})}}\right]+O(N^{-D}). $$

The calculation (3.7) in [13] shows that the expectation on the RHS of the previous estimate is $O(N^{-2\kappa})$ for some $\kappa>0$ fixed depending only on $L>0$ . Thus, we can choose $\delta_{V},\epsilon>0$ small enough so that $\mathbb{E}|\mathrm{II}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ . Finally, bounding $\mathbb{E}|\mathrm{III}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ uses the same argument as for $\mathrm{II}$ , except we only need the bound $\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)=O(1)$ , which can be deduced from (2.12) in [13]. We have shown $\mathbb{E}|I_{0}^{\eta_{0}}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ . The proof of $\mathbb{E}|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ follows by the same argument. In particular, note the deterministic bound $|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}|=O(N^{200})$ ; this and $|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(z)|=\mathcal{O}(N^{4\delta_{V}})$ give

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}| \displaystyle\leq N^{4\delta_{V}+\epsilon}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}|}{\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})}}\right]+O(N^{-D}). $$

By the proof of Proposition 3.3 in [13], the expectation on the RHS is $O(N^{-2\kappa})$ . So, if we take $\delta,\epsilon>0$ small, we get $\mathbb{E}|I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ . The proof of Theorem 2.4 in [13] now gives $\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{-\kappa})$ . In particular, the comparison in Proposition 25 amounts to comparison of $I_{\delta_{V}}(A,f^{(j)})$ and

$$ \displaystyle I_{\delta_{V}}(\tilde{M}_{t},f^{(j)}):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}}^{N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z,t}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

where $G_{z,t}$ is $G_{z}$ but with $\tilde{M}_{t}$ instead of $A$ . Precisely, by the proof of Proposition 2.5 in [13], we have the following.

#### Lemma 26.

Suppose there exists a constant $c>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}I_{\delta_{V}}(A,f^{(j)})\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}I_{\delta_{V}}(\tilde{M}_{t},f^{(j)})\right]=O(N^{-c}). $$

Then Proposition 25 follows.

### 7.2 Proof of (7.10)

We start with the following construction.

#### Definition 27.

Take $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ as in Lemma 18. Define the matrices

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{0}:=\tilde{\mathcal{H}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tilde{M}_{t}\\
\tilde{M}_{t}^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathcal{H}^{1}:=\mathcal{H}=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\
A^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Let $\rho_{ij}^{0}$ and $\rho_{ij}^{1}$ denote laws of $\mathcal{H}^{0}_{ij}$ and $\mathcal{H}^{1}_{ij}$ , respectively, and for any $\theta\in[0,1]$ , define the interpolated law $\rho_{ij}^{\theta}=(1-\theta)\rho_{ij}^{0}+\theta\rho_{ij}^{1}$ . Now, for any $\theta\in[0,1]$ , let $\mathcal{H}^{\theta}$ be a matrix of size $2N\times 2N$ that satisfies the following properties. First, the triple $(\mathcal{H}^{0},\mathcal{H}^{\theta},\mathcal{H}^{1})$ is jointly independent. Second, the marginal distribution of $\mathcal{H}^{\theta}$ is given by the product measure

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{i,j}\rho_{ij}^{\theta}(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{\theta}). $$

Next, for any indices $(i,j)$ and any $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ , define the matrix $\mathcal{H}^{\theta,\lambda}_{(ij)}$ as

$$ \displaystyle(\mathcal{H}^{\theta,\lambda}_{(ij)})_{k\ell}:=\begin{cases}\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{\theta}&(i,j)\neq(k,\ell)\\
\lambda&(i,j)=(k,\ell)\end{cases} $$

Finally, for any $\eta>0$ and $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , define the resolvents

$$ \displaystyle G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta):=\left[\mathcal{H}^{\theta}-\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\
z^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}-i\eta\right]^{-1},\quad G_{z,(ij)}^{\theta,\lambda}(\eta):=\left[\mathcal{H}^{\theta,\lambda}_{(ij)}-\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\
z^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}-i\eta\right]^{-1}. $$

We note that we do not require $\mathcal{H}^{\theta_{1}}$ to be independent from $\mathcal{H}^{\theta_{2}}$ for $\theta_{1}\neq\theta_{2}$ . By calculus, we have the following for any smooth $F:\mathbb{C}^{2N\times 2N}\to\mathbb{C}$ , provided all expectations exist:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{2N}\mathbb{E}\left[F\left(\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{\theta,\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{1}}\right)-F\left(\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{\theta,\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{0}}\right)\right]. $$

Now, we combine (7.11) with equations (1.7)-(1.8) in [26]. This gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta}) \displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\ell}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}K_{n,(ij)}^{\theta}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})\right]+\mathcal{E}_{\ell}, $$

where the coefficients are defined by

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}K_{n,(ij)}^{\theta}t^{n}=\frac{\mathbb{E}e^{t\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{1}}-\mathbb{E}e^{t\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{0}}}{\mathbb{E}e^{t\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{\theta}}}. $$

Because $A$ and $\tilde{M}_{t}$ match up to three and a half moments, one can easily check that

$$ \displaystyle K_{n,(ij)}^{\theta}=\begin{cases}0&n=1,2,3\\
O(N^{-2-\delta_{t}})&n=4\\
O(N^{-n/2})&5\leq n\leq\ell\end{cases} $$

where $\delta_{t}$ is from Lemma 18. Next, $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ satisfies the usual Taylor series estimate below, where $N^{-\ell/2}$ comes from bounding the $t^{\ell+1}$ coefficient in $\mathbb{E}e^{t\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{\tau}}-\mathbb{E}e^{t\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{0}}$ uniformly in $\tau$ as in the $K_{n,(ij)}^{\theta}$ estimate above:

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{E}_{\ell}| \displaystyle=O\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}N^{-\frac{\ell}{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{\theta\in[0,1]}\left|\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{\ell+1}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})\right|\left(1+|\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}-\mathcal{H}^{0}_{ij}|^{\ell+1}\right)\right]\right) \displaystyle=O\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}N^{-\frac{\ell}{2}}\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{\theta\in[0,1]}\left|\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{\ell+1}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})\right|^{2}\right]\right\}^{1/2}\right). $$

The second bound uses Cauchy-Schwarz and moment bounds on $\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{\theta}$ uniformly in $\theta\in[0,1]$ and $i,j$ . So, we have the following.

#### Lemma 28.

Suppose $F:\mathbb{C}^{2N\times 2N}\to\mathbb{C}$ is smooth and satisfies the following for any $\ell>0$ fixed:

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{i,j=1,\ldots,N}\sup_{4\leq n\leq\ell}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})\right] \displaystyle=O(N^{\frac{\delta_{t}}{3}}N^{C\delta_{V}}), \displaystyle\sup_{i,j=1,\ldots,N}\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{\theta\in[0,1]}\left|\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{\ell+1}F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta})\right|^{2}\right]\right\}^{1/2} \displaystyle=O(N^{C\delta_{V}}). $$

Then for $\delta_{V}>0$ small, we have $\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{1})=\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{0})+O(N^{-\frac{\delta_{t}}{2}})$ .

Now, define the function

$$ \displaystyle I_{\delta_{V}}(\theta,f^{(j)}) \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}}^{N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

where we recall $f^{(j)}(z)=N\tilde{f}^{(j)}(N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0}))$ with $\tilde{f}^{(j)}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ . Let $\mathcal{I}:=[N^{-1-10\delta_{V}},N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}]$ and $m:=m_{R}+m_{L}$ for convenience. We compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m}I_{\delta_{V}}(\theta,f^{(j)})\right]=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}\int_{\mathcal{I}^{m}}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Delta f^{(j)}(z_{j})\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z_{j}}^{\theta}(\eta_{j})-\mathrm{Im}m_{z_{j}}(i\eta_{j})\rangle\right]\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\eta_{j}\mathrm{d}^{2}z_{j} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}N^{m}\int_{\mathcal{I}^{m}}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(w_{j})\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}^{\theta}(\eta_{j})-\mathrm{Im}m_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}(i\eta_{j})\rangle\right]\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\eta_{j}\mathrm{d}^{2}w_{j}, $$

where the second line holds by change-of-variables $w_{j}=N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0})$ and the observation $\Delta f^{(j)}(z)=N\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(N^{1/2}(z-z_{j}^{0}))$ . Thus, by Lemmas 26 and 28, we are interested in the function

$$ \displaystyle F(\mathcal{H}^{\theta}):=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}(w_{j})\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}^{\theta}(\eta_{j})-\mathrm{Im}m_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}(i\eta_{j})\rangle. $$

In particular, by Lemmas 26 and 28, to complete the proof of Theorem 1, it suffices to prove (7.12)-(7.13) for this choice of $F$ . Indeed, this would give

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}I_{\delta_{V}}(A,f^{(j)})\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}I_{\delta_{V}}(\tilde{M}_{t},f^{(j)})\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m}I_{\delta_{V}}(1,f^{(j)})\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{m}I_{\delta_{V}}(0,f^{(j)})\right] \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}N^{m}\int_{\mathcal{I}^{m}}\left[\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{1})-\mathbb{E}F(\mathcal{H}^{0})\right]\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\eta_{j}\mathrm{d}^{2}w_{j} \displaystyle=O\left(N^{-\frac{\delta_{t}}{2}}\int_{\mathbb{K}^{m}}N^{m}\int_{\mathcal{I}^{m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}\eta_{j}\mathrm{d}^{2}w_{j}\right)=O(N^{-\frac{\delta_{t}}{2}}N^{C_{m}\delta_{V}}). $$

The last line follows by Lemma 28 and the fact that $\tilde{f}^{(j)}$ is compactly supported in $\mathbb{C}$ (here, $\mathbb{K}\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is a compact subset). Then, we use the fact that $|\mathcal{I}|\leq 2N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}$ . Now, by the Leibniz rule, to show (7.12)-(7.13) with the above choice of $F$ , it suffices to show that for any $n\geq 0$ and locally uniformly in $w_{j}\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{I}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{C_{n}\delta_{V}}\right), $$

where $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ either has the form $g(V(z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j},T))$ with $T$ finite-rank and Hermitian and $g\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ or the form $\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}^{\theta}(\eta_{j})-\mathrm{Im}m_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}(i\eta_{j})\rangle$ . (Such $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ have $m$ -th order derivatives that are deterministically $O(N^{C_{m}})$ if $\eta_{j}\geq N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}$ and $\delta_{V}>0$ is small; this can be checked by elementary resolvent perturbation identities. Thus, an $\mathcal{O}$ -estimate is enough. We also note that straightforward regularity bounds in $\theta$ of $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ let us use a net argument to extend (7.14) to the same estimate but with a supremum over $\theta\in[0,1]$ , upon possibly changing the constant $C_{n}>0$ .)

We are left to prove (7.14). First, the assumption $g\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ and the local law (see Theorem 2.6 in [12]) imply (7.14) for $n=0$ , so we focus on $n\geq 1$ . By definition of $V(z,T)$ , it suffices to show that locally uniformly in $z\in\mathbb{C}$ and uniformly in $\eta\in[N^{-1-10\delta_{V}},N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}]$ , for any finite-rank, Hermitian $T$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{C_{n}\delta_{V}}) \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\mathrm{Im}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{1+C_{n}\delta_{V}}). $$

For this, we record the following consequence of resolvent perturbation identities:

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta) \displaystyle=C_{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\left[\Delta_{ij}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\right]^{n},\quad(\Delta_{ij})_{k\ell}=\delta_{ik}\delta_{\ell j}+\delta_{i\ell}\delta_{jk}. $$

Using this identity and a spectral decomposition $T=\sum_{a=1}^{\ell}\tau_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}^{\ast}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}^{\eta}(\eta) \displaystyle=C_{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)[\Delta_{ij}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)]^{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{\ell}C_{n}\tau_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{e}_{i}\ldots\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{a}, $$

where the product has at most $n+2$ many factors of the form $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{y}$ with $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}$ deterministic unit vectors. By rigidity and delocalization, i.e. Proposition 30, for eigenvalues $\xi_{k}$ and eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_{k}$ of $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ , we have the following for some $c>0$ independent of $N$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{y} \displaystyle=\sum_{k}\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}\mathbf{u}_{k}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}}{\xi_{k}-i\eta}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\frac{1}{\xi_{k}-i\eta}\right)+\sum_{k:|\xi_{k}|\geq c}\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}\mathbf{u}_{k}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}}{\xi_{k}-i\eta} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}\eta^{-1})+O(1)=\mathcal{O}(N^{10\delta_{V}}). $$

The last term in the first line has the form $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}Y\mathbf{y}$ , where $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , hence it is $O(1)$ .

Combining the previous two displays gives (7.15). To prove (7.16), we write $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)=G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)-G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ . In particular, it suffices to prove (7.16) but with $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ replaced by $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ and $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ . We prove (7.16) with $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ replaced by $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ ; for $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ , the same argument works. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\ast}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta). $$

The estimate (7.15) with $T=\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\ast}$ implies that the RHS of the previous display is $\mathcal{O}(N^{1+C_{n}\delta_{V}})$ . This proves (7.16), so as mentioned right before (7.15), this shows (7.14) and thus completes the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

### 7.3 Proof of Proposition 23

This argument has three steps. First, we reduce to proving the estimate for $\xi_{2}^{z}(t)$ , the second-smallest singular value of the matching matrix $\tilde{M}_{t}$ from Lemma 18. Then, we further reduce to proving the estimate for the second-smallest singular value of a Ginibre matrix. Finally, we cite known estimates for the Ginibre case. As argued in the proof of Lemma 24, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]. $$

Now, define $G_{t,z}(\eta):=[\mathcal{H}_{t,z}-i\eta]^{-1}$ , where $\mathcal{H}_{t,z}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{t,z} \displaystyle:=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tilde{M}_{t}-z\\
(\tilde{M}_{t}-z)^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is smooth and compactly supported, we can use (7.16) and $\eta\leq N^{-1}$ and Lemma 28 to deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{t,z}(\eta)\right)\right]=O(N^{-\delta_{t}/2}). $$

(The input (7.13) to use Lemma 28 can be shown, again, by (7.16) and a standard net argument.) As argued in the proof of Lemma 24, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{t,z}(\eta)\right)\right]\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}), $$

where $\xi_{2}^{z}(t)$ is the second-smallest (positive) singular value of $\tilde{M}_{t}$ , and $\delta_{2}$ is any fixed number strictly smaller than $\delta_{1}$ . Summarizing so far, we have proven

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}. $$

We now use Theorem 3.2 in [11]. This gives the following. There exists a matrix $W(t)$ whose entries are i.i.d. standard complex Gaussians mutiplied by $(1+t)^{1/2}$ such that if $\{\mu_{k}(t)\}_{k}$ are the singular values of $W(t)$ with $\mu_{k}(t)\leq\mu_{k+1}(t)$ for $k\geq 1$ and $\mu_{-k}(t)=\mu_{k}(t)$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\xi_{2}^{z}(t)-\mu_{2}^{z}(t)|\leq N^{-1-\kappa}\right)\lesssim N^{-D} $$

for any fixed $D>0$ , where $\kappa>0$ is fixed. (This requires that $\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{t,z}(\eta)\rangle=\mathcal{O}(1)$ for all $\eta\geq N^{-1+\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$ fixed. Such an estimate follows by the local law in (3.6) in [17] combined with (3.7) in [17].) Since $\kappa>0$ is fixed, for small enough $\delta$ , we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\mu_{2}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}=\mathbb{P}((1+t)^{1/2}\mu_{2}(0)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}. $$

We now use Theorem 2.10 in [19]; this shows that the first term on the far RHS of the previous display is $O(N^{\epsilon}N^{-8\delta_{2}})$ with $\epsilon>0$ fixed but otherwise arbitrary. If we choose $\epsilon>0$ small enough and $\delta_{2}$ sufficiently close to $\delta_{1}$ , then the far RHS of the previous display becomes $O(N^{-2.1\delta})$ for $\delta>0$ small enough. This completes the proof.

## 8 Green’s function estimates

The purpose of this section is to record various auxiliary bounds for Green’s functions. These bounds are mostly standard. First, recall the Hermitization $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ of $A$ and Green’s function:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{z}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&A-z\\
(A-z)^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad G_{z}(\eta):=[\mathcal{H}_{z}-i\eta]^{-1} $$

for $\eta>0$ . Green’s function can be written as

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}i\eta\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)(A-z)\\
(A^{\ast}-\bar{z})\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle H_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}. $$

We assume $A$ has entries that satisfy $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}=0$ and $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}^{2}=N^{-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}|A_{ij}|^{p}\leq C_{p}N^{-p/2}$ for all $p\geq 2$ . As in Definition 20, we let $\xi_{k}^{z}$ be eigenvalues of the Hermitization $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ , and we let $\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}$ be the corresponding eigenvalues. We adopt the convention $\xi_{k}^{z}\geq 0$ for all $k\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ , and $\xi_{k}^{z}=-\xi_{-k}^{z}$ for any $k\in\llbracket-N,-1\rrbracket$ . We also impose $\xi_{k}^{z}\leq\xi_{\ell}^{z}$ for $k\leq\ell$ .

We now introduce a deterministic local law approximation for $G_{z}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle M_{z}(w):=\begin{pmatrix}m_{z}(w)&-zu_{z}(w)\\
-\overline{z}u_{z}(w)&m_{z}(w)\end{pmatrix},\quad u_{z}(w):=\frac{m_{z}(w)}{w+m_{z}(w)}, $$

where $m_{z}(w)$ satisfies the self-consistent equation

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{m_{z}(w)}=w+m_{z}(w)-\frac{|z|^{2}}{w+m_{z}(w)},\quad\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(w)]\mathrm{Im}[w]>0. $$

#### Proposition 29.

Fix any deterministic matrix $Y\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ with $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ and any deterministic unit vectors $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{2N}$ . Fix any $\tau>0$ . Fix any $\eta\geq N^{-1+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ , and fix $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\langle Y(G_{z}(\eta)-M_{z}(i\eta))\rangle \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-1}\eta^{-1}\right) \displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\ast}(G_{z}(\eta)-M_{z}(i\eta))\mathbf{y} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1/2}\right). $$

In particular, we have (A3.1)-(A3.2).

#### Proof.

The first two bounds are (3.6) in [17]. We now show (A3.1); the proof of (A3.2) is similar. We use the first two bounds with $Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&I_{N}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{y}^{\ast}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf{w}_{2}^{\ast}\end{pmatrix}$ , so

$$ \displaystyle i\eta\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}H_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-m_{z}(i\eta)\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1/2}) \displaystyle\langle i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\rangle-m_{z}(i\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}\eta^{-1}). $$

This gives (A3.1). ∎

Define the following limiting empirical spectral density of $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ for $E\in\mathbb{R}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{z}(E):=\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\frac{1}{\pi}|\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(E+i\eta)|. $$

With this, we define two objects. The first is the quantile $\gamma_{j,z}$ for any $|j|\leq N$ via the equation

$$ \displaystyle\frac{j+N}{2N}=\int_{-\infty}^{\gamma_{j,z}}\rho_{z}(E)\mathrm{d}E. $$

Note that $\gamma_{j,z}=-\gamma_{-j,z}$ . The second is the $\kappa$ -bulk $\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}:=\{E\in\mathbb{R}:\rho_{z}(E)\geq\kappa^{1/3}\}$ , where $\kappa>0$ . These notations are taken from Section 2 of [12]. By Example 2.5 in [12], if $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ with $\tau>0$ fixed, then we can take $\kappa>0$ small enough depending only on $\tau$ such that $\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}$ contains an interval around $0$ .

#### Proposition 30 (Rigidity and delocalization, Corollaries 2.8 and 2.9 in [2]).

Suppose $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ for some $\tau>0$ . Fix any $\kappa>0$ small enough, and suppose $\gamma_{k,z}\in\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}$ . We have $|\xi_{k}^{z}-\gamma_{k,z}|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1})$ . Moreover, we have $\|\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|_{\infty}=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ .

Next, we note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}[M_{z}(E)] \displaystyle=\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(E)]-\frac{E+o(E)}{\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(0)]}\begin{pmatrix}0&-z\\
-\overline{z}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(0)]=\sqrt{1-|z|^{2}}. $$

#### Proposition 31 (Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, Theorem 2.7 in [12]).

Fix any deterministic matrix $Y\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ such that $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{|i|,|j|\leq N}\left|\mathbf{u}_{i}^{z,\ast}Y\mathbf{u}_{j}^{z}-\delta_{ij}\frac{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})Y\rangle}{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})\rangle}-\delta_{-ij}\frac{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})(E_{11}-E_{22})Y\rangle}{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})\rangle}\right|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-\frac{1}{2}}), $$

where $\mathcal{O}$ is with respect to randomness of $A$ , while $E_{11},E_{22}$ are the $2N\times 2N$ block matrices

$$ \displaystyle E_{11}:=\begin{pmatrix}I_{N}&0\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad E_{22}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&I_{N}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Thus, by (8.2), if $\langle YE_{11}\rangle,\langle YE_{22}\rangle=0$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{i}^{z,\ast}Y\mathbf{u}_{j}^{z}=\delta_{|i|=|j|}O(N^{-1}i)+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}). $$

#### Proposition 32.

Suppose $|z_{1}|,|z_{2}|\leq 1-\tau$ for some $\tau>0$ and $\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in[N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}},10]$ . Define $\eta^{\ast}=\max\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ . Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $D>0$ we have

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}\right)\leq N^{-D} \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}\right)\leq N^{-D} \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq\frac{c}{\eta^{\ast}\left(\eta^{\ast}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\right)}\right)\leq N^{-D} $$

for large enough $N$ uniformly in $z_{1},z_{2},\eta_{1},\eta_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Define $\eta_{\ast}=\min\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ . To show (8.3), we note that

$$ \left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle G_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}G_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})E_{22}\right\rangle. $$

Now we use Theorem 3.5 of [15] to approximate this trace by a deterministic quantity

$$ \left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{22}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{N^{-3\epsilon_{0}}}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\right). $$

Here $\mathcal{B}:M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ is a linear operator given by

$$ \mathcal{B}(\cdot)=Id-M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\mathcal{S}(\cdot)M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2}). $$

By a straightforward computation we see that

$$ -\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{22}\right\rangle=\frac{|m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|}{|1-z_{1}\bar{z_{2}}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}}\geq c $$

for some constant $c$ . Here we used that $|m_{z_{j}}(\eta_{j})|$ is bounded below by a constant; for $\eta\geq c_{0}$ for any fixed $c_{0}>0$ , this follows by continuity of solutions to (8.1), and for $\eta\leq c_{0}$ , this follows by Lemma 3.2 in [17] if $c_{0}>0$ is small enough. We also used that the denominator is bounded above by a constant, which can be readily checked using properties of $m_{z_{j}}(\eta_{j})$ , and positive since we know that $\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle>0$ . This concludes the proof of (8.3). The bound (8.4) is proved the same way.

Now we prove (8.5). If $|z_{1}-z_{2}|<N^{-\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}}$ , we use Theorem 3.3 of [17] and if $|z_{1}-z_{2}|\geq N^{-\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}}$ , we use Theorem 3.5 of [15] to get

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle G_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}G_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})E_{21}\right\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{N^{\epsilon_{0}}}{N\eta_{\ast}^{2}}\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\right). $$

(The quantity $\hat{\beta}_{\ast}$ in Theorem 3.5 of [15] is bounded below uniformly by Lemma 6.1 in [15].) Since $\eta_{\ast}\geq N^{-1/3+\epsilon_{0}}$ , the error term $\mathcal{O}(N^{\epsilon_{0}}N^{-1}\eta_{\ast}^{-4})$ is much smaller than $\eta_{\ast}^{-1}$ . Thus, we can drop the $\mathcal{O}$ -term in the second line. Again, we can directly compute

$$ \displaystyle-\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{|m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|\left(1-(|z_{1}|^{2}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2})(|z_{2}|^{2}u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}-m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2})\right)}{|1-z_{1}\bar{z_{2}}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}}. $$

Now from the self-consistent equation (8.1) for $m_{z}(\eta)$ , we see that

$$ 0\leq|z|^{2}u_{z}(\eta)^{2}-m_{z}(\eta)^{2}\leq 1-\eta|m_{z}(\eta)|\leq 1-c\eta. $$

Thus

$$ -\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle\geq c(\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}) $$

for some constant $c$ . The denominator of (8.6) is the determinant of $\mathcal{B}$ . From the calculations in Appendix B of [17] we see that

$$ \det\mathcal{B}\lesssim\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}. $$

This concludes the proof of (8.5). ∎
